chapters.title: The Wrong Nail
chapters.html:
The door was locked, which was right, and the cat was not in the window, which was wrong, and I stood on the step of the Marigold Bindery at ten to seven on a Friday morning with a bag of buns going soft in my hand, trying to decide which of the two to be cross about.

I had come up from Hocking’s, where Elsie Hocking sold me six currant buns without lifting her eyes from the till. “Fine morning, Mrs Pellow.” “It is.” “Tide’s making.” “So I see.” That was the whole of it, and I do not hold it against her. At fifty-eight, in a grey cardigan, with my hair cut by my own hand with the kitchen scissors, I am a kind of weather in Trevenna. People are glad of me and could not tell you what colour I was.

Fish Cellar Lane climbs from the harbour like something that has been asked to and means to make a point of it. The lanes here are named for what was once done in them: Net Loft Row, Pilchard Steps, and mine for the cellars where the catch was salted down in the days when there was a catch. Nobody has salted anything there since 1920, though on a warm morning the granite still remembers. The hydrangeas were out in their tubs, blue as bruises. There was a gull on every chimney, one to a pot, like clergy. Behind me the tide was half way up the Hard and the first boats had begun to lift on it.

At the top, where the lane gives up and turns into a track to my cottage twenty yards on, stands the Bindery: shop at the front, press room behind, and over both a net loft that nobody has hauled a net into since Ned’s father’s day, and which I use for millboard and the sort of paper one cannot bring oneself to throw away. You reach it by granite steps up the outside wall. The third one creaks. The door is yellow because Ned’s mother loved marigolds, and when Ned married me he named the place for the door, which is the sort of romance I was brought up to trust.

That Friday the Trevenna Antiquarian Book Fair was to open in St Petroc’s hall at noon, with Aubrey Trevithick, chairman of everything, cutting a ribbon. I had agreed, for thirty pounds and the novelty of being asked, to sit at a trestle there with a pot of paste and mend loose hinges at fifty pence apiece, beneath a card in his own firm hand: MRS PELLOW OF THE MARIGOLD BINDERY, REPAIRS WHILE YOU BROWSE. Hence the buns. Paste wants cooking at first light so that it has cooled by ten, and Ned’s rule, which I have never had the nerve to break, was that the first bun of the day is eaten standing beside the pan.

I had two keys to my own door. One was in my cardigan pocket. The other, a brass Yale on a loop of green wool, had been in Aubrey Trevithick’s waistcoat since a quarter to six the evening before, and I had half expected to find it on the mat with a note of thanks in violet ink. There was nothing on the mat. I let myself in with mine.

The shop was cool and smelled as it always does, of leather and size and the ghost of Ned’s pipe, which three years and two coats of whitewash have not shifted. No cat on the sill. I said “Quire?” to the room and the room declined. The door to the press room, which I keep shut against the draught from the lane, stood open the width of a hand, and the air that came through the gap was warm.

I pushed it with two fingers.

The first thing I saw was the cane, ebony with a silver collar, lying across the boards like a rule dropped on a drawing. Then the shoes, good brown brogues, side by side, as though he had stepped out of them into his own length. He lay on his side between the nipping press and the bench with one arm under him, the silver moustache combed, the summer tweeds buttoned for the last time by himself. His Panama had come off. It lay a foot from his hand, crown down, like a bowl set out for coins. The back of his head was dark, and I looked at that for as long as it takes to understand something, and then I looked at the hat instead.

“Mr Trevithick,” I said, which was foolish. Then, “Aubrey,” which I had not once called him in twenty-seven years, and neither of us seemed to mind.

I have seen how a body looks when whatever ran it has gone. It is not a thing one mistakes, and it was not a thing I could improve by fetching anyone. I put out a hand to steady myself and found the stove. It stands against the back wall, an iron thing the size of a small cow, and I light it for paste and for nothing else; I had let it die on Wednesday after the last pot. The iron was warm under my palm. Not hot. The warmth of a flank. In July, with the skylight shut and no fire of mine in it for two days, I stood with my hand flat against it like a woman feeling a child for fever, and could think of nothing sensible to say to it.

On the bench under the skylight lay the book. I knew it before I had decided to look, as you know a neighbour’s back in a queue: the Carne Rutter, Loveday Penhallow’s pilot’s book, which Ned had mended in the winter of 1971 while I made tea and was told not to breathe. It lay open and wrong. The back board had been lifted away and the endpapers were gone, torn out so hard that the board showed raw where they had been, like the inside of a loaf. The gatherings had been half unpicked from their cover, and the thread still hung from them in long brown lengths, trailing off the edge of the bench like the roots of something pulled up in a hurry.

I touched nothing. I would like that on the record, along with the stove. I looked, which costs nothing and in my experience is the part most people skip. The back door to the yard was bolted on the inside, as I bolt it. The window to the lane was latched. The skylight was shut. On my way to the telephone I looked at the lock of the yellow door and found nothing in it, and no green wool on the counter, none on the bench, none on the floor that I could see without bending. A locked door, a dead man behind it, and no key anywhere.

The telephone is a black Bakelite thing on the shop counter that Ned bought second-hand in 1963 and that rings like a person clearing his throat. I dialled the three nines with a finger in the little holes, waiting each time for the dial to come home.

“Emergency. Which service?”

“The police, please. And I suppose an ambulance, although I don’t believe he’ll be wanting it.”

There was a pause with a click in it, and a second voice, a man’s, asked where, and I told him. “Trevenna?” he said. “That’ll be Kitto,” in the tone of someone glad of a shortcut. The line went away and came back, and at the other end of it somebody was swallowing hard.

“Kitto.”

“It’s Dot Pellow, Demelza. I’m at the Bindery.”

“Mrs Pellow.” Another swallow. “Sorry. Toast. Go on.”

“There is a man dead on my press-room floor.”

“Who?”

“Aubrey Trevithick.”

There was a silence with a crumb in it. When she spoke again the toast had gone out of her voice. “Right. Facts. Are you certain he’s dead?”

“I’m fifty-eight, Demelza. I’m certain.”

“Anyone else there?”

“Only me. And the cat, somewhere.”

“Have you touched anything?”

“The stove. I leant on it.”

“Right. Don’t touch anything else. Stay in the shop, let nobody through, and shut that door if it’s open. Four minutes.”

I gave her seven, allowing for the hill and the toast. From behind the paper rack Quire came out, torn ear first, and hissed at me. It is her usual greeting and I found it, that morning, very nearly a comfort. She went up onto the windowsill and sat with her back to the press room and her white bib to the street, and would not look round, which I put down to temper. I filled the kettle. I mention this because I am told it is the sort of thing that goes in a statement, and because it was the only thing in the building I could think of to do.

Then I went back and stood in the press-room doorway, because I had been told to shut the door and I have been told a good many things in my life by people who had not seen the room. It was while I stood there that I noticed the hammer.

There are two nails in the wall by the lying press, a hand’s breadth apart. The left one was Ned’s. It had held nothing since March of 1986, and I would not have let anyone hang a coat on it. The right one is mine, which Ned drove in the first winter I was married so that I need not reach across him, and on mine, face to the wall, by the leather loop through the end of its shaft, the backing hammer has hung every working day for three years. I could find it blind. This morning it was not on mine. It was on Ned’s, and it had been hung face-out, the round steel of it turned toward the room and looking at me, the way he always hung it and the way I never have.

I thought: someone has been in my room and touched my hammer. I did not think the other thing, because nobody does, not at once. One takes it for a strangeness, like a picture hung crooked in a house where one has lived a long time. I stood and looked at it until the shape of it began to seem like a word I had written too often.

What I thought about, in the doorway of my own press room with a dead man and a kettle, was the evening before.

He had come into the shop at a quarter to six, as I was thinking of turning the sign, leaning on the cane because of his hip, with a flat leather satchel held to his chest as though somebody had threatened to take it. “Mrs Pellow. I require a bench, a lamp and a door that locks.”

“It’s a quarter to six, Mr Trevithick.”

“Then I shall be brief.” He was never brief in his life. He looked round the shop as he always did, as if it were a small tidy country he had thought about annexing. “There is something I wish to look at properly. I have not the light at Seagate, nor the tools, nor, I regret, the nerve.”

“What sort of something?”

“Tomorrow I shall have something to say to you. I would rather be accurate than prompt, and I am not yet accurate.” The swan on his signet ring tapped the head of the cane. “Accuracy is a form of courtesy.”

“So is closing at six.”

I gave him the spare key mainly to get him out of my shop. I would like that understood. I took it off its nail and told him I wanted it back first thing, and he said I should have it, and a word with it, and bowed, which he did to women, waiters and bishops, and I never worked out which of the three he thought I was. Then he went out in a cloud of camphor, with the satchel.

I went down to the Lantern. Quire Straits came fourth at the quiz, which I maintain was robbery and said so, at length, to anyone with an ear. I came up Fish Cellar Lane at eleven or a little after, with my cardigan buttoned one out and my mind on the fact that Elsie Hocking’s husband had written Brahms for a piece that was plainly Elgar. The press-room window looks onto the lane, under the loft steps. It was dark. I saw it, in so far as you see a thing you have walked past ten thousand times; I did not turn my head, because there was nothing in it to turn for. I went on up to my cottage and my bed and slept like a woman with nothing on her conscience.

I did not think I should tell anyone that. A woman walks past a dark window: it is hardly the stuff of a statement. (I thought a great deal, afterwards, about what is and is not.)

Down in the shop the bell over the door rang, and the draught of it came through to me along the floor. I did not turn round. I was watching the hammer, which had begun to move on Ned’s nail, a quarter of an inch one way and back, as though someone had only just let go of it.

chapters.title: Saffron Cake and Sympathy
chapters.html:
“Keys,” said Constable Kitto. “How many, and who’s got them?”

She had been in my shop eleven minutes. In that time she had looked at Aubrey Trevithick for exactly as long as duty required, shut the press-room door on him with the flat of her hand, and strung blue-and-white tape across the top and bottom of Fish Cellar Lane from a roll in her bicycle bag. Now she stood on the far side of my counter with her helmet upside down beside the till like a bowl put out for the cat. She was short and wide in the shoulder, with a plait pinned so tight beneath the helmet that it had left a groove in her hair, and a notebook with an elastic band round it. She held the band the way another woman might hold a rosary. Quire had hissed at her on the way in, and she had taken it as a formal caution.

“Two,” I said. “Mine, which has not left my cardigan since I put it on, and the spare, which I lent to Mr Trevithick at a quarter to six yesterday evening.”

“Lent.”

“Gave. I’d say I was bullied into it, but one should not speak ill of the dead, and it would be untrue. I gave it to him to be rid of him.”

Her pencil stopped. “What did he want it for?”

“A bench, a lamp and a door that locked. He wouldn’t say what for. He said he’d something to tell me in the morning, and that he preferred to be accurate.”

“About what?”

“About whatever he was being accurate about, Demelza. He was a man who made a speech out of the time of day.” I heard how that sounded and moderated it. “I took it to be the price of a trestle. We’d had words about the trestle.”

She wrote that down. She writes everything down; I have never seen anyone take such trouble over a sentence she did not quite believe. “Door was locked when you got here?”

“Yes.”

“Locked, with him inside it, and the spare not on him, not in the lock, not on the bench.”

“I looked at the lock. I did not look in his pockets. I am a bookbinder, not a magpie.”

“Right,” said Demelza, which she says the way other people say amen.

I did not mention eleven o’clock. I had meant to. There was a gap where I might have, and she was looking at her notebook, and the sentence went past like a bus I had no real wish to catch.

The shop bell went, a tall shape filled the doorway, and the top of it hit the frame.

“Sorry,” said Kit, to the frame.

He is my late husband’s nephew, thirty-four years old, and the longest, reddest, most apologetic man in west Cornwall: ginger hair standing up on the side he had slept on, a chin gone rusty with a night’s stubble, the left thumbnail bitten to the quick. He had run up the lane. He gripped the doorpost like a man on a boat. Quire, on the sill, hissed at him, and he apologised to her too.

“Sorry. Auntie Dot. Elsie Hocking said, and I said she’d got it wrong, sorry.” He saw who was behind the counter. “Constable.”

“Mr Pellow.” Her voice came out as flat as a ruler. “You’ll have to stay on the step, please. The press room is closed.”

“Is it true? Only he was going to be at the hall at nine to see the stalls go in. I rang the Court, and Miss Penhallow said he hadn’t, and I thought, sorry, I thought—”

“Kit,” I said.

“Sorry.”

“Inspector Garrow is coming from Truro,” Demelza said. She had turned a page of the notebook with the briskness of a woman making a bed in a hurry. “He’ll want a word. Stay in the lane. Don’t go anywhere.”

“No. Right. Sorry.”

He went out backwards, which with Kit is not a figure of speech, and the bell shook for a long time after. Demelza watched the door and I watched Demelza. As she turned the page her sleeve rode up on the left wrist, and below the regulation navy showed a cuff of grey wool, darned at the thumb-hole in a thread that did not quite match. I knew that darn. I had done it myself in the winter of 1986, on a boy who went through thumbs. I said nothing. It is one of the few advantages of being furniture.

Beyond the window and the tape a girl was sitting on the net-loft steps with her knees drawn up. I knew her by sight and a little by hand: Sheila Bray’s daughter, sixteen, whose mother cleans at Penhallow Court, and who had spent most of May at my counter with a school project on dying trades and a pen she chewed in place of a plait. Black hair cut to the jaw, a stripe of it bleached at the front, ink to the second knuckle. She was not watching the constable or the tape or the people beginning to collect at the foot of the lane. She was watching my window and, I thought, me. When I raised a hand she was not there. The third step gave one creak, as if it had been told off, and the steps were empty.

Detective Inspector Garrow came up the lane at twenty past eight in a belted raincoat, although the sun had been up three hours, with the look of a man bound in rexine: easy to wipe, and giving nothing back. He stopped on my step and took in the shop, the tape, the constable and me, in that order.

“And this is?”

“Mrs Pellow, sir,” said Demelza. “She found him.”

“Ah. The lady of the house.”

“Mrs Pellow will do.”

“Quite. If the lady of the house would show me through to—”

“The constable has shut the door and I would hate to undo her work. And the kettle’s on.”

“I shan’t trouble you for tea, Mrs Pellow.”

“It’s no trouble. It’s boiling.”

I have a gift for waiting; I have been practising since 1962. He waited too, with his hands in the pockets of the raincoat, until the kettle had finished and the pot had stood its three minutes, and I will say for him that he did not once look at his watch. Quire had come off the windowsill to inspect him. She looked him up and down, torn ear cocked, and hissed with a thoroughness I had not heard from her since the vicar’s wife came in with a spaniel.

“Does it bite?”

“Only the deserving.”

I had not known that a man could be carried out through one’s shop under a grey blanket, past the counter and the paste pots and the cat. They were very good about the step. There were two ambulance men from Truro and a doctor with a bag, who said “Mrs Pellow” as if I might be a patient, and on the blanket, over the chest, a hat. In the lane perhaps thirty people who had been ostentatiously on their way elsewhere took off their caps, those who had caps. Elsie Hocking put her apron to her mouth. Quire, on the sill, stood up and put her back into a hoop.

It was into this, at twenty past nine, that Morwenna Hext came up the lane like a small round tug through a regatta.

She had the silver perm, the pearl studs and the large handbag on her arm, and in her other hand, in a checked cloth, a saffron cake. Nobody has ever known Morwenna reach a crisis without one. Trevenna has been got through on her cakes: the lifeboat year, the chapel fire, the winter the harbour wall went, and the morning Ned died, when she was on my step at half past seven with a loaf still hot, and said nothing at all but “Sit. Eat.” She walked under Demelza’s tape as though it were a washing line, and Demelza, who had been ready to stop the Chief Constable, held it up for her.

“Dot, my handsome.” She took my face in both hands, quickly, as if testing a loaf. “Sit. Constable, you’ve toast on your chin. Inspector, I don’t know you, and you may stand where you like so long as it isn’t on my cloth.”

“Madam—”

“Hext. Women’s Institute and the regatta purse. I’ll thank you not to lay that coat on the cake.” She took the brown pot out of my hands, which I had not known I was holding, tipped out the tea I had made without a word on what she thought of it, and began again.

I will not say it was a relief to sit down. But I sat. The shop was small for five people and a cat, and Kit had been let in to stand against the paper rack, apologising to it, and the saffron was yellow as the door and still warm, and I ate a slice with my eyes on the floor. Morwenna cut and poured and passed. She gave the Inspector the biggest slice and his tea sweet before he had said he took sugar, and he took it, and sat down on my stool, which I had not offered.

Quire had by then hissed at the constable, the inspector and my nephew, in that order, and retired to the top of the paper rack to consider the rest of us. She came down when Morwenna sat. I want that on the record. She came down the front of the rack like water down a slate, crossed the counter, the floor and the whole width of the shop, and climbed into Morwenna’s lap and turned round once and settled, like a bun into a tin.

“Well,” said Garrow.

“She doesn’t do that,” said Demelza.

“She doesn’t do that for anyone,” I said. “She’s never done it for me, and I feed her.”

“Cats know who’s brought cake,” said Morwenna comfortably, and put a hand on the black back. Quire shut her eyes. “She was always a sensible animal. How long’s she been yours, Dot?”

“She turned up in March of ‘eighty-six. The month Ned died. She came in fat as a pudding, and I’d forgotten to feed myself that spring, never mind a cat. Somebody did. I never found out who.”

“A cat will always find somebody.”

“So I’ve been told.”

Garrow had his notebook out and his tea untouched, and was looking round the room with the particular patience of a man who has decided to be patient. “I shall want elimination prints from everyone who has been in the press room recently. Mrs Pellow, yourself. Mr Pellow.”

“Sorry,” said Kit. “Most days, sorry. I bring the post through.”

“Mrs Hext?”

“Not since Ned died, Inspector, God rest him.” She said it to the cat. “It was his room, you see. I never went in without Ned there to ask me, and after he’d gone I hadn’t the heart. I hardly come up the lane now. My knees. Dot comes to me, and we meet at the hall, and that’s very nearly all the conversation I get.”

“Very good,” said Garrow, and wrote it down. I watched his pencil. It wrote Morwenna as it had written me, and Kit, and the cat, if he had thought of it: a name and a few words, to be forgotten by lunch.

Garrow went through to the press room again, and Demelza after him, and Kit fled to the lane to be told off by nobody. When they had gone the shop was very quiet. The kettle ticked on its ring. Morwenna went on stroking the cat with her thumb behind the torn ear, where I had never been allowed to put a finger.

“Was it quick, do you think?”

“I don’t know. I’m not allowed to think.”

“You were always the one for thinking. Ned used to say you’d read a bus timetable for the plot.” She cut a second slice and put it on my knee without asking. “Eat.”

“He said he had something to tell me this morning,” I said. “He came in at a quarter to six, wanting my bench, and I was short with him. He said he’d rather be accurate than prompt. I told him closing was at six. Those were very nearly the last words I ever said to Aubrey Trevithick, Morwenna, about closing.”

“That’s Aubrey. Never so much as the time of day without a lecture on being right about it.” She looked at the slice on my knee until I picked it up. Her hand on the cat did not stop. “He always did choose the worst places to be right.”

I thought she meant the Bindery, and the stove, and the floor. I thought she meant church halls and funerals and committees, all the places Aubrey had stood up to correct a date. I thought she meant nothing at all, which is what people say at such times. I did not ask. I ate the saffron cake, which was very good, and I kept the sentence in my head the whole of that day, the way you keep a button from a coat you no longer own, without knowing why.

chapters.title: What the Spine Remembers
chapters.html:
Demelza gave me ten minutes, and she gave them to me by turning her back.

“I’m not here,” she said, from the press-room doorway, where she stood facing the shop with her arms folded and the helmet under one elbow. “I’m not watching you do it and I’m not hearing what you say to the furniture. The man from Truro’s stuck behind a tractor, and when he comes he’ll put the book in a bag and you won’t see it again till the trial. Ten minutes, Mrs Pellow. Gloves.”

“I have cotton ones. In the drawer under the plough.”

“Don’t touch the drawer.”

She fetched them herself, hooking the drawer open with her pencil and lifting the pair out on the end of it like a dead mouse. I put them on. They were the gloves I wear for fine work, and my hands, which are not fine, went into them with an air of embarrassment.

By ten the press room had been photographed, powdered and given up on for the time being. The aluminium dust lay grey on the edge of the bench and along the stove door. On the boards, between the nipping press and the bench, there was a dark patch the size of a tea tray, and I decided to be a stranger to it. The room smelled of powder and cold iron and the stale breath of a place that has had too many men in it. The book lay where it had lain at seven o’clock. I took my loupe out of my cardigan pocket, put my glasses up on my forehead on their bootlace, and began, as Ned taught me, at the beginning.

A book is a record of what has been done to it. That is the whole of the trade. Sew a gathering, unpick it, sew it again, and the paper keeps the account like a bad tooth: every hole stays, and each is a scar that tells you something. Ned used to say that a good binder reads a book as a doctor reads an old soldier.

I knew the Carne Rutter better than I had thought. I remembered Loveday Penhallow coming in the door in the winter of 1971, in gumboots under a tweed coat, with the book wrapped in a pillowcase, and saying to my husband, “Don’t fuss, Pellow,” before he had said a word. He told her he never fussed; he dithered, with intent. Five weeks he had it. He took the spine off and made a new one, a tight back, so well that you could not find the seam, and he did it by lamplight because he said the skylight was too honest.

Now I held it open under that honest light and counted. The sewing of 1631 had been done by a man who measured by eye: four stations to a fold, two crowded at the head and a long gap and then two more, like a drunk’s staircase. Ned had sewn through those same holes in 1971 and made two new ones of his own at the tail where the old thread had rotted the paper. I found the four old and the two new, on the first gathering and on the last, small and sad and exactly where he would have put them.

In the fat middle of the book there were five holes to every fold. They were clean and they were evenly spaced, an inch and a half apart, as if someone had used a ruler and a spirit of tidiness, and there were no other holes at all. The paper had never been sewn before. Those leaves had not been in this cover when Ned finished with it. They had come to it as strangers.

I turned a middle leaf to the skylight with my gloved fingers, as one lifts a sleeping child. The chain lines were close as the teeth of a comb. In the corner, pale against the light, sat a lion in a little paling fence with a hat on a pole; any schoolchild in Holland could have named it. The ink was a clerk’s brown and the hand a neat round one, and the lines went down the page in columns. To Wm Tresidder for thatching, 3s. 6d. To a ewe sheep, 14s. A rutter tells a man where the rocks are. This told him what he owed the thatcher.

The first two leaves were different, and I could feel the difference through the cotton. They were heavy, soft, the colour of oatmeal, with the chain lines wide apart like furrows on a hill seen from the road, and across them a seaman’s handwriting in ink gone the brown of tea: from Falmouth to the Lizard keep well off. The last two were the same. Between them, somebody had sewn a farmer’s accounts into a pilot’s book and made a good job of it.

I will say I stood there some while. Behind me Demelza shifted her weight and said nothing. The heart had been taken out of the Carne Rutter, and there was nothing in its place that any man could sail by.

The boards had lost their pastedowns as well, both of them, torn away in strips and scrapings so that the millboard showed through like a scraped knee. I could not think what a person wants with the endpapers of a book. They are blank, most of the time, or hold a name and a date, an owner’s pencil, a price. Aubrey wrote in pencil on everything; it was a habit that had driven Ned to distraction. I looked about the bench for the stub he carried in his waistcoat, and for any paper he might have written on, and found neither.

There were two things left, and I made myself take them in order, as Ned would have. The last gathering was the first. I lifted it free and turned it to the foot, where the margin is widest and a man might do something nobody would ever see. I took it at first for a flaw in the paper. It was a pin-prick, round and clean, made with a point and not a tear, through the foot of the fold and through every leaf of the gathering at once. I put the loupe to it. It was no larger than a full stop in a hymn book.

I knew it. I do not know how; I had never seen it in my life. I knew his hands, and the fine awl in the tin, and the way he finished a job, holding the book up to the window with his head on one side and his tongue between his teeth, and then the little movement of the wrist that I had taken for a man shaking off a cramp. Twenty-four years I watched my husband finish books. He signed them where nobody would look, and he never told me, and I do not know whom he thought would find them.

I found the cutting-board stool with the backs of my knees, which is how I know it is where it ought to be.

“Mrs Pellow?” said Demelza, to the shop. “Seven minutes. Are you all right?”

“I’m sitting down.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the one I’ve got.”

She did not turn round, which was a kindness I have thought about since. I sat with the gathering held in my gloved hands like a bird. On the shelf above the stool the cupboard where I keep the alum and the clove oil, and Ned’s old tins, stood shut, and I could see from where I sat that the little brass lock was turned, as I had turned it on Wednesday. Nothing in that room had been taken or touched, as far as I could see, but the book and the hammer. I got up, because I had two things left and not much time.

The second thing was the kettle stitch. It is the knot at head and tail where one gathering links to the next, and in the middle of the book every one of them turned left. Mine turn right. Ned’s turned left, and it was one of the three things we quarrelled over in twenty-four years of marriage, and on the other two he was wrong. I looked along the whole run of knots at the head and then at the tail, and each leant the same way, with a little hooked tuck at the finish that I had stopped seeing in my own kitchen because I had stopped seeing him do it. Whoever had sewn the middle of that book had been taught at Ned’s elbow.

There were not many people it could have been. I did not count them. I put the thought down the way one puts down a hot dish, carefully, and with the other hand already reaching for a cloth.

I lifted the back board, which was loose in my hand, toward the skylight, and from the hinge came a smell I knew at once and could not, for a moment, place in that room. Cloves. Oranges and nutmeg and string; the week before Christmas; my mother-in-law’s kitchen. Ned’s paste. One drop of oil of clove to a pint of wheat starch and alum, against the mould, and the smell outlasts the paste by years: I have opened a book Ned pasted in 1964 and been sent back to Christmas. It was there in the hinge, fresh, sweet and sharp, a Christmas smell in a room where a man had died in July.

“Time,” said Demelza.

Garrow came in at ten past, with a young man in a car coat who carried a case like a doctor’s and had the grey face of one who has been behind a tractor since Truro. I had the Carne Rutter laid open on the bench with the lamp on it and the gloves still on. The Inspector looked at the gloves.

“Mrs Pellow, dear. I hope you have not been interfering.”

“Reading,” I said.

“Reading what?”

“Your evidence. It isn’t what it says it is.” I told him. I told it quite plainly and in order, the holes and the paper and the lion in the fence; the heart of the book that wasn’t; the pin-prick I did not mention, because I did not yet know how to say it aloud. I said the cover was Ned’s work of 1971 and the middle was not the Carne Rutter at all, and that whoever had put it there had done it since the spring, because the paste in the hinge was still sweet.

He heard me out with his head tilted, the way one listens to a child recite. “The middle of the book is not the middle of the book.”

“Yes.”

“A forgery, in effect, of a work Mr Trevithick was valuing.”

“It would appear so, Inspector.”

“And who in Trevenna could do a job like that?”

“Anyone who could sew. Anyone who knew how. It takes years.”

“How many bookbinders are there in Trevenna, Mrs Pellow?”

“One.”

“Quite,” said Garrow, and let it lie there between us for the length of time it takes a man to enjoy his own pause. “And she was in the Lantern on Thursday night, was she? With witnesses?”

“With a quiz team and a pint of cider and the whole of the Lantern Regulars, who would be delighted to tell you I was wrong about Elgar.” I kept my voice level, with some effort. “I said it was done by someone who had been taught. I did not say by whom.”

“I see.” He turned to the young man, who held out a long brown paper sack. “We’ll have that looked at by somebody with the proper letters after his name, Mrs Pellow, dear, and I’ll want it in a statement. You’ve been most helpful. Most observant.”

“I’ve twenty-seven years at that bench,” I said. “They don’t give letters for it.”

“Quite.” He lifted the Carne Rutter in both hands, as if it were a hot plate, and set it down in the sack. It looked very small. He smiled at me. “And in the meantime I’d be obliged if you wouldn’t leave the village.”

“Where would I go? I haven’t been further than Truro since 1974.”

“Then it’ll be no hardship,” said Detective Inspector Garrow, and went out with the sack, and the young man after him, and neither of them looked back at the room.

I took the gloves off one finger at a time. Demelza had been writing again, and she did not look up. I stood at the bench, where the lamp still burned on nothing, and said it aloud in the end, because there was nobody else to say it to.

“Someone sewed that book the way my husband taught, with my husband’s paste.”

“Then someone’s been in your shop,” said Demelza, not looking up from her notebook.

chapters.title: Bunting and Bargains
chapters.html:
The Reverend Arthur Nance opened the Trevenna Antiquarian Book Fair an hour late, by apologising to God and then, since nobody else seemed to be in the habit that day, to the dealers.

“Forgive me, I am sure it is nothing,” he said, standing on the dais in St Petroc’s hall with his bicycle clips still round his ankles and a cough drop travelling from one cheek to the other, “but our chairman cannot be with us. Let us ask a blessing on the stalls, and the floor, and the roof, which is not what it was, and on those of you who have come a long way and found us, which is not easy. And on Aubrey.” His voice went on the name. A woman from Bristol with a box of Penguins put her hand over her mouth. “There will be no ribbon,” said the Reverend, and sat down on the wrong chair.

Twenty-six trestles stood under Jago Rowe’s regatta bunting, two hundred yards of it, red, white and blue and a yellow nobody could account for, strung across the rafters because Aubrey had said it would add tone and Jago had said it would add bunting. Beneath it the dealers stood among their boxes in shirtsleeves and tweed, speaking in the low reverent voices of people about to be rude about one another’s prices. I sat at my trestle at the end, beside the tea urn, with a pot of Ned’s paste, a bone folder, a card in a dead man’s handwriting, and no customers.

I had not wanted to come. But Garrow had told me not to leave the village, and the village had seemed to me that morning very small, and there was nothing to do in the Bindery but listen to it. Also, though I did not say so to myself, a woman at a trestle with a paste pot is the best-placed observer in any room. People talk across her as they talk across a hat stand. At fifty-eight I had been wasting the talent for years.

“I wonder, my dear,” said a man in a bow tie, “if you could tell me who is in charge of repairs?”

“I am,” I said, and mended his Trollope.

He was a Mr Fosdyke, from Hay, and while the hinge dried he told me, unasked, that Aubrey Trevithick had once sent back one of his catalogues with eleven corrections in red ink, including a Latin ablative. “He was right about every one. I have never forgiven him.” That was how people spoke of Aubrey, I found, all that afternoon: with exasperated care, as of a clock that struck the hour correctly and at the wrong people. Nobody in the village had believed him an honest man. They had thought him too tidy for it.

“Mrs Pellow.”

A shadow came across the trestle, a large pale one. Pieter de Vries was from Rotterdam and dealt in maps, and he wore a linen jacket the colour of milk and round tortoiseshell glasses and a clipped grey beard, and he stood at my table with his hands behind him, as a man stands at the edge of a museum.

“I am sorry for your trouble. Very terrible, this.”

“Thank you, Mr de Vries.”

“The inspector has been to see me this morning. He asks me about paper.” He took off the glasses and polished them on the jacket, which made both paler. “A paper with a lion in a fence, from the seventeen-sixties. Is it Dutch, he asks. I tell him, probably, yes. Such paper we have sold to the whole world, to your Navy, to your Bank of England. Every dealer in Europe has a drawer of it.” He put the glasses back. “And while I say it, I hear how it sounds. A Dutchman, in a large white jacket, who tells the policeman the paper is Dutch.”

“It sounds like information.”

“It sounds like a confession with good manners.” The smile was very small. “I came for the maps, Mrs Pellow. Only for the maps.”

He went back to his stall and began, with the elaborate calm of a man carrying a full cup across a room, to straighten a chart of the Scheldt that had not moved.

I took my paste pot, because I could not think what else to take, and went to the far corner by the door, where Morwenna Hext had her honey.

She had a trestle to herself and a gingham cloth, and on it the honey of eight hives in jars with gingham lids, set in ranks like a small yellow army. Beside them lay the candles: rolled tapers in sheets of honey-coloured wax, tied in threes with raffia, and cakes of beeswax in muslin for polishing furniture and freeing sticking drawers. A card said ALL PROCEEDS TO THE LIFEBOAT in her upright hand. The whole stall smelled like a church that had been given a holiday.

“Dot, my handsome. Have you eaten? You’ve not. Take this.” A jar landed in my free hand. “No, I won’t hear it. You’re skin and bone, and it’s for the lifeboat, so you’re doing a service.”

“Morwenna, I only came to say—”

“You came for a look at the Book,” she said, and tilted her head at the end of the trestle. “Go on. I’m minding it for Jago. It can’t be left lying about with all these strangers, and it isn’t safe in the hall safe, either, I’m told, since the chairman’s key went with him.”

It lay on a cushion of tissue paper, a fat ledger in half calf, brown with a green cloth side and a gilt label across the front: REGATTA, TREVENNA, WINNERS. I knew it as I know my own handwriting. Ned had bound it in the summer of 1964, two years after I came to Trevenna; I had watched him do it, and he had let me press the boards. Every winning crew since the war was written in it in the treasurer’s hand, and every treasurer had been a small anxious person who kept it in the airing cupboard.

At the back joint someone had made a repair. I looked at it twice. The old calf had been lifted and re-pasted, with a strip of Japanese tissue let in beneath, and the work lay flat and clean, in no hurry, and very nearly as good as Ned’s.

“Who did that?”

“I did.” She was straightening candles. “It was going, Dot, and I couldn’t have the Book come apart in Jago’s hands at the finish. Paste and a bit of nerve. Ned left a tin of his tissue behind once, years ago, and I never gave it back.”

“It’s a good hinge.”

“It’s an honest hinge. Don’t make a fuss, I’ll go red.”

She was already red. She was always a little red, in the cheeks, like a winter apple, and she looked at me with her small bright eyes as if to see whether I had said it to be kind. I had not. I put my thumb on the joint and felt it give not at all, and had the thought, which I put away, that it was a heavy book for a ledger.

There was a noise from the middle of the hall like a sheet being torn very slowly, and a hush.

Jago Rowe was on a stepladder under the rafters in his shirtsleeves, the largest man in Trevenna, bald as a harbour stone, with an anchor on his forearm so faded that it might have been a bruise, and a right hand with the little finger gone to a winch in ‘fifty-eight. He was Ned’s oldest friend and the only man I knew who could tie a knot with nine fingers and still be ashamed of it. He had a length of bunting in one fist and was leaning out over the aisle to reach a hook. Below him, in the aisle, in his raincoat, with his notebook open to take a statement from the Reverend, stood Detective Inspector Garrow.

The knot gave. The whole run of it came down from the beam in a long soft rattle of flags, red, white, blue and the yellow, and it landed on the Inspector from the crown of his head to his shoes, so that for a moment he was a pillar of pennants with a notebook sticking out of it.

Nobody laughed. I will say that for Trevenna. Nobody laughed for at least two seconds.

“Mr Rowe,” came a muffled voice, “was that deliberate?”

“A knot, Inspector.” Jago’s voice is like a slow tide; one hears it arrive a good while before it reaches you. He looked down at the pillar with an expression of great gravity. “Not a good one.”

“I see.”

“That’s the size of it.”

It was at this point that Imogen Mayne came in at the door in a black leather jacket.

It was July and the hall was close; she wore it like a position. She had her father’s height and none of his ease, a cropped head, a silver stud in the side of her nose, and a cigarette unlit behind one ear, and she walked past the bunting and the Inspector and the Reverend as if they were a wall she meant to get round. At the table by the door stood Kit, with the chairman’s grey tin box held against his chest in both hands, where the dealers’ stall fees went.

“I’ll take that.”

“Sorry, I was only minding it. Until someone—”

“It’s mine now. It’s his.” She took the box from him and set it down and opened it, and counted the notes with a fast dry thumb. “Where’s the float? Where are the receipts? Who has the catalogues, Kit?”

“They’re, sorry, they’re by the—”

“Sorry’s not an answer. It’s a noise.” She did not look up. She had found something in the box, a stub of pencil, one of Aubrey’s, chewed at one end, and she stood with it in her palm. “Daddy,” she said to it, quietly, and then closed her hand and looked up, and her eyes went over the hall and found nobody they wanted, until they came to me.

“You’re the bookbinder.”

“Dot Pellow.”

“He said you were the only person in the village who didn’t flatter him.”

“He said that?”

“As a complaint.” The nose stud flashed. She put the pencil in her pocket, and the box under her arm, and went away to count somebody else’s money.

I had not expected to feel hit. I sat back on my heels beside the honey and put the jar down carefully on the floor.

“Pellow!”

The hearing aid reached me first, a high thin whistle that crossed the hall ahead of its owner, and then Loveday Penhallow herself, in gumboots under a tweed skirt, seventy-four years old and as thin as a pen, with long beautiful hands on the head of a blackthorn stick. People moved out of her way as they would for a heron. She stopped in front of me and the whistle stopped, and she looked down.

“They have my Carne in a paper bag in Truro.”

“Yes, Miss Penhallow. I’m sorry.”

“Don’t fuss, Pellow. I did not ask you to be sorry.” Loveday barks; it is one of the pleasures of her. “They say it was damaged. Garrow says there’s some question about the book. What question? You were in the room.”

I thought of the ewe sheep at fourteen shillings and the lion in his fence. It is a hard thing to say to a woman of seventy-four in a village hall, between a honey stall and a man in a bow tie. “I think it will be looked at very carefully,” I said.

“That’s what people say when it won’t.” The hearing aid gave a short whistle, like a kettle thinking about it. “You found him. You have the nose for it. You found out what was wrong with my pump before the plumber did. Find out who did this.”

“I’m a bookbinder, Miss Penhallow.”

“Nobody looks at you,” said Loveday. “It’s what the job wants.”

I have been paid worse compliments, though not many.

Kit had come across the hall with a folder of typed pages, holding it out to her in both hands like a man handing over a cheque. “Miss Penhallow. Sorry. This is the list, the valuation, what Mr Trevithick and I did up to Wednesday. It’s, sorry, it’s all in order. I’d thought you should have it.”

She took it and turned the pages with her long fingers, and I saw over her arm the column of numbers going down the left in Kit’s careful capitals, and the last line on the last page. 114. Rutter, MS, c.1631, in contemporary calf, rebacked 1971. The “Carne”.

“That’s as far as you got.”

“Yes. Sorry. We’d done the north wall, and the Carne’s the, it’s the last on it.”

“Last on the list,” said Loveday. She closed the folder. Her hand found my sleeve and held it, and the fingers were cold as a bell, and surprisingly strong. “Aubrey valued my library as far as the Carne, Pellow, and not one inch past it. The sale is in September. I have a roof.”

She went. The whistle went with her, up the aisle and out through the door into the afternoon, and the hall began again at its ordinary murmur, and a woman asked if the person with the paste could do her Georgette Heyer.

I went back to my trestle and did her Heyer. From there, across the hall, I could see the honey stall, where Pieter de Vries had come to buy a candle. I could see him over the heads. He picked the cheapest, a single yellow taper, and put a note on the cloth, and Morwenna, small and round and unhurried, folded it into tissue paper and tied it with raffia and held it out to him. He took it as if it might still be lit. He did not look at her face, nor at her hands, nor at the jars. He looked at the tissue paper the whole time, as if it were being read aloud to him.

chapters.title: The Quarrel at the Lantern
chapters.html:
The ceiling of the Drowned Lantern is hung with glass fishing floats, a hundred and forty of them in their nets, and in every one a small lamp burns. Jago’s grandfather began it in 1880, one float for each man lost off Trevenna, and nobody since has had the heart to take one down. The effect, if you sit under it long enough, is of drinking at the bottom of a green sea with all the lights on. It is the only pub I know where the decorations have a casualty list.

I had not been in since the quiz. I stood in the doorway at seven that Friday evening with the smell of chips and old beer coming out to meet me, and a dart that had been on its way to the board seemed to stop in mid-air, consider me, and then arrive in the wall. The Lantern’s darts team, five men in their working shirts, looked round together, as people look at someone they have been discussing.

“Mrs Pellow,” said the nearest.

“Evening, Alan.”

I walked the length of the room under the lamps, and the talk closed behind me like water. Jago Rowe was at the pumps with a cloth over his shoulder, as big as a door and as silent. He did not say good evening, which in twenty-seven years he had never failed to do. He drew me half a cider without being asked, put a mat under it, and slid it along the wood with the three fingers and thumb of his right hand, and went to the other end of the bar to attend to a customer who was not there.

I took the cider to the table under the window. Kit was not there; Garrow had borrowed him for the evening, I learned, and installed him in the vestry of St Petroc’s with a pot of tea and a great many questions. Demelza was. She sat at the far end of the bar in her uniform with a lemonade she was not drinking, and she looked at me once and nodded, a short level nod, which I understood to mean that she was on duty and would pretend not to be listening, and that I was to say nothing she would be obliged to write down.

I had not been seated a minute before Bert Tregear, eighty years old and coxswain of the lifeboat until his knees, came across in his cap and sat down opposite without being asked.

“You’ll want to know about Thursday,” he said. He had been waiting for the question since I came in. “I’ll tell you about Thursday.”

It took an hour. The Lantern on a Friday night had, I understood, appointed itself my witness, and it gave its evidence in the manner of the place, which is all at once, with corrections. Alan Polglase the postman came over from the dartboard, and Elsie Hocking and her husband Len from the settle, and a couple of the Chapel men who disapprove of the Lantern and were passing through it on the way to the gents. Between them they reassembled the night as a woman reassembles a torn page, with paste and argument.

“It was a good night,” said Elsie. “Till it wasn’t.”

“We came fourth,” I said.

“We came fourth because the Regulars cheated.”

“Elsie Hocking,” said Alan, with dignity, “the Lantern Regulars came second on merit. You gave a Brahms for an Elgar.”

“Len gave a Brahms for an Elgar.”

“I gave,” said Len, who is a quiet man, “a considered answer to a difficult question, and it was robbery.”

“It was the Nimrod,” I said. “It is always the Nimrod. Anyone who has been to a funeral has heard it.”

“That’s what I said!” said Len, and Elsie hit him with her handbag, quite gently, as one punctuates.

I will say it was a comfort. For about four minutes the whole of Trevenna was reduced to a dispute about a piece of music, and I was cross with the right people for the right reasons, and a man was not dead. Then Bert coughed, and the table remembered itself, and the green light settled back on our faces.

They did the room first. The Jam Tarts at the next table, third place, as they have come every Thursday since the Coronation, with Morwenna in charge of the pencil, as she is of everything. The noise. The chips, which Jago does on quiz nights in a pan the size of a bath. Quire Straits in the corner by the fruit machine, Elsie and Len and Kit and myself, and a chair for the Reverend Nance that stayed empty all night because he had promised us and did not come. We had been a man short, which in my view also accounted for fourth.

Then they did the quarrel.

“Twenty past eight, near enough,” said Bert. “Right in the middle of the geography. She come in from the back, the daughter, in that coat.”

“Leather,” said Elsie.

“I know it’s leather, Elsie. And Mr Trevithick was stood at the bar with his whisky, very upright, like he’d swallowed a ruler, and she said, ‘You sold Mother’s piano.’”

“She said, ‘You sold Mother’s piano and you kept the stool,’” said Alan.

“It was about money,” said Elsie. “She wanted four thousand pounds for a workshop up in London and he said accuracy obliged him to ask for a business plan.”

“It was about her mother’s money. He said it was held in trust. She said it was held in a drawer.”

“I heard the word Mother,” said Alan, “and the word piano, and another word that I shall not repeat in front of Mrs Pellow.”

“I’m fifty-eight, Alan.”

“I’d still not repeat it.”

They agreed on two things only, and I counted them on my fingers under the table as they went by: that the girl had said Mother, and that she had said money. They agreed also that she had gone out at five and twenty past eight like a door slammed in a gale, and that Aubrey had stood a moment looking at his glass, and had drunk it, and straightened his waistcoat, and said to the room at large, “I beg your pardon, ladies and gentlemen. A family matter.” Which, said Elsie, was the most human thing she had heard him say in twenty years.

I had no pencil. Alan lent me the chalk from the dartboard, which was no use on a sheet of paper, and then, being a postman and a man of resource, produced a stub from behind his ear. I took a beer mat from the next table, one with a printed pasty on it, turned it over, and began to write.

8.00 Quiz begins. 8.20 A. and Imogen. 8.25 Imogen out.

By nine o’clock the room had thinned and taken a new colour. Demelza had gone at half past eight, her lemonade untouched. The Chapel men had gone. Bert’s wife had sent for him by a child. I sat with the mat and the cider, and the lamps in their nets swung a little each time the door opened, and I watched Jago work the pumps with that large slow back, until there was no one near the bar but the Reverend Nance, who had come in at ten to nine with his bicycle clips on, and ordered, in a voice of the deepest apology, his one small sherry.

He took it to the end of the bar, to a stool under a float with a green lamp, and sat with it in both hands like something that might go off.

“Arthur.”

“Mrs Pellow! Forgive me. I didn’t see you there.”

“Nobody does,” I said. “You didn’t come to the quiz on Thursday.”

“No. No, I am afraid I was detained.” The cough drop travelled from one cheek to the other. He looked at the sherry. “By the roof. There is a matter of the roof, which wants a man to look at it, and one cannot always, forgive me, predict.”

“At half past nine?”

“At half past—” He stopped. His mild eyes, which are the colour of weak tea, came up to mine with an air of actual pain. “Was there a question about half past nine?”

“I’m only asking where everyone was, Arthur. Garrow will ask. I thought you’d rather be asked by someone who liked you.”

“I walked,” said the Reverend. “I do walk, you know, in the evening. I think about my sermon. I could not tell you which way, precisely. Up, I think, and down. It is a very small village.” He laughed, rather high, and drank the sherry in one swallow, though he generally makes it last the evening, and put down a coin more than the price. “Forgive me, I am sure it is nothing.”

Then he took his clips off, which he had not done, and put them on again, and went out, and the bell swung on the door for some while after.

I looked at the beer mat. I wrote 9.30 Nance? and, after thought, left the question mark, because it was the only honest thing on the card.

At twenty to nine on the Thursday, Jago told me, when at last he came down the bar, Aubrey had used the payphone. He told it to the glass in his hand, with the voice that moves like a tide. It hangs on the wall at the back by the gents, behind the dartboard, he said, and the dartboard had been in use, and Aubrey had stood against the wall with his cane hooked on his arm and the receiver an inch from his mouth, as if he distrusted it.

“Who did he ring?”

“He didn’t say.”

“What did he say?”

“’Half ten, then.’” Jago wiped the glass. “That’s all I heard. He put it down. He had a second whisky, which he never did, and he went out. Ten to nine. That’s the size of it.”

“Half ten where?”

“He didn’t say.”

“Half ten, then.” I said it twice, to hear what it did. It was the hour the quiz ended, when the whole Lantern would be on its feet hunting for coats. A good hour, I thought, for a man to be somewhere else without being missed.

I wrote it on the mat under the rest, with the time, and then the rest of the night as the room had given it to me: Imogen out at 8.25. Aubrey at the bar, then the telephone, then gone by ten to nine. Nance a question. Quiz ended half past ten; the Jam Tarts, third; Quire Straits, fourth and robbed. I went out at ten to eleven, up the hill, and it was dark.

Then there was the key. I sat looking at it for some time before I wrote it, because I did not care for what it did to my feelings.

The door had been locked behind him, with the spare. A person who kills a man does not stop to go through the pockets looking for a key unless he knows there is one to find. Someone had known. I had known; I had handed it over. Aubrey had known, naturally, and could tell nobody anything now. And Kit had known, because he had told me so himself that afternoon at the trestle, between a Georgette Heyer and a Dornford Yates, with his face white and his thumb in his mouth. He told me on Thursday he’d got your spare key, Auntie Dot. Sorry. He said you’d been kind.

Three people. It was a short list, and I did not like the third name on it, and I wrote it down all the same.

“Jago.”

“Dot.”

Aubrey had held the lease of the Lantern for eleven years, and in all that time Jago had never said a word against him, which in a Cornishman is either a testimony or a confession. I did not say so. “Who would want to see Aubrey Trevithick at half past ten at night in my press room?”

He did not answer. He took up a glass, a tumbler, and began to wipe it with the cloth. Round and round the inside, with the thumb that had only three fingers to keep it company. He wiped it for a full minute by the clock over the fruit machine. I counted. Above his head one of the green floats turned slowly on its net, and the lamp inside it flickered, as a lamp does that has been listening.

“Leave it, Dot,” he said.

“I don’t think I shall.”

“Ned’d have left it.”

“Ned would have asked twice as many questions as I have, only with a pipe in his mouth, so that nobody noticed.” I finished my cider. I did not leave it. I put the beer mat face down on the wood, and on the clean side of it, with Alan Polglase’s stub, I began a second list, headed in my best capitals with the question that had been sitting in the room since seven o’clock, wearing a green lamp and waiting to be asked: Who was going to meet him?

chapters.title: Paste, Thread and Wax
chapters.html:
Ned’s paste is made in a dented enamel pan that is used for nothing else and has a handle mended with a bootlace. Wheat starch, never flour, mixed cold to a cream with a wooden spoon; then boiling water poured in a thin stream, stirring, until the whole turns from milk to glass in the space of a breath. A pinch of alum. And off the heat, from the brown bottle with the cork in the cupboard, one drop of oil of clove, no more, which Ned counted aloud in a whisper like a man at a christening.

Demelza had taken down the tape at half past seven on Saturday morning with a face like a shut door, told me the press room was mine again, and left. The aluminium powder still lay grey along the stove door. I found I could not lay a hand on that stove. So I made the paste on the gas ring in the shop, in the small pan, as I had the winter of ‘seventy-nine when the flue fell in, and I had Kit stir, because his arm is longer than mine and he needed something to do with it.

He had come when I rang, at eight, in yesterday’s shirt, unshaven, and stood in the press-room door a full minute before he would come in. He looked at the boards where Aubrey had been. Somebody, and I think it was Demelza, had put a sheet of newspaper over the patch and weighted its corners with four bone folders from Ned’s tin. Kit stepped round it the way you step round a sleeping dog.

“Sorry. Is it, I mean, are you sure about doing this today?”

“Paste goes off. There is a fair on. I have forty hinges promised, Kit, and a man from Bristol who wants a Surtees back by Sunday.” I unlocked the cupboard and took out the brown bottle, which stands on the second shelf behind the alum, beside Ned’s green notebook with its rubber band. “Stir. Slowly. As though it had done you a kindness.”

The starch cleared. I held the bottle over the pan, counted one in a whisper, and the smell came up out of the steam like a door opened on a lit room: oranges, nutmeg, string, the week before Christmas.

I stood very still with the cork in my fingers.

It was the same. I do not mean similar. I had put my nose to the hinge of the Carne Rutter at ten o’clock on Friday, with a policeman’s back turned to me, and what I smelled now was that exactly, down to the faint sharp edge underneath it, the spike like a pin in a cushion that clove oil gives when it has been in the cupboard a month or two. Whoever had pasted that board had used this bottle’s cousin. They had used Ned’s recipe, in Ned’s quantities, and counted, I would have said, aloud.

“That’s Uncle Ned’s,” said Kit, working the spoon. “That’s just, sorry, that’s what it smells like in here.”

“It is. Who else makes it?”

“You. Me.” He stopped stirring. “Sorry. Nobody else, Auntie Dot. It’s not written anywhere. You’d have to have stood where I’m standing.”

“Yes,” I said. “You would.”

We let it cool. I told him the rest, because somebody had to hear it who knew what a signature was: that the middle of the Carne was a farmer’s accounts on Dutch-looking paper, and that the cover and the ends were genuine. I did not tell him about the pin-prick. I had not yet found a way to say that to a living person. Kit listened with his head down, and his bitten thumb went up to his mouth and was removed again, and a good deal of colour went out of his freckles.

“Garrow thinks it was Mr Trevithick,” I said. “That he was the forger, and fell out with a partner.”

“Sorry. No.”

“No?”

“He wouldn’t have.” He said it to the pan. “He was, sorry. He was very particular.”

“Yes, Kit, I know.” I looked at him, but he was looking at the paste, and I put the matter away on the shelf with the other things I did not understand that week.

When it was cool I carried the pan through to the press room and set it on the bench, and ran my hand along the cutting board for the bone folder I wanted. The board is a slab of beech the size of a tea tray, and thirty years of knives have scarred it into a country of rivers and roads, with Ned’s long diagonal cut across the middle like a border. In one of the cuts, down by the edge of the lying press, something brown caught my thumbnail.

It was a tail of thread, three inches, wedged in the groove where the policeman’s tweezers had missed it. Kit found me my glasses, which had slid under the bench. I took the loupe from my pocket and laid the thread across my palm in the light from the skylight.

The thread was sound, linen, twisted three-ply, the colour of a toasted crust. I had expected tallow and paraffin, which is what I use, and what Ned used, and what leaves a thread slightly grey and stiff and smelling faintly of a stable. This was golden. There was a bloom on it as fine as the bloom on a plum, and when I rubbed it between my finger and thumb it warmed, and gave off an odour, thin and sweet and entirely out of place in a room that smelled of a dead man and a policeman: honey.

“Beeswax,” I said.

“Sorry?”

“The thread’s been waxed with beeswax. I’ve never used it in my life.” I held it to his nose. “Nor did Ned. He called it a wax for ladies who sew their own buttons. It’s a hobbyist’s choice; it’s kinder to the thread and it costs three times as much.”

“I use yours.”

“I know you do.”

He sniffed the thread and took his head away, and I put the thing in an envelope from the shop drawer and sealed it with a bit of Ned’s paste, for reasons I cannot defend. Then I took a breath. I told him about the hammer, because it had been in my head since the doorway on Friday and I had reached the point of needing to say it aloud to anyone who would not write it down.

“It was on Ned’s nail. Face-out. I’ve not hung it there since the funeral.” I nodded at the wall, where both nails stood bare, the police having taken the hammer away in a paper sack with a label on it, and I had not asked what the label said. “Ned was left-handed, you’ll remember, and he hung it to suit himself, round side to the room and the handle to his left. I could find it in the dark on my nail. Whoever was in this room put it on his, in his way. It isn’t a thing you do by accident. You do it if you have watched a man reach for it ten thousand times.”

“Sorry.” Kit’s voice had gone a long way off. “Who’d have watched Uncle Ned reach for it ten thousand times?”

“You. Me.” I counted on my fingers, as I had under the table at the Lantern. “Jago, I suppose, in the early days, before the boat took up his time. Nobody else ever worked at that bench beside him. He was a private man, Ned, about his work.”

“Only me and you and Jago.”

“I did not say—”

“Only us three.” He put the bone folder down, rather he did not put it down, he let it go; it fell with a small clean sound on the boards and lay there between his shoes. He looked at it as though it belonged to a stranger. What colour he had went out of his face and left the freckles standing on it like type on a page. “Sorry. That’s, sorry. That’s all of us, then.”

“Kit.”

“No, sorry, I only. Sorry.”

“Kit, listen to me. You turn your kettle to the right. I have unpicked enough of your head and tail stitches to know it blindfold. Ned gave up on you at eleven and said the boy had hands as God made them.” I made myself say it lightly. “I am only saying who might have stood beside him. I am not saying who.”

He nodded, three or four times, and bent for the bone folder, and missed it, and bent again. I took an end of the thread out of the envelope and tried not to look at his bitten thumb.

“I can see your shoes under the door,” I said, rather loudly, to the shop.

There was a silence in which somebody inhaled. Then the door to the street, which stood ajar, moved a few inches, and the girl came out from behind it as if she had been slid on a tray: Sheila Bray’s daughter, with her jaw-length hair and the bleached stripe, ink to the second knuckle, a pen in the corner of her mouth.

“Right,” she said. “So.”

“How long have you been standing there?”

“Not long.” That was certainly untrue. She looked past me at the press room, at the newspaper on the boards and the four bone folders, with an expression I could not read, not curiosity quite, and not the hunger of the village. She looked at it like someone seeing a church. “I could sweep.”

“No,” I said.

“I’m quick. I don’t touch anything. I’d do the yard and the front step and not the bench.”

“No, thank you. I’ve no money to pay anyone and I’ve enough on my conscience without the Education Authority.”

She stood her ground. She is a thin small person in a big jumper, and she did not argue; she merely went on standing there, with her hands behind her and the pen in the corner of her mouth, looking at the Bindery as if it were the last warm room in the county. I thought of the Fish Cellar Lane steps, and the third that creaks, and the girl on them the morning before.

“The yard,” I said. “And the step. And I’ll not be paying you.”

“Right. So.” She vanished, and a minute later I heard the broom begin in the yard, a brisk skilled whisper, the sound of a girl who had swept before and liked the work.

I went back to the cupboard for the alum, and it was Ned’s notebook on the second shelf that I looked at. A small green cloth book with a rubber band round it, much handled, which had lived in that cupboard since before I was married. Every job he ever did was in it, and every boy who ever held a needle for him, in his own tiny horrid hand. I had lent it to Sheila Bray’s girl for an afternoon in May, for a school project on dying trades, and she had brought it back in a Co-op bag with a thank-you note in a far better hand than mine, and I had locked it away again without opening the cover. I cannot read Ned’s writing. It is like being shouted at by a man in a gale.

“Kit,” I said. “Ned kept every pupil he ever had written down. In that book. Every job and every name, with the dates.” I took the alum from the shelf. “If someone learned his way of sewing, he’d have put them in it. It might be that there’s a name.”

“Have you read it?”

“I cannot bear his hand. I’ve never read it. It’s been in that cupboard for—”

“Dot, my handsome! Are you in?”

It came from the shop, bright and unmistakable, and the bell over the door, which jangles when the door is pushed open, jangled a moment after her voice. Morwenna was standing at the counter with a tin open in her hands and her large bag over her arm and the face of a woman who has arrived that very instant. In the tin lay saffron buns, a dozen, yellow as the door.

“I heard they’d given you your room back, and I thought, she’ll not have eaten. No cake this morning, the oven let me down, so it’s buns. Kit, you look dreadful. Sit down before you fall.”

“Morwenna, you’re a saint.”

“I’m a woman with a tin. Eat.”

We ate. She stayed ten minutes, and talked about the bunting committee and whether the lifeboat would get a new tractor, and admired the paste, and said she wouldn’t set foot in the press room, if I didn’t mind, not today; and then she took her tin and her bag and went down the lane without looking back, as she always does, a small round person moving through the morning like a well-run errand.

When she had gone I took Ned’s notebook out of the cupboard, and weighed it in my hand, and put it back. I turned the little brass key. It was Ned’s key, a flat thing with a bow like a clover, that had hung on the third hook of the board in the shop between the yard bolt and the loft padlock since his day, and I had turned it in that lock out of habit and never out of fear. I looked at it on my palm. I threaded it on the bootlace that holds my glasses, and put the lace over my head, and felt it settle against my breastbone, cold, with a small weight like a coin.

I felt a fool, doing it, and not nearly enough of one.

chapters.title: Somebody Else's Key
chapters.html:
The otter came up as lot forty-one, and the hall lights found both its eyes at once.

It stood on its hind legs in a glass case a yard high, on a riverbank of green baize and cotton wool, with a pewter-coloured trout clamped in its jaws and one paw raised, as if it had been about to ask a question and been interrupted. Someone had stuffed it around 1890 and never forgiven it. The eyes were amber glass, enormous, and under the new tube lights of St Petroc’s hall they blazed like a pair of headlamps on a wet road. The front row, which was entirely Women’s Institute, leaned back together.

“Lot forty-one,” said Jago Rowe. “An otter.”

The Saturday auction had been Aubrey’s idea and Aubrey’s gavel, and with its owner lying in a drawer in Truro the whole business had fallen, as things in Trevenna do, to the nearest large man. Jago stood at the lectern in a waistcoat last buttoned in about 1974, the gavel lost in his right hand (the one with four fingers), and ran the sale in the voice of a tide coming up the Slip: slow, unhurried and certain to arrive. He had not looked at me once all evening. I had been sitting at my trestle by the tea urn for three hours, mending the hinges of other people’s Bibles, and I was used to being looked past. It was only that he did it so carefully.

“Who’ll start me at five pounds?”

Kit, who had carried the case up onto the table in both arms like a man bringing in a drowned relative, said “Sorry” to the otter and stepped back.

“Five,” said Mrs Bolitho.

Ada Bolitho keeps the post office and has not been outbid on anything since the Coronation. She wore a raspberry felt hat that needed both hands to remove, and she had already turned round in her chair to tell the row behind what the otter was for. “Hats on the paw,” she said, “umbrella through the trout. I’ve the very spot in the hall. Twenty years I’ve been looking for a thing to put in that spot.”

“Seven,” said a voice from the back.

Heads turned. Pieter de Vries sat at the end of the last row in a folding chair that did not contain him, his white jacket spread over its edges like a tablecloth, his round glasses holding two small otters. He had raised one finger perhaps half an inch from the catalogue on his knee. He was looking at nothing at all.

“Seven pounds, from the gentleman at the back,” said Jago, as if announcing a drowning. “Eight?”

“Ten,” said Mrs Bolitho.

“Twelve.” The finger went up half an inch, and came down.

It was a good deal like watching a heron and a terrier dispute a ditch. At twenty-five the room sat up. At forty it began to enjoy itself, and somebody at the back had to be told to stop whistling. Mrs Bolitho bid with her whole body, rising on the balls of her feet to do it, hat tilted like a mainsail, and Pieter bid with nothing but the finger, in a stillness so complete that by sixty pounds I had begun to find it ghastly. He did not look at the otter, or at her, or at the roof. At seventy, Imogen Mayne, behind the cash table in her leather jacket, put down her pencil. At ninety, Mrs Chegwidden said “Disgraceful” in a voice of deep contentment.

“I’ve had that hall in my head since nineteen sixty-one,” said Mrs Bolitho to the room at large, “and I’ll not be beaten by a map.”

“One hundred and thirty,” said Pieter.

“A hundred and thirty-five!”

Pieter turned his head and for the first time looked at her. Then he rose, the whole pale length of him, and bowed from the waist, and the hall, which has a great sense of occasion, went “Ahh.”

“Madam,” he said. “I give way. It will look very well, this, with hats.”

“It will,” said Mrs Bolitho, and sat down hard.

Jago brought the gavel down on a hundred and thirty-five pounds. At the side of the hall the Reverend Nance, who had been standing with his lips moving, visibly added it to the roof.

At the interval I joined the queue for the urn and found myself behind forty inches of white linen.

“Mrs Pellow.” Pieter inclined his head. “You will tell me I am a fool, I think.”

“I was going to say eccentric. What would you have done with an otter in Rotterdam?”

“I do not know. Posted it, perhaps.” He took his cup from the urn lady and considered it as he had considered the otter. “Please to think. A man has died in a village. Here is a foreigner with maps and the wrong kind of paper, and every person in this hall has watched him two days to see what he will do. So. Now they have seen. He wanted an otter.” He tasted the tea and bore it. “People forgive a great deal in a man who wants an otter, this.”

“And if she had stopped bidding?”

“Mrs Bolitho does not stop. I watched her at the tombola.”

He went off down the hall with his cup held out in front of him like a candle, and I thought, not for the first time that day, that there are more kinds of honest than one, and that Pieter de Vries had chosen a narrow one.

I went back to my trestle, where a water-stained Pilgrim’s Progress lay with its back joint split from head to tail. I had the bone folder in my hand when I became aware of a presence at my elbow. The Reverend Arthur Nance has a way of arriving as if he has been there some time and been too polite to mention it. He stooped over the trestle, a cough drop clicking against his teeth, his bicycle clips still on, though he had walked forty yards from the vestry.

“Mrs Pellow. Forgive me. I wonder if I might put a, a hypothetical.”

“You may put what you like. I’m only mending Bunyan.”

“Quite. Quite.” He looked at the book, and at the urn, and at the ceiling, where a brown stain the shape of Ireland had been advancing since Easter. “A book. Let us say a book that has, ah, left its owner’s keeping by irregular means. Might it be, in your experience, possible to buy it back?”

“Stolen, you mean.”

“I did not say stolen.” The cough drop travelled from one cheek to the other. “I am sure it is nothing. A friend, merely. A friend of a friend.”

I have known Arthur Nance for twenty-seven years and I do not believe he has a friend of a friend. He has a cousin in Hayle who sells insurance, and a dentist.

“It depends where it’s got to,” I said. “If it’s in the thief’s attic you can’t buy it back, you can only tell the police and wait. If it’s been sold on, you can find the man who has it and offer him what he paid, and then something on top for his trouble, and then something on top of that for his pride. It’s always possible, Reverend. It’s the money that’s difficult.”

“Ah.” His eyes went to Ireland again. “Yes. The money.”

“Is it a parish matter?”

“No! Gracious, no. No.” He patted the trestle, apologised to it, and was carried off by Mrs Chegwidden, who required a blessing on the tombola. I looked at Bunyan’s broken joint for some while. A book that had left its owner’s keeping by irregular means: I had one of those on my mind already, and it was in a paper sack in Truro.

The otter took forty minutes and the rest of the lots took another hour and a half, and after that there were the unsold boxes to stack, and the takings to count. Kit went off to the Lantern at nine with a darts match in his pocket, apologising to the door. Imogen counted the money three times on the vestry table, a cigarette burning in a saucer that Mrs Chegwidden had provided with the expression of a woman signing a treaty, and I stayed to help her, or to be near other people. Every night that week I had climbed past the press-room window as one passes a dog one does not trust. It was midnight before Imogen shut the cash box with a snap, said “Well, that’s that, then,” in a voice that was not about the money, and let me out into the dark.

The tide had turned. It was making small sucking noises at the foot of the Hard, drawing the harbour off like a cloth from a table. I climbed Fish Cellar Lane slowly, between the old pilchard cellars with their holiday curtains drawn, and a smell of wet rope came up with me from the quay. The lamp at the bottom gave out at the third house. After that there was only the grey of the granite and the yellow of my own door, which at night turns the colour of old cheese.

On Thursday I had walked up this lane at eleven o’clock and looked at the press-room window and seen only dark, and gone on to bed. I had told no one. I have told several people since, and it has not got lighter.

The window was not dark. The lower sash stood four inches up, a black wedge in the grey paint, and on the sill lay a curl of white paint like a pencil shaving. Someone had worked a blade in between the sashes from outside and slid the catch back as neatly as you open a tin.

I stood a minute with my hand on the cold stone. Then I went round to my own door, let myself into the shop with my own key, and took the yard rule down from its hook. It has killed nothing larger than a wasp, but it is the only weapon on the premises I trust.

The shop was as I had left it. The till drawer held fourteen pounds sixty and a button. I stood at the press-room door and listened, and somewhere low down in the dark, behind wood, there rose a long, thin, rising complaint, like a kettle with a grievance.

“Quire?”

The complaint ceased, drew breath, and resumed at a higher pitch.

I put on the light. The strip over the nipping press, which was fitted last year against all my objections, ticked and buzzed and came on in three stages like a man getting out of a chair. Cold air poured through the open window and brought the harbour with it. The bench was bare; the lying press stood where it had stood; the chair was in its place. The only thing out of true was the paste cupboard to the right of the stove, a tall pine thing with a ledge door, because the noise was coming out of it.

It was shut. I took the key off its bootlace, where it had hung against my breastbone since Saturday morning, and turned it in the lock, and the door swung out on a flash of white bib and a torn ear, and Quire came out of it like a cork. She went over my foot, hissed at the yard rule, hissed at me, and stalked to the stove where she sat down with her back to the room and began to wash. There was a saucer on the floor of the cupboard. She had drunk every drop of what had been in it, which did not in her opinion lessen the offence.

On the second shelf, between the alum and the clove oil, there was a clean oblong in the dust where a small green book had lain for longer than I had been married.
