I shut the door again and turned the key. It went round as sweetly as a clock. I bent with the torch from the shop drawer and looked at the keyhole, at the brass plate, at the pine around it. Not a scratch. Not a bruise. Whoever had been in that cupboard had opened it with a key, and had locked it again with a key, and the only key I knew of was lying on my chest.

I stood with that for some time. Then I went into the shop and rang Demelza.

She was there in six minutes, which is quick for a woman who has had to find her boots. She came in under the bell wearing her police overcoat buttoned one hole out, tartan flannel pyjama bottoms, and a pair of green gumboots, with her plait over one shoulder and a torch the size of a rolling pin. At her wrist, where the coat sleeve rode up, was a grey cuff that I had darned myself in 1987. I looked at it and then, with great care, at the till.

“Right. Facts,” she said. “Door?”

“Locked. I used my key.”

“Window?”

“Up. Forced from outside, I should think. I’ve touched nothing but the cupboard.”

“Anyone inside?”

“Only the cat. She was in the cupboard.”

“In the cupboard.”

“Shut in. With a saucer of milk.”

Demelza looked at me. Then she went through into the press room and shone the torch round it, slowly, left to right, and stopped on the sill and on the bright curl of paint. She put her face to the glass. “Chisel,” she said. “Thin one. Not a boy, a boy would have put his elbow through. Somebody who knew what they were doing and wasn’t in a hurry.” She straightened. “Mr Trevithick’s spare key is still missing, so whoever’s got it had no need of a window.”

“Then why use one?”

“To say they hadn’t a key.” She wrote it down. “What’s gone?”

I had decided on the walk from the shop what I would say. I said it. “Ned’s notebook. A small green cloth one, with a rubber band. Every job he ever did and every pupil he ever taught, from 1951. It was in the cupboard.”

The pencil stopped. “Every pupil.”

“I’ve never read it. I can’t bear his hand.”

“A list of everyone your husband taught to bind a book,” said Demelza, quite gently, “has been sitting in a cupboard for two days after a man was killed over a forged one, and you are telling me about it at ten past one in the morning.”

“I did mean to.”

“We’ll come back to that.” She tapped the pencil on the book twice. “And the cupboard was locked. Who has the key?”

“It hung on the third hook of the board in the shop, by the yard bolt, for thirty years. Anyone who ever worked here knew where it was.”

She went and looked at the board with her torch. Eleven hooks, ten keys, and the third one bare. “Not there.”

“No.”

“So someone’s had it off the hook, opened the cupboard, taken the book, put the cat in, locked up, and walked off with the key in their pocket.” She nodded, pleased with it, as she should have been. “I’ll want that cat’s saucer. And nobody in that room till the Truro man comes at eight.”

I want it understood that I did not lie to her. I have been over every word. Everything I said was true, and I let her have the rest, as one lets a child have the last biscuit. It was a good deduction and a wrong one. I could not have told you why I held my tongue, except that a second key meant a second person who had once stood close enough to Ned to be given it, and I did not care to hand that to a woman in pyjamas at one in the morning. I wanted to turn it over by myself first. That is what I told myself, with the thing lying cold against my breastbone, where it was heavier than it had been at supper.

Demelza taped the sash, and set the shop chair against the press-room door, and sat in it with her coat round her knees and the torch in her lap, and I took the stool. We did not speak for a while. Quire stayed by the cold stove with her back to us both, washing the same shoulder, which is how she sulks.

Before the door was shut I had looked once more into the cupboard. The saucer sat on the floor under the bottom shelf, licked to a bright circle. It was one of mine, from the blue-rimmed set that lives on the tea shelf in the shop, bought with Co-op coupons the year we were married. And beside it, laid straight on the boards with its bowl turned up and its handle pointing to the door, as you lay a spoon for a guest who has come to stay the evening, lay one of my teaspoons.

chapters.title: Quire Gives Evidence
chapters.html:
The cake was on my step at ten to six, under a tea towel with a faded lighthouse on it.

I had slept in my clothes and not well. Demelza had walked me up the twenty yards to my own door at two, and stood on the cobbles until she heard the bolt go home, and I had lain on top of the counterpane with my shoes on listening to the cottage tick. When I opened the door the light was the colour of weak tea, the gulls were already shouting about it, and there it sat on the granite: a saffron loaf the size of a hymn book, still faintly warm through its greaseproof, with a corner cut off to show it was meant to be eaten and not admired. Morwenna’s, of course. Nobody else in Trevenna gets the crust that colour.

Nobody had knocked. Nobody ever does. In Trevenna, when there is a death or a flood or a husband gone off with a woman from Redruth, the cake appears on the step before the news is round the harbour, and the person who has baked it is never anywhere about. I had found one on my own step twice before in my life. The first was in 1962, when I was a bride nobody had asked for, and the second was March 1986.

I took it in. I stood at the kitchen table, in my shoes, and ate the corner and then another corner, and then I was crying with my mouth full, which is not a thing I recommend to anyone with a good set of teeth. I was furious as well. It is a peculiar sensation to be both at once; it leaves the face with nowhere to go. Somebody had come up the lane in the dark to leave me a cake, and in four days nobody had come to ask whether I was all right, except a constable who wished to know why I had not mentioned a cupboard. I ate standing up and I finished the slice, and I wiped my eyes on the lighthouse, and I thought: well. That’s the first decent thing that has happened since Thursday, and it is flour.

Demelza was in the shop by half past eight, in uniform, with her helmet under her arm and her eyes ringed like a pair of pennies. The Truro man had been and gone. He had a case of brushes like a lady’s dressing-table and left the press-room window the colour of a chimney-sweep’s glove. The saucer and the spoon had gone in a bag. Quire sat in the middle of the counter with her back to the constable, as she had since Friday.

“You should have told me it existed,” said Demelza.

“I have said it was remiss.”

“It isn’t remiss. It’s the one thing in this whole business that points at a person and not at a piece of paper. Who taught whom. Who stood at that bench.” She did not raise her voice. Demelza never does. She lowers it, until you have to lean in, which is a great deal worse. “I rang the Inspector at six. I told him I’d seen that notebook on Friday, during the search. I said I’d had it in my hand and judged it to be old repairs.”

“Did you?”

“No. I didn’t open the paste cupboard. I thought a paste cupboard was where you kept paste.”

“It is.”

“Thank you, Mrs Pellow.” She looked at the ceiling for a moment, where the shop bell hung on its curl of brass. “So I told him I had read a book I’d never touched, and now it’s gone, and any minute he’s going to ask me about it in front of you, and I need you to nod.”

“I don’t lie to policemen.”

“You’ll be lying to a policeman, then, but only on my account.” She said it quite flatly. “If I say I never knew there was a cupboard, I’ve searched the scene of a murder for four hours and missed it. If I say I knew and thought nothing, I’m a fool who can be forgiven. Either way I’d rather be the fool. Nod.”

“Demelza—”

“He’s turning in at the bottom of the lane. I can hear that raincoat.”

You could, in fact. Detective Inspector Garrow wears his raincoat in all weathers, and it makes a noise on the steps like a man folding a tarpaulin. He came in under the bell with the sun full on his back, and stood looking about the shop as if he were trying to put a price on it.

“Mrs Pellow, dear,” he said. “A burglary.”

“Of a sort.”

“Of a sort. Yes. I’d say that’s about right.” He lowered himself on to the customers’ stool, which he had not been invited to do, and opened his notebook, which is bound in rexine. “A window opened with great delicacy. A cupboard opened without a mark on it. A till left with fourteen pounds sixty in it. And the single article taken is one that nobody in the kingdom would pay a penny for. Would you call that an ambitious thief, Constable?”

“No, sir.”

“A careful one?”

“Yes, sir.”

“A very careful one. Careful enough to leave a lady with a fright and a story.” He turned to me, kindly, which was worse. “Mrs Pellow. A woman on her own. A husband three years gone. A business that, shall we say, is not what it was. Then a dead man in the back room, and half the village not knowing where to look. I’ve seen it before, my dear. A little disturbance. Something to be fussed over, something that makes people come round.”

I let him finish. I find it saves time.

“Inspector, I have never in my life wished to be fussed over,” I said. “It’s such a messy thing to be given.”

“Quite.” He wrote something. “And the notebook, Constable. You saw it on Friday?”

“Yes, sir. A record of old jobs. I took it to be of no relevance to the scene.”

“Of no relevance.”

“At the time, sir.”

“Mrs Pellow?”

I nodded. I have been nodding all my life, at weddings and sermons and the accounts, and it came to me quite easily, which was the worst of it.

The door bell went again. Kit came in backwards with a box of linen thread in his arms, saw the raincoat, and said “Sorry” to the bell.

“Mr Pellow.” Garrow beamed. “Just the man. Saturday night.”

“I was at the Lantern. Sorry. From about nine, I think. Darts.”

“Darts.”

“A match. A friendly.”

“Against whom?”

“Porthcurno. Some of them.” Kit shifted the box. “Or, no, I think they didn’t come, I think it was the Seconds against, we played ourselves in the end.”

“And who won?”

Kit looked at the ceiling as if the result might be written there. “Sorry. I think I did. Or Eddy Tonkin.”

“And Mr Tonkin can tell me so?”

“He went home about ten to feed his ferrets.”

“And from ten to whenever you left?”

“I was at the board. Sorry. It was full, the Lantern, on a Saturday, they must have, somebody would have seen me.”

“Somebody will have seen you,” said Garrow, in the voice of a man who has never believed it. He closed his notebook. “I’ll ask. Don’t leave Trevenna, either of you. The lady of the house will understand that.” And he went out in a rustle of tarpaulin.

Demelza stood perfectly still with her eyes on the middle of the counter. Kit put the box down very slowly, as one puts down something that might go off. Neither of them looked at the other; the shop had more than enough to look at.

I went to church. I go to St Petroc’s at Christmas and for funerals and on the rare Sunday when I wish to see how a thing is done, and that Sunday I went because the Inspector had gone, and I wanted to watch what he looked at.

He was in the back pew with his notebook propped on the hymn board. St Petroc’s choir is nine people, of whom two are sure, and they sang “Eternal Father, strong to save” about a quarter-tone under the organ, with the particular courage of people who have buried a great many fishermen. The Reverend Nance preached on the lilies of the field and apologised twice during the sermon, once to the lilies. Morwenna was in her usual pew with her handbag on her lap. She did not turn round, but I saw her shoulders settle when I came in, as a hen’s do.

I took the back of the hymn sheet, and a stub of pencil I keep for measuring, and wrote three words down the margin: till, key, cat.

The till first. Fourteen pounds sixty and a button, and a bag of coppers I would not have left either. Whoever it was had gone through the shop in the dark, past the cash and the good shears and Ned’s brass dividers, which would fetch ten pounds in Truro, and gone straight to a small green book of other people’s names. A thief who cared about a notebook more than a till.

The key next. Demelza thought a key had been taken from the hook. But the key had been on my chest since Saturday morning, and it was on my chest now, under the hymn sheet and my good blouse; and the lock was as unmarked as the day Ned fitted it. So there was another. Ned had been a man who bought two of every tool, because the first always walked, and I had never in thirty years seen or looked for a second key to that cupboard. Somebody had one. Somebody had been given it, once, by a man who gave out keys the way other men give out advice, which is to say when he was sure of you.

And the cat. I had it from Demelza, in the small hours, that Quire hissed at her on Friday, bit her on Saturday, and had that afternoon taken a piece out of the Truro man’s cuff. I had seen her take the skin off a plumber. Whoever had carried Quire to that cupboard had done it without losing a drop of blood, and had then poured her milk, and laid a spoon.

Well. I could not make a person of that. I could make only an outline, like the pale shape on a pastedown where a print has hung and been taken down. Somebody who valued a list of names above a till, who held a key I did not know existed, who had been kind to a cat in the middle of a crime. I looked down the church for such a person, and found a great many cardigans.

By four the fair had been packed into its crates and the church hall smelled of damp card and old men’s tweed. I took my trestle apart, and Kit took the other end, and we carried it out to the van without a word. I could do nothing for him. I took myself down to the Lantern.

Jago was in the cellar, as usual, which means that his voice came up through the trap in the bar like a ship’s sounding. “Darts?” it said. “There’s always darts, Dot. Whether it was a match or a lot of men throwing things at a board on a Saturday, I couldn’t tell you.”

“Was Kit there?”

“Saw him at nine. Saw him at eleven with his coat on. Between, I’d a barrel to change and a flood to mop. I was down here, the best part of an hour.” The voice paused, and came up again with its owner under it, wiping his hands. “That’s the size of it. Take the Dutchman this, will you? He’s not eaten since breakfast. He’s in the back.”

He put a pasty on a plate, and the plate in my hand, and went down again.

Pieter was in the back room on his trunk. It stood by the dead dartboard with its straps done up and its brass corners polished, and he sat on it with his white jacket across his knees like a man on a railway platform in a country where the trains had been cancelled. His round glasses turned to me. He did not look surprised. I do not think anything surprises that man; he simply reorders.

“Mrs Pellow. You have come to arrest me?”

“I’ve brought you a pasty.”

“Ah.” He took it with two hands. “The Inspector says I stay. I say, I have a ferry on Tuesday. He says the ferry will wait. A ferry! It is not a man, a ferry, it does not wait.” He ate a mouthful. “I said the paper was probably Dutch. Probably! In my trade this is a word you say like bless you. Now I am the man who knows about Dutch paper. It is a sad thing, I tell you, to be honest in a small place.”

“Are you?”

He looked at me over the glasses, and I had the impression of a man weighing me, leaf by leaf, for chain lines. “I am what is usual in my trade, Mrs Pellow. I buy from people. I do not ask what is in the attic. Everyone in my trade is exactly this honest.”

“And what’s usual in this village is saying nothing.”

“Yes! It is extraordinary. I ask a question and I am told, that’s the size of it, or proper job, or dreckly. I do not know what any of these mean. I ask the landlord, who says, that’s the size of it.”

“That’s the size of it,” I said, and left him with his pasty and his strapped trunk, and he laughed, a single bark, the first sound of the sort I had heard from him.

It was dusk when I put the rubbish out. I pulled the dustbin from its place by the yard wall to empty the bucket, and behind it on the flags, in the dust, lay a flat tin with its lid rolled back on the key like a snail. It had been licked so clean it shone. Gulls make a mess of a tin; they leave it ruined and glittering on a roof. This had been done as a cat does it, patiently, to the corners.

I picked it up. I turned it over and read the Portuguese on the bottom. Then I stood a moment with it in my hand and an idea going round in me that would not come to a stop, like a coin on a table. I could not have said what it was. I put the tin in the bin, and the lid on the bin, and by the time I reached the shop door the thing had come out again like a splinter.

I sat down in the shop chair to take off my shoes. I intended to sit for the length of a boot-lace. The next I knew the lamp was lit and the window was black, and something heavy and warm and quietly vibrating lay across my knees: Quire, who has sat on my lap on perhaps six occasions, all of them when I held a sardine. She had her eyes shut. Her torn ear was twitching.

“You snore,” said Demelza.

She sat on the customers’ stool, where Garrow had sat, with her helmet in her lap and her notebook closed on the elastic band. I do not know how long she had been there. I do not think she did either.

“I’ll tell you what I’ve not told the Inspector,” she said, “because I don’t know yet what it is. If you find something, you tell me first. Not Garrow. Not Kit. Me.”

“That’s a great deal to ask.”

“I know.” She got up and put the helmet on, and pulled the strap with two fingers, which is how she shows she has stopped being a person and become the force. “I’ll ask it anyway.”

I thought of the green notebook, and the other key, and the cake, and Quire’s pulse going on my knee like a small engine. I have never promised anything lightly in my life.

“I promise,” I said.

chapters.title: Ash in the Stove
chapters.html:
Nobody rakes out a stove in July, which is why I did.

The press room had been given back to me on Saturday and taken away again on Sunday, and on Monday morning at half past seven it was mine once more, with a board nailed over the broken sash and a fine grey powder over everything the Truro man had thought worth touching. He had been thorough with the stove. The black iron lid wore a coat of fingerprint dust like mildew on a loaf, and the fire door, the damper and the little brass knob of the oven were furred with it. I could not lay paste on a bench that had that in the room. I put on Ned’s old gardening gloves, filled a bucket in the yard, and started at the top.

It is a squat, cross-tempered stove, older than I am, with a rocking grate and an ash pan the size of a bread tin, and I had lit it last on Wednesday for the paste and let it die by supper. That is the thing I kept coming back to as I scrubbed. On Friday morning, when I put my palm flat on the lid beside a dead man, the iron had been warm. A stove that has gone out on Wednesday night does not hold its heat till Friday. It had been fed since, and fed late, and nobody had said so; and nobody had said so because it was July, and nobody lights a stove in July, and a policeman who sees cold grey ash in a firebox in a summer month looks at it exactly as long as he looks at the weather.

Looking at it myself, I realised, I had not seen it either. I had been looking at the floor.

The kindling box beside the stove, a fish crate of split pine, was down by a good double handful. If you had asked me on Thursday I should not have been able to tell you how many sticks were in it. But I had filled it myself on Wednesday, and I knew the look of a full box, and this was not one.

I opened the fire door and the smell came out to meet me: cold ash, flat and grey and slightly sweet, the smell of the morning after bonfire night, quite wrong in a room with the sun coming down through the skylight and a bumblebee working at the glass. I put the shovel in. The ash was fine as flour and white as a miller’s hat. I shook the grate, and the rest of it dropped, and I drew out the pan and carried it into the yard and set it on a sheet of newspaper, and went in for the sieve from the shop.

A spoonful at a time I sieved it, like a woman making a very poor cake. There were clinkers the size of walnuts. There were the pale curls of burnt kindling, and a black shred of something that had been cloth. And on the third pass, when the pan was nearly bare, I looked into the dark of the firebox with the torch, down past the grate bars to the iron floor where the draught pulls things, and something lay curled there like a dead leaf.

Touching it was out of the question. I went to the shop, and came back with a sheet of blotting paper, and slid it under the thing as Ned taught me to lift a dried flower, an inch at a time, holding my breath so as not to blow it to pieces.

It was a corner of paper about the size of a playing card. It had been laid paper once, buff coloured, with the faint ribbed pattern you can see against the light; the burn had taken the rest of it and left this, black and brittle, the edges rolled and glittering. On the back clung grey fibres, and I knew them at once. They came off a board. This had been pasted down to the inside of a cover.

On the flat of my two hands I carried it to the bench. I clamped the lamp, and swung its arm down, and turned the shade until the light came in low across the char instead of down on it, a trick I use for reading the ghosts of old blind-tooling on a leather spine. And the black woke, and showed me silver.

Pencil. A soft one, a 2B, in a small upright hand with the sevens crossed in the continental way. Graphite is only carbon, but it holds a polish that soot has not, and under that slanting light the lines stood up off the burn like writing in frost. There were two of them, and the second was cut off by the char in the middle of a word.

K. – cat. 114 –

And lower down, further in:

Mrs P. in the mor

I sat down on the cutting-board stool. I know that hand. I have seen it on every invoice and every note that ever came down Fish Cellar Lane from Aubrey Trevithick, signed yrs, A.T., with a full stop after each initial as if the letters might otherwise run off. Booksellers pencil their notes on the endpaper; they always have. A man holds a book as the buyer, and he writes down what he finds, small and light so that it can be rubbed out. He had written on the endpapers of the Carne Rutter while he sat at my bench on Thursday night with his cane across his knee, and someone had torn those endpapers out and burned them in my stove.

The bumblebee banged at the glass for a while, and I let it.

Mrs P. in the mor. It did not take a binder to finish the word. He had said it to me himself, at a quarter to six on Thursday, in the shop doorway with his hat on, while I was handing him a brass key on a green wool loop and wanting only to be rid of him. Tomorrow I shall have something to say to you, Mrs Pellow. I would rather be accurate than prompt. And I had said something about the buns. I had come at ten to seven, on Friday, with the buns in a paper bag and a pot of paste to set, as I had told him I would. And he had been there, or had been there for eight hours, with the book open on the bench and his notes ready.

Mrs P. in the morning. I was Mrs P. He had written it down so as not to forget, and then he had waited.

I make a poor detective and a worse liar, but I can reason from a bench. Whoever burned those pages had not burned the book. It lay on the bench on Friday morning with its thread hanging out of it like roots, and it was worth, as Kit had told Loveday, a figure with a comma in it. A stolen book is money; a pencilled note is a rope. Anyone with a head would burn the rope and keep the cash. They had taken the notes out of the covers and fed them to my stove and left the rutter to whoever came next, and what that told me, sitting on the stool with the light on the scrap, was that the person who did it had cared about being named a good deal more than about being rich.

Nothing about that pleased me. It made them neater than a thief. It also made them somebody who had known what to look for, which was a thing Aubrey had written on a page of a book that only Aubrey, and perhaps Kit, had been reading.

I turned the lamp a little. K. A letter with a full stop; a man’s initial or a woman’s. Cat. 114 was a number I knew. Kit had given Loveday his typed valuation on the Friday of the fair, a good clean list of her library, ending at lot 114, the Carne Rutter, as far as the Carne and not one inch past it. K. for Kit. Kit’s catalogue. I told myself that was all it was, a clerk’s reference. A man pencils the cataloguer’s number beside his note about a book. It is what you do.

Several times I told myself so, and each time it sounded more like a thing one tells oneself.

Well. I had promised. I got up, and went into the shop, and rang the police house.

Demelza came in eight minutes, in uniform, her plait pinned up under her helmet, and I took her through to the bench without a word and swung the lamp. She bent over the blotter with her hands behind her back. I watched her read it. I saw her get to the K and I saw her go still, the way Quire does at a sound in the wall.

“Kit,” she said. “Or Kitto.”

“It’s Kit’s catalogue number. He numbered the Carne lot one-fourteen. It’s the number on the list.”

“It’s a K and a number, and one of the two Ks in this village is me.” She said it quite pleasantly. “He didn’t know me from a hole in the road, Mr Trevithick. But he might have, by the end of the week.” She straightened. “And the other one?”

“Mrs Pellow. In the morning. He told me he’d have something to say on Friday. I came at ten to seven.”

She did not answer that. She took out her notebook, took off the elastic band and put it on again, and put the notebook away without writing in it. In the quiet I could hear the bumblebee still working at the skylight.

“I ought to bag that,” she said. “I ought to put it in a bag with a label and take it to Truro and give it to Inspector Garrow, and by lunchtime he’d have Kit in the back of a car.”

“On a pencilled K.”

“On a pencilled K, a hammer from Ned’s nail, a man who was at the Bindery twice that week and a cataloguer’s name on the thing that was stolen.” She pushed her helmet back an inch. “I’d like a day. I’d like to find out who K. is before somebody else decides. It stays here. In your hands, in whatever you’ve got. I’ll come with a bag when I know what I’m going to say and to whom.”

“That isn’t procedure.”

“No. It’s Monday.”

The shop bell rang.

I had the blotter folded into my apron pocket before I knew I had moved. Kit stood in the doorway between the shop and the press room with a pint of milk in each hand, as he does every morning, because I will not drink tea made with milk that has stood. He looked at the uniform, then at a spot politely beside it.

“Sorry. Morning.”

“Mr Pellow.”

“It’s Kit.” He said it to the milk. “It was Kit, anyway. When I last, sorry.”

“I’m on duty.”

“I know. I only wanted to say. About Saturday. The darts. I was at the board, sorry, I was, and I know it’s not, it isn’t much of, I didn’t mean to put you in the middle.”

“You were at the board,” said Demelza, “with a man and his ferrets.”

“Sorry.”

“That’s the thing, isn’t it.” Her voice had not risen. It had gone small and level and extremely clear. “I told you in March last year that I’d been passed over for sergeant, and you said sorry. As if you’d done it.”

“I wished I had, so there’d be somebody to shout at.”

“I didn’t want somebody to shout at. I wanted you to shout. I wanted a plate thrown.”

“Not at my paste pots,” I said, from the corner.

Neither looked at me. Kit said, very low, “You didn’t ask me to stay. You said you were going to Plymouth for a course and I said, sorry, I said I thought.”

“You thought. You think a lot, Kit. You stand there thinking in a pair of boots.” She had her helmet strap in two fingers and she was pulling it so hard it must have hurt. “Fourteen months, and the first word you have for me in a doorway is sorry. It’s a weather report. It isn’t an answer.”

There was a silence in which nobody breathed in the right order.

“Don’t be kind to me,” Demelza said. “Anyone but you. I can’t do the job if you’re kind.”

She went out past him, not touching, and the bell took the whole quarrel and shook it out into the lane. Kit stood with the milk in his hands. After a while he said “Sorry,” to nobody, and took both bottles into the shop, and I heard him fill the kettle, carefully, like a man with a limb in plaster.

When the kettle began to sing I took the blotter out of my pocket. I stood at the shelf where Ned’s things stay, and took down his tin of bone folders, a toffee tin with the Silver Jubilee on the lid, gone brown at the corners, in which his tools still lie in the order he left them: the long folder with the chipped tip, the little one for the hollows, the curved one that he said was a whale’s rib and I always knew was a shin of beef. I eased the scrap into the cloth lining and set the lid on the top. It closed with a sound like a held breath.

In three years I do not think I had said a word aloud to the empty room. I said it to the tin, and the stove, and the board over the window, and the silver on the black that was no longer there to be seen.

“He was waiting for me.”

chapters.title: Smelled Like Church
chapters.html:
The third step of the net-loft stair has creaked under every foot since 1962, and at ten past five on Monday morning it had creaked under one I could not account for.

I heard it from my bed, twenty yards up the lane, with the window open and the harbour as quiet as it ever gets: a short dry complaint, a long pause, then a second one, softer, as of someone going up a ladder in her stockinged feet. It might have been a gull. A gull can make a surprising noise on slate. But I had lain awake four nights listening to that lane and I knew what a gull sounds like on a roof, and this was not one.

So at half past two that afternoon, with the stove clean and the Silver Jubilee tin shut on its secret, I put the last of Saturday’s saffron buns in a paper bag, for no reason I could have defended, and climbed the steps.

There are eleven of them, granite, up the outside wall to a door under the eaves, with an iron rail that Ned painted black every Easter and that I have not painted since. The padlock hung open on its staple. It has not truly locked since the winter of 1979, when the screws gave up the wood, and Ned used to say it was there to be a conscience. I pushed the door with the flat of my hand and went in.

The net loft runs the length of the building under the slates, one long room with a floor of broad boards worn silver, and from the rafters three seine nets still hang as they have hung since before the pilchards went: tarred and stiff with salt, grey as old sails that have forgotten the wind. Nobody has fished with them since 1953. I keep the stock I cannot sell up here, broken boards and spoiled paper and a press with a cracked screw, and the smell is tar and hemp and slate and ancient fish, which is the smell of the whole village if you take the people out of it.

Under the far gable, beneath the little window that looks down the lane, somebody had made a bed.

It was a sleeping bag, army green, zipped to the chin of nobody, with a folded anorak for a pillow. Beside it stood a milk crate holding six library books stamped with Truro’s blue date, a jam jar of pencils, and a rubber torch of the square-headed sort that takes a battery the size of a brick. I looked for a candle. A candle in a loft hung with tarred twine is the kind of thing that gets onto the front of the Cornishman, and I was glad to find none. Four exercise books were stacked on the crate, edges squared, blue covers, with the Truro school crest on the front.

I opened the top one. I am not proud of that.

It was full of spines. Page after page of them, drawn in biro on the feint-ruled paper, each in its own tall oblong: spines with raised bands, spines with gilt panels worked up in the fine crosshatch of a girl who has measured how a real gilt line catches the light, spines with the tails of the headbands curled just so. She had given them titles. The Tides of Trevenna, Vol. III. A Short History of Mackerel. Letters from a Pilot’s Widow. There were forty to a page, and the books on the shelves of the Bindery have never looked as good. Near the back there was a full-page drawing, in blue, of a sewing frame, upright, with the cords strung and the tapes laid and the needle caught in the thread, and notes down the margin in brackets, in a hand much better than mine. (tapes: five, linen.) (kettle stitch, head and tail.) (this is the bit that matters).

“Right,” said a voice behind me. “So.”

I did not jump. I would like that recorded. I closed the exercise book and put it back on its stack, squared, as she had left it, and turned round.

She stood at the head of the stairs with her hands behind her back and her jaw stuck out. The bleached stripe had fallen across her left eye, the way a flag drops in no wind. I had not heard the third step. I realised that she had stepped over it.

“It’s private,” said Tamsin Bray. “Up here.”

“The loft belongs to the Bindery. Which on a bad month is me.”

“I haven’t broken anything.”

“I never said you had.”

“You’ve got a face on.”

“It’s the only one I have.”

She sulked as other people paint: with depth, in layers, over several sessions. She sat on the milk crate with her knees drawn up and her chin on them, and said nothing for a minute and a half, and then said “Right,” and nothing again. I took the bun out of its bag, to give my hands something to do. Her eyes went to it as a cat’s go to a mouse that has dared to move.

“That’s two days old.”

“I don’t mind.”

I held it out. She took it and ate it with the concentration of a communicant, and half-way through, in a different voice, she said, “Mum doesn’t know.”

“About the loft.”

“I’ve been up here since the exams. There’s five of us in two rooms, and Terry’s on lates, and the dog sleeps on my feet.” She brushed crumbs off her knees. “Up here it’s quiet. Nobody wants anything. You can see the whole lane from that window, and your door, and the corner of the press room.” She looked at the little square of glass as at an old friend. “Nothing happens in Trevenna, so you have to watch it quite hard.”

I let that one stand. I have been watched hard in my time and I know what it is worth.

“Thursday,” I said.

She did not pretend. I will give her that. A grown woman would have had a dozen expressions to choose from, and she used none of them. “I was up here,” she said. “I’d got my torch and a book. I didn’t see anything till about half past nine.”

“Tell me what you saw.”

“Right.” She put the last of the bun in her mouth, swallowed, and wiped her hand on her jumper, the great grey one that has been through two brothers. “Half past nine, the Reverend. Mr Nance. In his bicycle clips. He’d left the bike at the bottom, I saw him push it, and he came up and knocked, and Mr Trevithick opened the door, and the Reverend started on at him. I couldn’t hear all of it. Something about the roof. And, ‘you know what it’s worth, Aubrey.’”

“And what did Aubrey say?”

“He said, ‘Not tonight, Arthur.’ Quite kind. Then he shut the door.” She frowned. “Very quietly. Like when you shut a door on a baby. And the Reverend stood there and said sorry to it.”

“He would.”

“Then he went down the lane pushing the bike, and he was coughing.” She counted on her fingers, which were inky to the second knuckle. “Five past ten, the lady with the nose stud. The one in the leather. The daughter. She didn’t knock, she banged. She was in there fifteen minutes. I couldn’t hear the words but I could hear the shape of it, and the shape was, shouting, and then not shouting, and then quite a lot of nothing.”

“And she left?”

“Twenty past. I’ve got a watch, it was Dad’s.” She showed me: a man’s steel wristwatch on a strap punched with new holes. “She came out with her face all, like this.” She dragged the heel of her hand across both eyes. “And then she stood in the lane and kicked the wall. Twice. I think she hurt her foot.”

I thought of Imogen Mayne on Saturday night, counting a hundred and thirty-five pounds for an otter with a cigarette going, and saying well, that’s that, then, in a voice that was not about the money, and found I had stopped being able to dislike her.

“And after that?”

“After that nobody for ten minutes. Then half past ten.” Tamsin pulled her knees in. “A lady came up from the bottom of the lane. In a mac, the pale sort with a belt, and the hood up. Not a scarf, an actual hood. She’d a big bag on her arm. She didn’t knock. She put her hand flat on the door, like that, and it went in.”

“It wasn’t locked.”

“It must have been on the latch. He’d have been expecting her.”

I did not ask her how she knew he was expecting anyone. “Who was she?”

“I couldn’t see. It was from above, and she had her head down, and everyone’s short from above.” She considered. “Not tall. Not fat. She walked like somebody carrying something that mustn’t spill.”

“Is that all?”

“No.” She hesitated, and for the first time looked like what she was, which is a girl of sixteen who has been on her own in a loft with a very bad piece of knowledge for four days. “I had the window open for the air. She went right under it, to the door. And I smelled her.”

“Smelled her.”

“Like church,” said Tamsin. “Polish and candles. Like the vestry on a Tuesday when Mum goes in to do the brass.”

I stood in a room of tarred nets with the afternoon coming in grey through the glass and understood that I was being given something very much heavier than a bun.

Church. In Trevenna, church is a quarter of the population by Sunday and a tenth by weekday, and every woman in that tenth had done the brass or the flowers or the linen at one time or another, and every man had been in the vestry to sign something. The Reverend Nance himself smells of his own vestry: Brasso and hymn-book dust and mouse and cough drop. But Nance had been at the door at half past nine and gone home down the hill wheezing, and Tamsin was clear it had been a woman, by the walk. I own a mac the colour of porridge. So does every woman I know, and a hood, and a bag on her arm. A woman in a mac with the hood up is the most invisible article in the English countryside; I have been that article myself for thirty years, and not on Thursday only. If I had gone up that lane to commit a crime I could not have chosen better.

“Did you see her come out?”

“No. I got cold. I went down in the bag.” She did not meet my eye. “I woke up when the church clock did twelve and there wasn’t anybody.”

“And me.”

I had not meant to say it. It came out like a tooth.

Tamsin looked at the floor. “You went by about eleven,” she said. “You were humming. You looked at the shop window and the front door, and you didn’t look in at the press room. The light was off by then.”

“Yes,” I said. I had told nobody that. I had told it, in the end, to a girl in a sleeping bag. “No. I didn’t.”

“I’m not going to say,” said Tamsin. “If you don’t tell Mum.”

I sat down on a tea chest. For a moment neither of us said anything. The torch lay on the crate with its square head turned up at the slates, and I reached across and switched it on, to be doing something, and the beam went up through the hanging nets and laid a great scale-pattern of knots and shadows on the underside of the roof, like the belly of a fish. In the middle of it the blue exercise book on the stack showed up, with the sewing frame drawn on the open back page. Someone had written under it: (Ned’s? ask).

“You are a witness,” I said. “A good one. You have the times and the smell and a direction of travel. You must tell Constable Kitto.”

“No.”

“Tamsin.”

“No, they tell your mum. They have to. It’s the law.” She said it with the heartbreaking logic of the sixteen-year-old. “And Mum’ll say I’ve been sleeping out with all sorts, and she’ll send me to Auntie Jean’s in Redruth. Auntie Jean’s got a launderette and a dog that hates me. I’d rather be stabbed.”

“That is not a remark you should make in this particular building.”

“I’d rather,” she said stubbornly, “be told off by Mr Nance.” She pushed her hair out of her eye. “If you tell, I’ll say I never. I’ll say I made it up for a laugh.”

“You would not.”

“I would. I’m good at it. Ask Mr Pascoe.”

I looked at her, at the jam jar of pencils and the library books and the careful, fierce, sixteen-year-old face, and I saw that the child would do it. She would deny every word, and a poor witness is no use to anyone. I know about stubbornness. I have kept the Bindery open on the strength of it.

“Very well,” I said. “A bargain. I will speak to your mother myself. Before anyone else does. I will tell her something true.”

“What true?”

“I’ll think of it on the way.”

“That’s what I’m scared of.” But she let out a breath that was almost a laugh. “And you won’t tell the constable?”

“I will tell her what I must when I must, and I shall do it so that your name is on the last line of the page and not the first.” I rose, because my knees were beginning to say things. “You are going to be sensible, in the meantime. No candles. No stairs in the dark; the third step is bad.”

“I know. I step over it.”

“I noticed.”

At the door I turned. She had not moved from the crate. She was sitting very upright, with the grey jumper pulled over her knees, and the torch-light was in her face, and for once she did not seem to have anything ready.

“Mrs Pellow.” It came out quickly, as if she had been carrying it all afternoon. “Can I watch you do corners next?”

I opened my mouth to say something about the Education Authority. What I said was, “Yes.”

I had said it before I had thought, which is not a thing I do. I went down the eleven steps in the grey light with the rail wet under my hand, and I did not step on the third.

chapters.title: Tea at Penhallow Court
chapters.html:
“You’ll want your mac,” said Morwenna, “and a scarf. Don’t look at me like that. It’s rain.”

She stood on my step at two o’clock on Tuesday with water running off the brim of her plastic rain-bonnet, a tin under one arm and her handbag on the other, in which there was a second tin, because there always is. I have never known Morwenna Hext go anywhere without cake in some form. She would take shortbread to a lifeboat launch.

“Loveday asked me to tea,” I said. “I didn’t ask for an escort.”

“Loveday asked you to tea, and I go up on Tuesdays regardless, so you can walk with me and save the Court the sight of a woman coming through the shrubbery like a drowned cat. And not another word, Dot. Mind the step.”

So we went up the hill together in the rain, two women in macs and headscarves, with our heads down and our shoulders up: the pale kind, with a belt, that every woman in Cornwall owns and none of us remembers buying. A man coming down the lane with a sack on his back looked at us without seeing us and touched his cap to the air between. Nobody on that hill could have told us from any other two. I have found it restful, on the whole, over the years, and that afternoon for no reason I disliked it.

The track runs up past the church and the last of the cottages, between walls so thick with fuchsia and montbretia that they look to be holding up the sky, and on to the long hill where the Court sits with its back to the sea. It is a fifteen-minute walk. With Morwenna’s knees it is twenty-five, and I did not mind that either. She told me about Ronald as she climbed. He had known her on Sunday. He had looked up from his chair in the day room at Gwithian House, and said, “Morwenna, who’s died?” and she had said, “Nobody, my handsome,” and he had looked so cross.

“On a good day he asks who’s died,” she said. “On a bad one he asks who I am, and I tell him I’m the lady with the cake, and he’s very polite.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be. He was never a man for long speeches.” She got a hand on a gatepost and heaved. “And you, Dot? I’ve seen how you look. Garrow’s been at you.”

“He thinks I broke into my own shop for the sympathy.”

“You would sooner be flogged.”

“I would.”

“Well, you’ve had cake instead, and I hope you ate it.”

“I ate it standing up. It was very good.” I found, to my irritation, that my voice was not quite level. “It was kind, Morwenna.”

“It was flour,” said Morwenna, and went on up the hill ahead of me, small and round and entirely cheerful, with the rain bouncing off her bonnet.

Penhallow Court was built when granite was cheaper than glass and has been paying for it since. It is a long grey house the colour of a tooth, with chimneys at the corners and gutters in which, in July, buddleia stands six feet high. Morwenna always goes in by the back, through the boot room, as family do, and I followed her into a stone passage that smelled of wet dog and floor polish.

Along one wall ran a row of pegs hung with macs, the pale kind, six of them, the colour of dishwater, and I added mine to the row with the sensation of joining a congregation. On a spread of newspaper by the door stood a pair of black rubber sea-boots, enormous, with their tops turned down, a rim of dried salt along the welts, and a white 12 painted on each heel. I noticed them as one notices a stranger’s umbrella.

“The gardener’s,” said Loveday Penhallow.

She had come up the passage behind us without a sound, in gumboots under a skirt of tweed so old it had turned green, with her blackthorn stick in one beautiful long hand and her hearing aid round her neck in its beige box on a cord. As she turned her head, the thing gave a thin shriek of feedback.

“I wasn’t going to ask,” I said.

“You were going to ask.” The aid whistled again, higher. “Don’t gawp, Pellow. Come in out of the wet. Morwenna, my dear, I’ve a headache and a hip and I’ve had to be civil to a solicitor, so you may tell me what the Institute wants and I shall give it to you.”

It is a peculiar thing about Loveday’s hearing aid that it whistles whenever anybody lies. I have never established the mechanism; I do not believe the makers know it. But in eleven years of taking tea at the Court I have never known it wrong, and it has led, in a house where a good many people say a good many things, to a rather noisy life.

At the far end of the passage a woman in a pinafore was doing the tiles with a mop. She did not look up. As we passed, the mop stopped, not for long, about as long as it takes to decide that a thing is not your business, and then went on. Sheila Bray has a face like a closed shop and the hands of a docker, and she is the only person in that house who has never once been thanked.

The library at Penhallow Court is forty feet long and has been drowning since the Coronation.

There is a bucket under every third shelf. I counted eleven, as the rain found its way through the plaster of the ceiling and let itself down in slow bright beads, and each bucket had its own pitch, from a bright tink to a deep mournful plonk, so that the whole room played a tune. It was a very slow tune with no end to it. Round the walls at the height of my knee ran a line of brown, a tide-mark, where the damp had risen from the floor, thought better of it and turned back. The books above the line were vellum and calf and good green morocco gone grey with age; the books below it were mostly a rumour.

And everywhere there were gaps. Little pink slips of Kit’s stood up like flags between the volumes, each with its number in his careful hand, and in places there was no book at all, but a clean oblong on the shelf and a cleaner one on the wall behind it, where something had stood since 1700 and had gone, in a cardboard box, to Truro, to be valued. It looked like a mouth that has lost its teeth and is trying not to smile.

“That is Sir Ambrose,” said Loveday, from her chair, “who held the Court for the Crown until he ran out of beer. And that is Captain Hannibal, who lost the silver to a Spaniard at cards in 1703. And that, over the door, is Honor Penhallow, who ran the contraband from Sennen to Mount’s Bay for thirty years and was never once found out. And that is my father, who lost the rest.” She rapped her stick on the boards. “Eleven generations on this hill, Pellow. Seven of them could read.”

The whistle that followed this was long and very shrill. Morwenna, setting out cups, did not even look round.

Sheila Bray brought the tea, put the tray on the table without a word, and went out without one. Loveday looked at Morwenna, who looked at the pot.

“Be mother.”

Morwenna took the big Georgian teapot, which was silver and had been dented by a Penhallow, in her left hand, and filled my cup with a long easy turn of the wrist that I remember thinking rather beautiful. Then she glanced down, and paused, and changed the pot into her right hand, and filled Loveday’s with the slight stiffness of a woman putting on her good gloves. Neither of them remarked on it. I did not, either. People pour as they please.

“Now,” said Loveday. “You have been to see me, and you have not told me what you have found. I asked you on Friday. What have you found?”

“I’ve found out how little I know.”

“Hm. That’s more than the Inspector.” She turned her good ear to me. “He came on Saturday. He said the Carne has been interfered with. I told him that was what the vicar said about the choir boys in 1951.”

“Loveday,” said Morwenna.

“Well, it was.” She sat back. “You needn’t tell me, Pellow. I saw his face. When you know, you’ll tell me, and I’ll know what to do about it, and we’ll say no more.” She looked at the wall where the ghost of a shelf-gap began, and her hand tightened on the stick. “Do you know the story of it?”

“Everyone knows the story of it.”

“Nobody knows the story of it. They know a pilot’s book.” She nodded to Morwenna. “Tell her.”

“It’s yours to tell, my dear.”

“Then I shall. November 1631.” Loveday lifted her chin and her voice dropped half an octave, into the register that I imagine her family reserved for the telling of this sort of thing. “A gale from the south-west, three days of it, and a ketch out of Bideford, the Hopewell, with a cargo of Spanish wine and a captain who did not know the coast. A pilot went out to her from Sennen in his own boat in the dark. Jory Carne. Forty years old, and a wife in the cove, and the finest pilot between the Lizard and the Bristol Channel. He took the Hopewell in towards the Longships to bring her round the Land’s End, and she struck.”

The rain went tink, tink, plonk.

“The Longships is a reef, a mile off the Land’s End. They say a man can drown there with his dinner in sight. Carne drowned. So did the captain, and so did the wine. Three days afterwards the sea gave back the pilot. He had a pouch of oiled wool strapped inside his shirt, and in the pouch, dry, because he had greased the covers with tallow, was his book.” She said the next as if reciting a lesson learned at a knee. “From Cape Cornwall to the Longships, two leagues and a half, keeping the Brisons well open to the west. My father made me learn the first line when I was six. The widow sold it to Sir Ambrose for a winter’s coal and a pair of boots. The Penhallows have kept it from that day to this.”

She looked at me. “I should like to know who has had their hands on it.”

“Who has handled it, since Christmas?” I asked. “Apart from Aubrey.”

“The boy with the clipboard, Kit. A man from the record office who took photographs and left a bill. Aubrey himself, three times. Sheila Bray dusts the shelves but I’ve told her she is not to touch that one, and she hasn’t, she’s not that sort.” The aid whistled, a small one. Loveday ignored it. “And Morwenna.”

“I read to her,” said Morwenna. “Tuesdays. Eleven years. Don’t I, Loveday? I’ve read you the whole of Gibbon twice, and Trollope, and half the Bible, and the minutes of the Rural District Council.”

“She is the only one of you I trust with the shelves.” Loveday jabbed her stick towards the third bay. “Fetch Pellow the Hakluyt. The one with the map. Mind the bucket.”

I watched her go. I would like to say I watched for any reason at all, but it was a binder’s habit and nothing else. Morwenna crossed the library, stepped round the bucket, and stopped at the shelf. She did what nine readers in ten do not. She pushed the neighbouring books back on either side, took the spine in the middle of her palm, and eased the volume out without once hooking a finger over the head-cap, which is how every spine in England gets its first wound. She carried it to the table on both hands, laid it on the cushion Loveday keeps for the purpose, and opened it with a hand under each board, so that the joints took no strain at all.

It was a first edition of Hakluyt, in limp vellum, the size of a paving slab. I have held perhaps two books of that age in my life. She laid it before me as one sets a plate before a guest, and stood back with her hands folded, and said, “Mind the map. It’s a fold-out.”

Well, I thought. Eleven years of Tuesdays. A woman picks up good habits from a shelf the way she picks up burrs from a hedge.

I asked for the lavatory at ten to four, and was sent down the back passage, past the boot room, and found it exactly where the Penhallows have kept it since the Restoration, behind a door with a china handle.

Sheila Bray was in the passage with her mop and her bucket. She stood up straight when she saw me, as if I might be an inspector.

“Mrs Bray. A word about Tamsin.”

The mop stopped. “She’s been up the Bindery, I hear.”

“She has been sleeping at the Bindery,” I said. “In the net loft, since the middle of June.”

“In that army bag from the Co-op.” Sheila Bray took the mop out of the bucket, wrung it with two quick turns, and put it back. “I’m not daft, Mrs Pellow. I wash her jumpers. They smell of tar and cat.”

“You never said.”

“She never said. If I’d said, she’d have stopped, and gone somewhere I couldn’t see.” She looked at me then, a flat grey look that went all the way through. “She has hands, that girl, and nothing to do with them. Will you have her?”

“I can’t pay her.”

“She’s not asking to be paid. She’s asking for a bench. I can’t give her one. I’ve five in two rooms and a dog.”

“Then she may come in the daytime, and say she’s working for me. It’s no more than she’s been doing.”

“And nights?”

“The stairs are bad.”

“They’re not so bad she can’t step over the third,” said Sheila Bray. “Don’t tell her I know. She’d stop.” The mop went round a tile. “And Mrs Pellow. She’s a good girl. She’s not a sneak. If she’s seen anything she shouldn’t, it’ll be because the thing was there to be seen.”

I looked at her. She looked at the floor. In a village you learn that a woman who has been told nothing for twenty years has learned to say a good deal in very few words, and that the polite response to these is to hear them as spoken.

The size-twelve boots stood on their newspaper by the door as I went back. I did not ask about them. It seemed to me that the mop had already answered that.

When I returned to the library Morwenna had the Hakluyt back on its shelf, and Loveday had her chin on her stick, and the buckets were still keeping time.

“We have settled the tent,” said Loveday. “The Institute may have my long tables and the big urn for the regatta, and a boy to carry them, and the proceeds to the lifeboat. I should like it recorded that I gave in handsomely.” She reached for her hearing aid and settled it. “And Pellow. If that raincoat of a man should ask you, as he asks everything, Morwenna sat up with me until midnight last Thursday. The night it happened. We played piquet.”

“Nobody has asked me.”

“They will.”

“She cheats, you know,” said Morwenna, brightly, picking up her tin. “She counts her tricks twice.”

“I do not.”

The aid gave a squeal that set the buckets rocking. Loveday closed her hand over it. Morwenna laughed, and I laughed, because it is impossible not to when a woman of seventy-four is being shrieked at by her own ear, and the laugh went round the library and was lost among the shelf-gaps.

I took it, I think, as one takes a stranger’s umbrella: as something offered, which I had no particular reason to refuse.

We said our goodbyes in the passage. Loveday did not come to the door. Sheila Bray opened it, and stood aside, and did not look at me, and the rain came in. It was four by my watch as I pulled on my mac among the others. Behind us, in the hall, the grandfather clock cleared its throat, thought about it, and struck four, eleven minutes late, and nobody in the house seemed to mind.

chapters.title: The Strip Light
chapters.html:
“Triangles,” said Mrs Chegwidden, “are not a matter of opinion.”

She held up a template cut from a cornflake packet. It was a long thin triangle with a base of nine inches and a height of eleven, and she held it at arm’s length as a priest holds up the Host. Across the trestle from her, Miss Hocking, who taught arithmetic at Truro for thirty-one years and has never forgiven the pupils, held up a second one, which was equal on all three sides.

“Bunting is equilateral,” said Miss Hocking, “by nature.”

“Bunting is whatever shape is left of the flag,” said Mrs Bolitho, in her raspberry hat, which she had not taken off since the otter. “Nobody ever cut a flag for the pleasure of the geometry.”

“That is a very common attitude, Ada, and a very sad one.”

It was ten past seven on Tuesday evening in the Women’s Institute hall, which is a green tin hut on Net Loft Row with a stove-pipe, a stage the size of a double bed and a hatch through which, for sixty years, the Institute has handed one another cake. Eight women sat round a pair of trestles under a single strip light that flickered whenever the urn came on. Three sewing machines stood among us: Mrs Rosevear’s mother’s treadle, a school electric that ran at two speeds, stop and flee, and a hand-cranked affair of Miss Hocking’s that she said had come to her from a Dutch sea-captain and I believed it had come from a bomb-site. Round our feet, in drifts, lay the sort of red and white and blue and yellow scraps that might in a better world have been somebody’s best flags.

I was the eighth woman. I should like it known that I had not wanted to be. Morwenna had caught me on the way down from the Court and said that bunting at seven was not a request, that the Institute had eight pairs of hands and four of them could not hem, and that I had a face on me that wanted company. I had said I would come if I could sit near the door. She had said I could sit where I liked, so long as it was in the hall.

“It was not,” said Mrs Rosevear, from the treadle, with the brimming eyes of a woman who has been rehearsing a grievance since Sunday, “from Pengelly’s.”

“Doris,” said Morwenna.

“It was a family recipe. It was my mother’s.”

“Doris, my handsome. There was a doily in your bin with Pengelly’s of Truro stamped on it in blue.”

“That might have been anybody’s bin.”

“It was in your bin, dear, in the Chapel Anniversary Tea, with your name on the entry, and it won.” Morwenna did not raise her voice; she doesn’t. She spoke as to a child who has fallen off a wall, and put down the hem she was turning. “Nobody’s saying a word. But a cake is a promise, Doris. That’s all it is. You say, I made this, and you put it on the table, and everybody eats it on your word.”

Mrs Rosevear cried, comfortably, into the flag she was supposed to be hemming. Morwenna patted her, and said she would show her how to make it right, a proper yellow loaf, and then she’d be the only other woman in Cornwall who could, and Mrs Rosevear blew her nose and said, “That’s very good of you,” in a voice of pure doomed gratitude. It had taken eleven minutes, start to finish. In the Institute, justice is a form of catering.

At half past seven Morwenna lifted a flour sack onto the end of the trestle, and it came down with a thump that made the cups jump.

“Now,” she said. “Before it goes under glass for the prize-giving. I want you all to see my hinge.”

She took the Regatta Book from the sack in both hands. It is a ledger of foolscap size, half calf, with marbled paper sides in the old Spanish pattern, a red label on the spine stamped REGATTA in gilt, and corners rubbed down to the board by twenty-five years of the thumbs of treasurers. Inside, in a score of hands, it holds the name of every crew that has won the gig race at Trevenna since 1921. Ned bound it in 1964. I remember him finishing it, at the bench, in March, humming “Bread of Heaven” in a different key every time he reached the bridge.

“There,” said Morwenna. “Back joint split clean from head to tail at Christmas, the poor thing. I did it with a strip of calf and a bit of paste and a great deal of prayer. Have a look.”

The Book went round the trestles. “Lovely,” said Mrs Bolitho. “You’d never know,” said Mrs Opie. “What?” said Mrs Trewhella, who is deaf as a kipper and sits near the stove. “THE HINGE,” said four women together, and she said, “Oh, yes,” with great conviction, and passed it on.

It reached me last. I took it on my knees as I would take any book that wanted looking at, with a hand under each board, and the thing took my knees with it. It is difficult to describe how it felt. A ledger of that size ought to weigh what a good-sized loaf weighs, and this settled down into my wrists like a sleeping child. Heavy, I thought. A great deal heavier than a ledger.

Well, it was Ned’s. He bound everything as if the book expected to be thrown downstairs.

I ran my thumb along the back joint, and then looked for the join, and for a good ten seconds could not find it. I looked for the pared edge of the new calf, the shine of the paste. I know where those things hide. I have spent twenty-seven years hiding them. Morwenna had not left me so much as a ridge.

“That’s very good,” I said. “That’s better than mine.”

“Paste and prayer, my handsome.”

“It’s a good deal better than prayer. Where did you learn to do that?”

“Oh, I’ve watched a good deal of mending in my time.” She took the Book back, gently, and set it in her lap. “You can’t live in Trevenna and not pick up a bit. It’s the only trade it has, Dot, bar fish.”

The door banged. The rain came in round it, and then Imogen Mayne, in black leather, with her cropped hair plastered flat to her skull and a cardboard folder clutched against her chest. She stood on the mat, with water running off her nose stud, and looked round the hall.

The three machines stopped, one after another, the treadle last. Eight women laid their hands in their laps and looked at her, like a jury that has not yet been told the verdict.

“We are only doing the bunting,” said Mrs Chegwidden.

“So I see.” Imogen looked at the folder as if it had spoken. “I was looking for the treasurer. I found Daddy’s regatta papers. The accounts, and the order of procession, and a lot of letters from the Harbour Commissioners in a tone I’d rather not describe. I thought somebody ought to have them. Unless this is a bad moment.”

“It is never a bad moment, my handsome,” said Morwenna, and was on her feet before the others. “Come in off that mat before you rust. Sit. Eat.”

Then they pounced. I have watched a flock of gulls take a dropped chip and I have never seen it done more thoroughly. In the space of four minutes Imogen was seated in the best chair, in front of the stove, with a cup of tea in one hand and an egg-and-cress sandwich in the other and a second sandwich, of unknown filling, put into her pocket by Mrs Opie for later. She had been asked whether she was eating, whether she was sleeping, whether she was staying, and where. (“The Lantern.” “With Jago?”) She had been asked whether it was true about the will, to which she answered, with admirable dryness, that she was not permitted to know until the solicitor had finished being sorry. She had been asked whether the Inspector was a Methodist. She was asked whether she would come to chapel, and by the end she had agreed to present the cup at the prize-giving, because Miss Hocking said it was the chairman’s daughter’s place, and Imogen said that Daddy would have been appalled, and Miss Hocking said that was a reason.

“He wasn’t an easy man,” said Mrs Opie, tenderly. “But he was a good chairman, dear.”

“He said no to most things,” said Imogen.

“He said it beautifully,” said Morwenna. She had a hand on the girl’s shoulder; Imogen did not shrug it off. “He never once said no to a flag.”

Imogen laughed, a short surprised sound, and put her hand to her mouth; and I saw her eyes go round the hall and find me, and rest, and move on. I knew where she had been at ten past ten on the Thursday, and what she had done to a wall after. I said nothing. I felt as though I had taken her purse.

She took out a cigarette, and a match.

“Not in the hall, dear,” said Mrs Chegwidden. “There’s a saucer in the kitchen.”

“Daddy let me smoke in the vestry.”

“The vestry has been thoroughly forgiven,” said Mrs Chegwidden. “The hall has not.”

I do not know how it began. A hall full of women who have been sewing for two hours is a hot, close, dangerous place, and the strip light had been going like a moth against a window for most of the evening. Someone complained of her sciatica. Someone else had a head. Mrs Rosevear had a head with the sun, and Miss Hocking said she had one with Mrs Chegwidden, and Mrs Trewhella said “WHAT?” and was told, and said that in her day nobody had a head, they had a duty. It went round the room like a hymn.

“It’s these strips,” said Morwenna. She had put the Book back in its sack and was pressing two fingers to her temple, with her eyes shut. “I’ve had a head on me since Easter. They flicker, you see, and it gets in behind the eyes. That one of yours over the press, Dot. I stuck my head in at Easter to say good morning and I came out with a head like a bell. Never again.”

“It does flicker,” said Mrs Opie. “The one in the post office does it. I told Ada.”

“It does not,” said Mrs Bolitho.

“Does it?” I said. “It’s a dreadful thing. Ned would have hated it. It makes everyone look like—”

At that moment Jenifer Opie, who had gone to the hatch for the tea, turned the tap of the urn. The urn is an immense copper vessel, the size of a drum, older than the Institute. It coughed, shrieked, and fired a jet of boiling water clean across the hatch and down the hall. It caught Mrs Trewhella in the feet. Gwen Trewhella, who had not run since the Coronation, ran. She went round the trestle in a half-circle with her skirt held up and her mouth open and a noise coming out of it that I had not heard from a woman of seventy since the Blitz, and Mrs Chegwidden said “Gwen, do sit,” and Mrs Bolitho’s hat came off, both hands, and fell into the trifle. I laughed. I laughed until I had to put down my hem and hold the table with both hands, and tears were running down my face, and for a minute or two there was nothing in the hall but women bent double, and the urn spitting, and the strip light going off and on above us like a lighthouse in a bad temper.

It was the first time I had laughed in a week. I would not have missed it.

The men arrived at a quarter to nine, together, which neither enjoyed.

Jago Rowe filled the doorway. The Reverend Nance came in under his arm, wheeling his bicycle backwards into the porch and apologising to it, and the two of them stood on the mat and looked at the bunting, which was now strung from the hall beam to the stage rail in a gaudy wet swag, to check the lengths, with Miss Hocking’s broom holding up the middle.

“We’ve come about the Book,” said Jago.

“The procession order,” said Nance, “if we might. Forgive me.”

Mrs Chegwidden took the folder from Imogen and read it with the voice of an usher. “The Regatta Book is carried from the Slip to the finishing line by the Chairman, who presents it to the winning cox.” She looked up. “There is no Chairman.”

“Then it’s the Vice,” said Jago. “Aubrey carried it. I’ll carry it. That’s the size of it.”

“Mr Rowe.” Nance had gone pink above the collar. “I would not dream of, ah. But in the circumstances. It is a, a sacred trust, I think, a record of, of the community, and since it will be carried, in some sense, in his memory, I had thought that the parish, that I might, with a blessing, be the right person to—”

“A blessing on a ledger.”

“A sacred—”

“It’s a list of who won a boat race, Vicar.”

“It is the record of a hundred crews, Mr Rowe.”

“You would drop it in the harbour, Mr Rowe,” said Nance, bravely.

“I have dropped nothing in forty years.”

“You dropped the gavel,” said Mrs Bolitho, from under her hat, which was now sticky. “On Saturday. Twice.”

I was sitting nearest the sack. I do not know what possessed me. I think it was a week of dead men and a night of mac-coloured women and a pint of laughter that had gone to my head, but I picked up the Book from where Morwenna had set it, and I stood, and held it out in front of me at arm’s length like the Lord Mayor’s regalia.

“Gentlemen,” I said. “We shall decide it by weight. Whoever carries the Regatta Book is going to want a back like a hod-carrier. Let us see what we are dealing with.”

I had my pocket gauge in my cardigan, where it has lived since 1963: a small brass thing like a clothes-peg with a dial on it, which tells you the thickness of a leaf or a board to the half-millimetre, and which I carry as other women carry a compact. I opened the Book’s front cover and set the jaws across the edge of the board, as formally as a doctor with a stethoscope. The little needle swung and settled.

“Three and a half,” I said.

“Three and a half what?” said Jago.

“Millimetres. Of board. For a ledger, gentlemen, that is a very stout board. You could stop a small bullet.” I snapped the gauge shut. “Whoever carries it, I advise you both to take a barrow.”

There was a roar. Jago laughed, a slow, deep, delighted noise like a barrel rolling down a cellar, and Nance laughed until his cough drop shot out on to the boards, and the women banged on the trestle, and I was the Lord Mayor, and for a moment I was entirely visible and it did not hurt. Morwenna took the Book gently out of my hands and slid it into its sack. “Don’t scratch it, Dot,” she said. “It’s the only one we’ve got.” She laughed too, the loudest of anyone.

It was Mrs Bolitho who did it. She had risen to her feet to cheer, and she stepped back to give her hat room, and she trod on the leg of Miss Hocking’s broom.

The broom went over. The beam nail, which had been holding the first end of the bunting since six o’clock out of pure obstinacy, came out of the plaster like a tooth, and the whole gaudy length of it, three hundred feet of red and white and blue and yellow, fell on the committee in a single piece with a long soft sigh. It covered the trestles, the sewing machines, the egg-and-cress, two bicycles and the Reverend Nance. The strip light flickered. Out of the heap rose a hand holding a cup, and then a face, with a small blue triangle caught on the top of its silver curls like a hat.

“Well,” said Morwenna, quite calmly, taking it off. “That’s the third time this week things have come apart.”

chapters.title: The Honest Man
chapters.html:
On Wednesday the rain stopped, which in Trevenna is treated as an announcement. By nine o’clock half of Fish Cellar Lane was standing in its doorway with a mug, looking up at a sky that had been replaced overnight by a better one, and the hydrangeas along the wall had gone from slate to a blue so hard it hurt to look at. The gulls, who had sulked on the chimneys for three days, rose in a body, circled the harbour once and settled again, having forgotten what for.

In the five days since the fair the Bindery had taken eleven pounds forty, most of it from a woman who wanted paste for her wallpaper. I had stopped looking at the till. One does not stare at a thing that cannot improve. I stood at the counter instead with one of Mrs Rosevear’s hymnals, which wanted a new spine and a talking-to, and Quire lay on the paste shelf in a bar of sun with her belly turned to the ceiling, a position she permitted only on days when nobody had the least wish to touch her.

Tamsin had arrived at eight without being told the hour. She had stood on the step with her hands in her pockets and the bleached stripe of her fringe sticking up like a question, and I had put her in the yard with a ream of waste paper and one instruction, which was to tear it. Along the grain first, then across, and then tell me the difference. It is the first thing Ned ever taught me, in the spring of 1962, in that same yard, with a sheet of Whatman and a look of enormous patience. Through the open door I could hear her at it: a long clean rip; a pause; a short ragged one; a longer pause, in which I knew she was holding the two edges up to the light with her teeth in her lip; and then a small noise that was not quite an oath.

“The grain goes up and down,” she called.

“The grain goes the way the paper wants.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It is the only one there is,” I said. “Again.”

The bell went at ten past ten, and then nobody came in, which is how I knew it was somebody who had not yet decided to.

Imogen Mayne stood on the mat in the black leather jacket, in July, with a brown document case held out in front of her in both hands like a verger with the plate. Her eyes were red at the rims and she had made no attempt to do anything about it. There was a cigarette between two of her fingers, unlit, which she seemed to be carrying on someone else’s behalf.

“No,” I said.

“I haven’t.”

“You were going to. Everything in this room is paper or flour, and I should like to keep both.”

She looked at the cigarette as if it had been put there without her knowledge, and tucked it behind her ear. It was exactly where a man keeps a pencil. I do not think she knew.

“I’ve come to show you something,” she said. “I’d like you to read all of it before you say anything. Not even ‘Well.’”

“How do you know I say ‘Well’?”

“Daddy said you did. He said it was the most complete sentence in the English language.” She told this to the shelf behind my head. “He said you could close a subject like a lid.”

I had not known that Aubrey Trevithick repeated things I said. It is a peculiar sensation to learn that one has been quoted. I came out from behind the counter and turned the sign on the door to Closed, and she watched me do it with the faint surprise of a person who had expected to have to ask.

She set the case on the counter and opened it. “The lining’s perished at one corner. Old glue. He’s had this case since Cambridge, and I thought, I’ll get it put right, because he’d have hated...” She stopped, and began again further along. “I ran my thumb under the flap and it was in there. Flat. Between the lining and the leather, the way you’d keep something you hadn’t decided about.”

It was a cream envelope of good laid paper, a little soft at the edges from a life spent against a man’s other papers. The stamp was already on it, a nineteen-pence stamp, stuck down square in the corner. He had licked the stamp. He had addressed the thing in fountain pen, in the upright hand I knew from every receipt he ever gave me, and then he had put it away, and on one corner a cup had left a brown crescent where he had not noticed it standing.

H. R. Tregear Esq., Messrs Tregear & Polglase, Boscawen Street, Truro.

“Loveday’s solicitor,” I said.

“And the family’s. He did the Trevithick wills.” She touched the flap, which had been slit along the top with something fine. “I opened it. With a nail file, so the glue would still show it had been shut. I know I shouldn’t. I’m his next of kin and I don’t know what that allows. I’m taking it to Constable Kitto at one, I promise you I am. I wanted somebody to read it first who isn’t paid to.” She tried to smile. “Daddy’s list of people who weren’t paid to be kind to him was a short one.”

She gave me two sheets. I read them standing at the counter, with the sun coming through the glass of the door and laying the word BINDERY backwards across my wrist.

12th July 1989

Dear Hugh,

You will have my valuation of the Penhallow library at the end of the month, and I shall ask you to read it before Loveday does. But there is one item on which I cannot wait, and I put it to you now in plain terms so that you may advise her accordingly. The Carne Rutter is not what it seems.

I am not yet in a position to say what it is, nor since when, nor at whose hands, and I do not propose to guess in writing. A guess set down in ink has a way of becoming a fact by the time it has crossed a village. I shall have the volume taken apart on Friday in the presence of Mrs Pellow of the Marigold Bindery, who has not flattered me once in twenty-seven years and will therefore tell me whether I am a fool.

Meanwhile I must ask three things of you. That the rutter is not offered in the September sale under any circumstances. That nobody handles it further. And that nothing of this is said to Loveday, who has loved that book for seventy years and may be spared a few days more.

I am aware that this is a poor letter. I would rather be accurate than prompt, and I find that I am neither.

Yours ever, Aubrey

I read it twice, and then I read one sentence a third time, and it was not the one about the rutter.

I have been called a number of things in thirty years in Trevenna. The bookbinder. Ned’s widow. The one with the cat. Never, until that moment, the person you send for. It is a foolish thing to be undone by, with so much else lying on my counter, but one does not choose which part of a page goes in.

“Well,” I said.

Imogen laughed, a wet, startled sound, and wiped her nose on the back of her wrist. “You’re allowed now.”

Nobody in Trevenna had ever quite believed that Aubrey Trevithick was an honest man. It was not that they thought him dishonest. It was that he held the Lantern’s lease and the regatta purse and a number of other people’s old debts, and a man who holds so much must surely have a manner where his scruples should be. I had been as bad as any. On the Friday I found him I had stood in my own press room looking at the rutter and thought: he borrowed my key, he promised to have something to say to me, and here is a book with its insides out and a collector beside it. I had made him a crook inside ten minutes. I had given him a partner, a quarrel, a hammer. It is such a comfortable shape, a crook and his accomplice. A crook is a man who has it coming. And when Garrow had said the same, in his raincoat, I had said “Well” and let him.

All the while Aubrey had been doing the one thing none of the rest of us did, which was to notice. He had held a book up to the light, seen what was wrong with it, and gone to considerable trouble not to say so until he was certain. He had put a stamp on a letter and not posted it, I thought, because he wanted me to see the book first. I was ashamed of every unkind word I had given him, from the hat to the cane, and there had been a good many.

And it turned the whole business round like a coat. If Aubrey was no partner, there had been no quarrel over spoils. Someone had made a false book, and Aubrey had found it out, and someone had learned that he had, and he had been stopped as one stops a sentence.
