The stamp on that envelope was as dry as the day he licked it. The words had never left the case. So the person who made the false book had learned of them some other way, between the Wednesday and the Thursday night, and I could not think how.

“I was there,” said Imogen.

I looked up.

“At the Bindery. On the Thursday. I’ve been trying to say it to you since the fair and I keep saying something about the weather.”

“I know.”

She went quite still. “How?”

“Someone saw you go in at five past ten and come out at twenty past. Not the police. Someone with reasons for keeping out of it, whom I shan’t name.”

“Five past,” she said. “Yes.” Her mouth worked. “Then you know what I did to the wall.”

“I know you did something to a wall.”

“I kicked it. Twice. Mrs Pellow, I swear to you, I didn’t touch him. I left him alive. He was alive and he was furious, he was in his shirtsleeves with that pencil behind his ear and the lamp on, looking like a boy with a frog, and he wouldn’t be got at. I’d gone to have it out. The piano, all of it. I’d gone to stand in front of him until he said one thing that wasn’t about accuracy.”

“And did he?”

“He said, ‘Immy, I can’t do this tonight.’ He said he had somebody coming at half past ten, and he meant to be kind to them, which was a good deal harder than being right, and he needed all the kindness he had.” She was gripping the case so hard that her knuckles stood up. “And I said something I would like back. I said ‘Daddy,’ in the voice. The one he hated. As if it were a diagnosis. And he said, ‘Tomorrow, then. I shall be accurate about the piano tomorrow,’ and he shut the door.”

In the yard the tearing had stopped. I did not turn my head.

Somebody coming at half past ten. Not a thief with a chisel, not a stranger out of the dark: an appointment, and one Aubrey had dressed himself in kindness for. I thought of a woman in a mac who had gone in without knocking. People do not knock when they have been told the door is open.

“Do you think I did it?” said Imogen.

“No.”

“Garrow does, or he’d like to. He’s been to the Lantern twice, asking who inherits as if he were asking the time. I do. Me. A house with a roof like a colander and a lease on a pub I’d give Jago tomorrow with a ribbon on.” She breathed out through her nose. “He thinks Daddy was in it, you know. I heard him on the stairs: ‘Trevithick’s hands weren’t clean.’ That’s what they’ll put in the paper. That’s what they’ll say at the funeral, in the car park, with their hats on.”

“When is the funeral?”

“Monday, if Garrow will let me have him. Mr Nance has promised a hymn Daddy would have corrected.” She hunted for the rest. “I don’t only mean the funeral. Everyone here was perfectly civil to him for thirty years and not one of them believed he’d lend them a pencil without wanting it back with interest. I want it said, out loud, in front of them, that he was the only one who noticed. That he was the honest one. I want to bury him as that.”

“I am not a person who makes speeches.”

“No. You’re a person who looks at a thing before she says what it is. He said that too.”

I said that I would do what I could. It was not a promise. It was a lid, and we both knew it, and she took it for what it was.

She put her hand inside the jacket and brought out one of the small brown envelopes the police use, and from it a ring. A gold signet, heavy, worn soft at the edges, with a swan cut into the stone and its wings half raised. I knew it as one knows the hand that has passed one change across a counter for a quarter of a century.

“They gave me his things in this, with a receipt in triplicate,” she said. “I can’t wear it. It goes on my thumb, and I’m not going about with my father on my thumb. I thought you should have it. Not to own. To keep, until it’s done.”

I took it to the paste shelf and set it down beside Ned’s old toffee tin, the Silver Jubilee one, which these days held a great many bone folders and one burned corner of paper. Quire came down from her patch of sun, sniffed the ring, and sat beside it as if she had been posted there.

Imogen lit the cigarette on the step, in the lane, in the sun, with the care of a woman lighting the first candle in a church. Then she went down the hill to see Constable Kitto, and the bell closed behind her.

“You were listening,” I said.

“I was tearing very quietly.” Tamsin stood in the yard door with a strip of paper in each hand. “That one’s with the grain. That one’s across. The across one’s rubbish, it fuzzes. So it isn’t a rule. It’s just what the paper does.”

“That is the whole of binding.”

“Right. So.” She looked at the ring and not at me. “Who did he tell?”

“That’s a different question.”

“How?”

“He told no one. The letter’s still got its stamp on. If he’d told someone, it would be someone who is now very careful not to say so.” I heard myself, the way I sound when I am being accurate, and it was his voice I had caught. “The question is who knew.”

I went to the drawer under the counter and took out Ned’s last order book, the black one with the cloth spine he had rebacked himself. I have never been able to read his hand. I do not open it at the pages, and I would sooner be seen in the street without my cardigan. But the inside of the front cover is clean board and paper, and his hand does not reach there. I took the pencil from behind my own ear and wrote, in capitals, so that I should not be mistaken:

WHO KNEW AUBREY KNEW?

Then I underlined it twice, the second time hard enough to dent the board.

chapters.title: Question Time
chapters.html:
The quiz at the Drowned Lantern began at eight, which is to say at twenty past, because the tide at Trevenna is the only thing that has ever been on time and nobody sees why the pub should compete. Low water was at twenty-five past nine. Through the open door the harbour smelled of mud and weed and old rope, and the gulls stood about on the Hard in the last of the light with the air of people waiting for the doors of a theatre.

Jago had put out forty packets of crisps for the teams, cheese and onion, salt and vinegar, ready salted, in drifts down the middle of the tables, so that the three leading sides faced one another over a sea of them like fleets. Quire Straits had the table by the dartboard: myself, Kit, who held the pencil because his handwriting looked like a catalogue and he had never been argued with about it, Tamsin Bray, who had been issued a lemonade by a landlord who chose not to ask her age, and the Reverend Nance, with his single sherry and his bicycle clips still on. The Jam Tarts had the long table under the window, five Institute women in cardigans arranged round Morwenna like petals. The Lantern Regulars held the bar end, led by Wilf Hosken, who was seventy-one and had been a pilot’s boy before the war, and Eddy Tonkin of the ferrets, who looked as innocent as a man can who is sitting on a book.

Demelza had come as a spectator. She sat alone at the next table with a half of shandy and her notebook shut in front of her, in the grey jumper under a cardigan, and she looked at nothing so firmly that it was plain she was looking at Kit.

Jago climbed on to his stool behind the bar with the cards in one great hand and his reading glasses pushed up on his forehead like a second pair of eyes. He rang the lifeboat bell over the till. The room went quiet by degrees, as a shingle beach does when the wave pulls out.

“Round one,” he said. “General knowledge. Question one. Which saint is patron of Cornwall?”

“Piran,” breathed Nance, “although there are those who would argue for Petroc, and of course Michael has a claim on the, forgive me. Piran.”

Kit wrote it down. Question two was the name of the Tottenham midfielder known as Gazza, and Nance looked at the ceiling and said he supposed it was a Sicilian martyr.

“Gascoigne,” said Tamsin, not moving her lips. “Paul.”

“Is that how it’s spelled?” said Nance, with real interest.

By question six he had given us a saint who was boiled, one who was roasted and one who was merely sat upon, and Tamsin had given us a goalkeeper, a Grand National winner and the Prime Minister’s maiden name, and I realised that I was watching an alliance form. They did not look at one another. They passed the pencil under the table with the delicacy of two spies at a station. When Tamsin noticed, from the corner of her eye, that Eddy Tonkin’s right hand had been below the level of the table for some minutes, she kicked the Reverend’s ankle once.

“Forgive me,” said Nance, rising, pink to the collar. “I am sure it is nothing. But I believe Mr Tonkin is reading under the table.”

It was Pears’ Cyclopaedia, the 1962 edition. Jago confiscated it in his enormous hand with the expression of a man removing a fish from a child, and deducted five points, and the Regulars arose in a body to say that a vicar had no business knowing what a cyclopaedia looked like from underneath.

“Round two,” said Jago, when the shouting was done. “Books.”

He stopped. He took the glasses down off his forehead, which I had never seen him do in public, and put them on his nose. From the inside of his shirt he drew a long brown envelope, a good deal handled, with writing on the front.

“Mr Trevithick gave me this a fortnight ago,” he said. “It says, Jago, for Thursday the twentieth, in order. I haven’t opened it before now. I’m going to read it as it’s written, and anyone who wants to say a word about that can say it to me after.”

Nobody said anything. At the end of the bar, by herself, Imogen Mayne sat with her hands round a glass and her face turned very slightly away.

I will not pretend it was a great round. It was what he would have set: elegant, a little vain and fastidiously exact. Who wrote Persuasion, and in what year? Both, please. The title page says 1818 and the book appeared in December 1817; any team that gives the former will receive a mark for pedantry and none for the answer. The room laughed at that. It laughed again at the third, which asked for the oldest printed book in the county and added, in Aubrey’s voice through Jago’s mouth, that he knew perfectly well it was in his own possession and that this was why he had not asked for it to be brought. I watched the laugh go round the room as one watches a wave go down a harbour wall, and I noted three people who took it late: Nance, who had missed the joke; Jago, who laughed at the end of his own sentence as though somebody had reminded him; and Morwenna, a full beat after the Jam Tarts, a beat in which she looked at the table and then smiled. It meant nothing. A woman at a quiz is generally thinking about something else.

They marked the sheets across the tables, as they always did, so that nobody should mark their own. Quire Straits had the Jam Tarts’ sheet, and Tamsin took the pencil and ran it down the right-hand column like a customs officer.

Morwenna’s hand was a pleasure to look at: quick, upright, small, every letter standing on the line with its feet together. At the foot of each round she had written the time, 8.40, 9.12, because Miss Hocking had decreed it, after a quarrel with the Regulars in 1987, to prevent disputes about who had been given longer.

“Question seven,” said Jago, reading from Aubrey’s second sheet. “What does a binder call a folded sheet, or a group of sheets, forming one section of a book? Gathering. Also signature. Also quire. All three are acceptable, and I will not hear a bookbinder insulted by a pedant.” He coughed. “Underneath he’s put, Accept ‘quire’ from one team in particular, who have been waiting three years to be right.”

The room turned and looked at us. Nance went the colour of a boiled ham. I would have liked to say something, and found that I could only smile at the table, which I did very hard.

“It says signature,” said Tamsin. She was holding up the Jam Tarts’ answer to the light. “Here. That’s not what’s on the card.”

“It is, my handsome,” said Morwenna, across the aisle. “Signature. It’s the proper word.”

“It says gathering.”

“It says gathering, signature or quire,” said Jago, “and I’ve just read it out.”

“A signature’s the mark at the foot of the sheet,” said Tamsin, with the stubborn gleam of the sixteen-year-old who has read the whole of one book thoroughly. “It’s not the sheet itself.”

“It was the sheet itself in 1780,” said Morwenna comfortably. “And it’s the sheet itself in the trade, today. And it’s also the mark. Both. I’d be surprised if you’d been told otherwise.”

They looked at each other across the aisle, the girl with the bleached stripe and the woman with the silver perm, and each, I could see, was perfectly certain, and each was right. Jago allowed the point. Tamsin gave Morwenna her mark with the expression of someone surrendering a fort and keeping the flag.

“Good girl,” said Morwenna, and winked.

Round two ended with the whole of Jago’s voice gone to gravel. The last note on the sheet was not an answer. He read it all the same, very slowly, as though each word were a plank he had to test before he put his weight on it. Jago: please read the answers slowly. People are generally cleverer than they look, and they like to be given time to find out.

Then he took the glasses off and laid them down, and there was no sound in the room at all. Wilf Hosken, who has stood for nothing since VE Day, put his hands on the table and pushed himself up. Chairs scraped. It went round the room like a wave in the other direction, the Seconds and the Regulars and the Jam Tarts one by one, and Nance with his sherry, and Tamsin, who did not look as though she knew why, and Kit, and I. Demelza stood. At the end of the bar Imogen did not move, and I saw Morwenna cross the floor and lay a hand upon her shoulder, and stay.

Sheets were exchanged for the other rounds, which I scarcely remember, except that the Regulars marked ours and passed it round the table before it went back, and that I saw Wilf’s lips moving as he came to the margin. I had not looked at the margin myself. Kit, who had meant to write the answers neatly and had then lost his place every time a grey cardigan moved at the next table, had begun by answering one question and finished by addressing another.

“Question nineteen,” read Wilf, with enormous gravity. “Which planet is nearest the sun? Mercury. Demelza, you have been at the next table for two hours with my jumper on, and I should say that you are not allowed to read this, because my handwriting has always looked like a ransom note. Question twenty: I am sorry about March last year. I know you didn’t want me to say it, so I haven’t said it, and it’s in the margin, which is not saying.”

You could have heard a crisp drop. Demelza was pink to the ears. She rose, crossed the three feet of floor, took the sheet from Wilf Hosken, read it right through to the end without moving her face, folded it in four, and put it in the breast pocket of her cardigan, where the police keep evidence.

“Is that a tick or a cross?” said Wilf.

“It’s a matter for the Crown Prosecution Service,” said Demelza, and sat down, and did not look at Kit again, or only twice.

The music round was Jago’s own. He fed coins to the Wurlitzer, whose cracked amber dome looks as though it had been through the war, and gave us ten seconds of ten records, and the Jam Tarts took the first six like a scythe. Morwenna did not confer. She heard four bars, wrote, passed the pencil, like a woman shelling peas. Then Jago reached the newer records, and the Institute went down in a heap. The seventh was a young man declaiming over a drum machine, and Mrs Chegwidden wrote Dance Band, and Miss Hocking wrote Gentleman’s lament, and Gwen Trewhella, who was deaf and knew all the tunes by the beat through the floor, was overruled four times in a row. At ten to ten Jago pulled the plug at the wall. Eddy Tonkin said it was robbery.

At twenty-five past ten the three sides were level on seventy-one, and Jago had a tiebreak card in his hand that was not Aubrey’s, because Aubrey had not written one. “Closest answer wins,” he said. “This is mine.”

The door opened as he began to read. It let in the smell of the flooding tide and a man in a pale linen jacket, who stood on the mat as if he had been told to wait in a room and had come to suspect that the room was the difficulty. Pieter de Vries had the round tortoiseshell glasses and the clipped grey beard, and he looked the Lantern over, floats and faces and the cold sea of crisps, and did not seem to see any of it. On the bar by the pickled eggs stood a one-pound jar of Morwenna’s heather and gorse honey with the lifeboat tin beside it, and his eyes went there and stayed, with an expression I cannot describe except to say that I have seen it on people looking at a witness.

“Tiebreak,” said Jago, when he had finished staring at the Dutchman. “Name the Trevenna lifeboat lost in 1910.”

Nance began: “There was one, I am almost certain, forgive me, I believe it was...” and trailed off. The Jam Tarts put their heads together and came up shrugging. “My grandfather’s,” said Wilf Hosken, “and he never said.” Nobody wrote anything. Jago turned the card over, as if the answer might be on the back, and it was not.

“Then nobody leaves till somebody knows,” he said. “Jory, bolt the door. It’s a lock-in.”

A cheer went up. Pieter de Vries, behind the bolt, moved to a stool at the far end of the bar and sat on it with his hands folded. Above us the hundred and forty glass floats burned in their nets, a drowned lantern for every drowned man, and not one of them would give us the name.

chapters.title: The Music Round
chapters.html:
Jago Rowe kept the Thursday answer sheets in a biscuit tin, and until that night I had supposed he did it out of sentiment.

By twenty to eleven the Lantern had shut its eyes and loosened its collar. The curtains had been drawn across the harbour windows, which was the whole of the ceremony, and forty people who had behaved themselves all evening began, behind a bolted door, to behave less carefully. Wilf Hosken had taken off his boots. The Seconds had resumed their darts at the far end, in the dim, with the exaggerated solemnity of men who cannot be fined. Nance sat in the inglenook with a lemon barley, appalled and wholly delighted, like a man who has been taken to a nightclub by his own churchwarden. Tamsin, on her fifth lemonade, lay along the settle with her boots on the cushion and her eyes shut, and announced to nobody that this was the best night of her life and that she would deny it.

Jago put the tin down on the bar in front of me with the sound of a coffin lid settling. Huntley & Palmers, the lid painted with a stagecoach in a snowstorm, the corners rusted brown and the sides ringed with forty-one weeks of other people’s beer.

“You’ve wanted this since Friday,” he said.

“I haven’t asked.”

“No. You haven’t. That’s how I know.” He rubbed the top of his head with the hand that has four fingers and a thumb. “I read that out tonight, Dot. His words, in his order. I told you to leave it, the first night, and I was wrong, and I’d be wrong again if I held my tongue. He told me for a year to file them properly. You’re good with paper.”

“Jago...”

“Take what you like. Put them back in order.” He lifted his coat from its nail. “I’ve a barrel to see to.”

He went out through the back, and the door sighed to behind him. It was a full minute before it struck me that a landlord who is keeping a lock-in does not as a rule see to his barrels in his coat.

I do not know what other people do with a heap of paper. My hands do one thing, which is to square it. I tipped the sheets out on the bar and knocked the edges true against the wood, and they fell into their weeks like dominoes: forty-one Thursdays since the first of October. You could read the weather in them, stiff in the cold months and limp and fingered in July. The Regulars’ sheets carried remarks in the margins, WE WUZ ROBBED in capitals, eleven times. The Seconds’ were a drift of scoring and thumbprints. Ours were as neat as a church notice, and had finished fourth on thirty-one occasions, which Jago had preserved like a parish register of a very consistent sin.

Jory, the potman, had been missing for a quarter of an hour, which nobody had remarked, a potman’s absence being the natural condition of a pub. He came in now from the yard, wiping his hands on his apron, with a five-pound note between his teeth like a retriever with a duck.

“Where’ve you been?” said Wilf Hosken.

“Quay steps. Dutchman’s trunk.” Jory took the note out of his mouth to be accurate. “Strapped up like a cow for market. He said he’d be along for it himself.”

“And he paid you?”

“A fiver.”

“Is it a Dutch fiver?”

“It’s got the Queen on.”

“Then he’s more English than he looks,” said Wilf, and went back to his boots.

Kit slid on to the stool beside me with his pint. He did not say “Sorry.” He looked at the sheets and then at me, and I think he knew what I was after before I did.

“Last week’s,” he said. “It’s on top. Jago never put anything in order in his life.”

It was. The Jam Tarts’ sheet for the thirteenth of July, folded once down the middle and stained with a ring of something brown. At the head, in a hand I should have known on the far side of the world, because it had written me eleven lines on the day Ned was buried: JAM TARTS. Capt. M. Hext.

I turned back through the weeks first, I do not know why, and the hand ran through them all, quick and upright and small, the hand of a woman who has never crossed a t twice. Then I came back to the thirteenth. The rounds went down the page one after another with the times at the foot of each in Miss Hocking’s fashion: 8.38, 9.10, 9.31. At the foot of the fourth, Music, stood 9.50, and underneath it the writing changed. It was round and backward-leaning and dotted its i’s with small circles, and I knew that too, because Doris Rosevear had once signed the Chapel’s Harvest returns with a smiling face.

Capt. changed 9.50. M.H. gone up to Loveday’s. D.R. now holding pencil. (J.R.’s rule.)

The rest of the page was in Doris’s circles to the bottom. The captain’s neat hand did not come back.

Kit leaned over. “Ten to ten,” he said, without being asked. “Jago pulled the plug at the wall. Eddy said it was robbery.”

“You remember the time.”

“I always remember the time. I catalogue.” He looked into his pint. “It’s about all I’m good for.”

“That is untrue,” I said, “and we shall return to it.”

I should say what I knew. Everyone in Trevenna agreed that Morwenna had gone up to Loveday’s after the quiz, in the way that everyone agrees on the date of the Armistice, without having been asked and without a doubt in the world. I had agreed myself. I had nothing against her in my hands but forty minutes and a woman called Doris.

The Jam Tarts were getting their coats. The Institute does not hold with lock-ins; Mrs Chegwidden had said so twice and had then looked longingly at her gin. Jory was to draw the bolt for them when they were ready. Morwenna sat a little apart with her big handbag open on her knee and the tin out of it, as it always is, and a greaseproof parcel unfolded beside her: saffron cake, cut in fingers. At the end of the bar, Pieter de Vries had not moved from his stool. He had a lemonade he had not touched, and since he came in he had followed Morwenna across the room with his head, the way a dog follows a plate.

“Sit,” she said, when she saw me coming. “Eat. You look like a dishcloth that’s been wrung by a strong man.”

I sat. I had meant to be clever, and found that I was not going to be. “I’m trying to put last Thursday in order, Morwenna, and I keep losing the middle. I wondered if you’d help me.”

“Whatever you like, my handsome.” She cut a finger of cake with the little horn-handled knife and gave it to me on the greaseproof.

“When did you go up to Loveday’s?”

“Half past ten.” She did not hesitate. “As soon as the last answer was in. She’d been after me for a hand of piquet all week and the damp gets into her chest. Mind the crumbs on Doris.”

“It’s only that I have your sheet.”

“Have you?”

“Jago’s tin. Doris has written the time on it, in your fashion, under the music round. M.H. gone up to Loveday’s. Ten to ten. And Kit says that’s when the jukebox went off.”

The lid of the tin went down on her knee, slowly, with a small click. She looked at the finger of cake in her hand with the attention of a woman choosing between two windows. Then she smiled, and it was the whole of her smile, with the cheeks in it.

“Then it was ten to ten,” she said, “and I’ve been telling myself half past for a week. There. Isn’t it dreadful, what the mind does.” She tapped her temple with a knuckle. “Ronald asked me on Sunday whether I was the new nurse. I said no, I was the old one. I put his tablets in the wrong pocket and found them in the lift. I’d have sworn on the Book it was half past. It’s no good, Dot, I’m sixty-three and I’ve mislaid whole months. That Doris. She wrote Alleluia on the Chapel quiz when she meant Armenia.”

“Well,” I said.

“Eat your cake.”

It was saffron cake, the true yellow kind with the currants, which I have eaten at every crisis of my life in this village, and it did what it has always done: it made a smaller thing of whatever I had been holding. I told myself that forty minutes is not a lie but a mislaid piece of an evening. I have mislaid whole years of mine. I put the sheet in my cardigan pocket, where it joined a pencil, a loupe and a lemon sherbet, and I ate the cake, and I should like it recorded that I knew perfectly well what I was doing.

At a quarter to eleven Jory drew the bolt back a hand’s breadth, and the Institute went out in a body, like a hen coop being moved. Morwenna was last. She stooped and kissed my cheek, smelling of woodsmoke and wax. “Sleep,” she said. “Promise me.” Her voice went off up Net Loft Row with the others’, saying something about Edna’s knees, and Jory shot the bolt behind them.

Demelza had come across for her coat. She did it as a person does who has been wanting to for an hour, standing too close to the bar and buttoning her cardigan over the pocket with Kit’s margin in it. She did not look at me. She looked at the pump handles.

“You said first,” she said. “If there’s anything.”

The sheet lay in my cardigan an inch from my hand, with its ten to ten and its Doris and my friend’s quick neat writing going out at the music round like a candle. I thought of the tin on Morwenna’s knee. I thought: it is forty minutes, and it is Morwenna, and I have been given a perfectly good explanation by the lady herself.

“Not yet,” I said.

“Right.” She nodded at the pump handles. “I’m off duty. I haven’t seen a lock-in. I’ve spent the evening in a tent.” Jory let her out like a cat, and the smell of the harbour came in and went out again behind her, and I understood that I had now kept four things from her, and that the fourth had come easier than the third.

Five minutes after that, at ten to eleven by the clock over the till, Pieter de Vries got down from his stool. He turned up the collar of the linen jacket, in July, in a bolted room, and said something low to Jory. Jory shot the bolt a hand’s breadth and let him out into the dark. The window was uncurtained at one corner, and I saw the pale shape of the jacket pass the glass and go downhill, towards the Steps and the quay, with the quick short walk of a man who has made an appointment and is afraid of being early.

I did not follow him. I will say that plainly, because I have been asked since, and by more than one person. I sat with the tin of Thursdays and squared another week, and then another, and the sheets would not stay squared. Tamsin snored. Nance, in the inglenook, had begun on a hymn under his breath and been told by the Seconds to carry on, as it was better than the darts. At five to eleven I got up, because the room had become unbearably warm and the saffron cake lay in me like a stone, and I asked Jory to let me out for air.

The Lantern’s door opens on the head of Pilchard Steps. Beyond the lamp over the step the dark began at once, and in it the whole of the harbour breathed, the flood making over the mud with that sullen thick lapping a young tide has, a rope creaking against a ring somewhere below, a boat knocking its fender on the wall. The air smelled of weed and diesel and, from the far side of the quay, a bonfire somebody should not have lit. I stood with my hand on the doorpost and the Jam Tarts’ sheet in my pocket and thought of nothing whatever, which I have noticed is the condition in which the worst news finds a person.

From the quay, below me in the dark, a man cried out. It was short, and it was cut off, as though a hand had been put across it. Then there was a splash, heavier than any fish.

chapters.title: Man in the Water
chapters.html:
Nobody runs in Trevenna after the age of forty, because of the steps, and I was fifty-eight, and I ran.

There are forty-three of them in three flights, cut out of the cliff by the pilchard-women with no thought for anybody’s knees, and the third flight is greener than the others and has a rope for a rail. I took the first two without noticing them. On the third I had the rope in my hand, and it burned, and I came off the bottom step on to the Hard with my glasses bouncing on their bootlace and my own breath loud in my ears.

The harbour was a black dish with the lamps of the Lantern lying broken in it. The tide had perhaps an hour and a half on it, over the mud, and the water at the foot of the quay steps stood higher than I would have guessed. At the top of the steps stood a steamer trunk with brass corners, strapped up for a journey, and on its lid a herring gull, which turned its head to look at me and did not trouble to move.

“Rope!” said a voice. “Dot. Anything.”

Jago was in the water. He was at the bottom of the steps with the flood to his chest, in his shirt, his coat thrown in a heap on the stone, hauling at something pale with both hands. I had seen him lift the end of an engine. I had never seen him look small. The pale thing was a man’s back, the linen jacket ballooned with air, riding face-down like a gull asleep, and it was swinging away from him on the swell and coming back, and each time it came back Jago got a little less of it.

There was a stack of lobster pots on the Hard, and across the stack lay a boat hook, the kind with a brass tip, which belonged to the Margery Jane moored under the wall. I took it. I went down the steps on my backside, because the weed on them was as slippery as soap, and I reached out as far as I could with my skirt in the water and caught the jacket by the collar.

“Pull,” said Jago.

“I am pulling.”

“Pull harder.”

“I am fifty-eight.”

“That’s the size of it,” said Jago, through his teeth, and the jacket came.

We got him in between the boat and the wall, where there was a gap of about a yard and a half, with the Margery Jane’s fender grinding against the granite on one side and the stone going by on the other, rough as a file. His head knocked on it twice. I heard it. Then Jago had him by the belt and the collar and went up the steps backwards like a man carrying a sack of coal out of a flood, and we laid him on the stones of the Hard among the lobster pots, which smelled of old bait and rope, and Jago sat down heavily where he was and let his arms hang.

I knelt. In 1943 I learned artificial respiration from Miss Treffry of the Third Plymouth Guides, who taught it with a sort of fury, kneeling astride a volunteer in the church hall and leaning like a woman rolling pastry. In 1972 Ned and I had spent six Tuesday evenings in the Methodist schoolroom with a man from St John Ambulance and a rubber doll called Annie, a course Ned attended in a rage of embarrassment with his cap on his knee. I remembered both. I could not remember which of them was supposed to be better, so I did the sensible thing and did what Annie had taught.

He was not breathing. I turned him on to his side and water ran out of him in a quantity I would not have credited, and then I turned him back, and tilted his head, and put my mouth over his, which tasted of harbour and Polo mints, and breathed, and pressed with the heel of my hand, and counted. I counted in the voice of Miss Treffry. I was aware of people arriving: the scrape of boots on the Hard, Kit’s torch shaking, Tamsin with a blanket from the Lantern’s settle, Wilf Hosken saying “Lord” over and over in a conversational tone, and under it all a thin continuous murmur which I took to be the Reverend Nance saying the Collect.

“Right,” said a voice above me. “Facts.”

Demelza came down the last flight at a dead run with her helmet in her hand, and went on her knees on the other side of him. She must have been halfway up Net Loft Row.

“Four minutes,” I said. “There was a pulse, I think. Thin as a thread.”

“Is there now?” Two fingers went under his jaw. “Right. Go on, Dot, I’ve got him. Kit! The Lantern, nine-nine-nine, ambulance and the Inspector. Trevenna Hard, the quay steps. Run.”

Kit ran. I let her take over. I had the strange sense of having been relieved from a watch, and I sat back on my heels, and my arms began to shake.

He coughed. It was an ugly sound, as though something were being dragged up out of a drain, and it was followed by a second and a third and by a long ragged pull of air, and Demelza turned him on to his side and held him there with her knee against his back. He did not wake. His eyes were half open and showed only white. There was a cut behind his right ear, welling thinly, and I looked at it and thought: the boat, or the granite. Or. I am not a doctor, and I said so, aloud, to nobody, twice.

The ambulance takes forty minutes from Truro. It is a statement about Cornwall as much as about the ambulance. We spent them on the Hard, in the lamplight, among the lobster pots: Demelza with two fingers at the Dutchman’s throat and her face quite empty, which is what her face does when she is working; Tamsin and Kit holding a blanket over him like a roof; Nance on his knees on the wet stones with his bicycle clips on, still murmuring; and the tide climbing the quay steps a stair at a time, behind our backs, so that I could count the hours in the weed lines, each one a darker green and a shade more wet.

Jago sat on a lobster pot with his shirt clinging to him and the sea running out of his trousers and passed his hands over his head again and again, as though to check that it was still there. He shook with a big slow shaking like a boat on a mooring. I put the second blanket round him.

“You were quick,” I said.

“I was close.”

“How close?”

He looked at the water.

“Where were you going, Jago?” Demelza did not look up from the Dutchman’s throat. She said it as she might have said the time.

“Walking.”

“The Lantern’s at the top of the Steps. Your door’s behind you. You were at the bottom, on the quay side, with your coat on.” She nodded at the heap on the stone. “You didn’t take it off to come out for the air.”

“I heard a man go in,” said Jago, “and I went in after him. That’s what I’ve got. That’s all I’ve got.”

And he shut his mouth. I knew that mouth. It was the mouth that had wiped one tumbler for a full minute on the Friday night and said, Leave it, Dot. He sat there steaming in the lamplight with his head down, and the only sound he made was the sound of a very large man trying to breathe quietly.

“Dot,” said Demelza. “His pockets. Anything that says what he’s taken, or who to ring.”

I did it because I was told. He was on his side with his sodden jacket rucked round his ribs, and I went through it as one goes through the pockets of a child’s coat. A hotel key on a brass tag, The Drowned Lantern, 2. A leather wallet, which I put into Demelza’s hand without opening. A handkerchief like a wet rag. And in the inside breast pocket a Dutch paperback, swollen to twice its size, the cover showing a woman looking over her shoulder at a house, the pages stuck together like a slice of cake. As I drew it out something slid from between the cover and the first leaf, where the board had held it dry, and fell on my knee.

It was a piece of paper folded in four. It was soft as a handkerchief, and it weighed what rag weighs. A binder knows old paper by the thumb before the eyes have caught up, and my thumb knew it, and it was dry at the middle and cool at the edges, and the fold had that faint crackle at the crease that only rag will give.

I did not decide to. I want that understood. My hand did it, the way it squares a pile of paper, and when I understood what it had done the leaf was in my cardigan pocket with the Jam Tarts’ sheet and a lemon sherbet, and Demelza was bent over the Dutchman with her back to me, and nobody on the Hard was looking in my direction. It is the one advantage of being fifty-eight and in a cardigan. I have never in my life been looked at in an emergency.

Headlights came down the lane at twenty to twelve, two pairs, a long way apart. The ambulance came first, its light turning blue on the wet of the Hard, and two big calm men got out of it and did everything without speaking, and took the Dutchman away in a red blanket on a stretcher, with Demelza walking beside it with her hand on the rail. Behind it, at his own pace, came the Inspector’s Rover. Garrow got out in the raincoat bound in rexine and looked at the wet stone, the trunk, the lobster pots, the gull (which at last had gone), and Jago Rowe in a blanket. He took a long time about it.

“Mrs Pellow, dear,” he said. “Again.”

“Inspector.”

“Mr Rowe. You’re wet.”

“I am.”

“I should like to know why.”

“I pulled him out.”

“And the rest of it?”

Jago said nothing. It was his entire statement. Garrow looked at him with the face of a man being shown a locked door, and then at me, and I put my hands in my cardigan pockets, and one of them closed on a folded leaf of paper, and I looked at the harbour with my most innocent expression, which is the one I use for customers who ask if I do gold-tooling.

I got up the first flight and the second. On the third, where the rope is, my knees went all at once, as though someone had cut a thread, and I sat down on a step. It was cold and wet and I found I was very interested in the weed on it. A hand came under my elbow. It was a thin hand, bony, with a gentle strength in it, and I thought absurdly of a stranger offering me his seat on a bus. I looked up. It was Nance. His bicycle clips were still on.

“Forgive me,” he said. “I am sure it is nothing.”

We went up the lane at the pace of the very old. He wheeled his bicycle in one hand, which he had fetched from the wall of the Lantern without being asked, and held my elbow with the other, and said not one word, which I had not known he could do. At my gate he waited until I had found my key.

“Good night, Mrs Pellow.”

“Good night, Mr Nance. Thank you.”

“Not at all,” said Nance. “I am sure it is nothing.” And he went off down the hill with the bicycle ticking beside him.

Quire was on the kitchen table, offended by the hour. I put on the forty-watt bulb and took the leaf out of my cardigan and unfolded it under the light.

It was damp at the edges, where the paperback had held the water out like a man holding a door, and dry at the middle. Laid paper, rag, with the chain lines as wide apart as a woman’s finger. Brown ink gone the colour of weak tea in the thin strokes, in a careful upright hand with the long s, the hand of a man writing with his tongue between his teeth. I laid it between two sheets of blotting paper from the dresser drawer and put Ned’s Cruden’s Concordance on top, a book which has been of use to me exactly once, and then, because I could not help it, I lifted the corner.

At the head of the page, ruled off with a line that had taken some trouble, was a heading, put there so that a man could find his place in the dark. Cape Cornwall to the Longships. The leaf had been folded in four. The creases were soft with handling, and none of them was mine.

chapters.title: Wet Boots
chapters.html:
At ten past five on Friday morning I sat up in bed and said “Loveday” aloud, to Quire, who had spent the night on the foot of the bed for the first time since Ned died and did not consider the remark addressed to her.

I had not slept, exactly. I had lain with my eyes shut while the evening went past me in the wrong order, the sheet and the cake and the splash and the weed lines on the steps, and somewhere towards four the line from the leaf had come and stood beside another thing I knew, as two people who have not met come to stand together at a funeral. From Cape Cornwall to the Longships, two leagues and a half, keeping the Brisons well open to the west. Loveday had said it in her library, with the buckets under every third shelf, in her bark, with her eyes shut, and I had thought it a beautiful sentence and put it away.

A pilot heads his pages. A man who copies out directions for two leagues of bad water takes several leaves to do it, and he puts the stretch he is writing at the top of each, so that by a lantern in a gale, with his thumb on the line, he can find his place. The first two leaves of the Carne Rutter were in a plastic bag in Garrow’s keeping, wearing their Cape Cornwall like a hat. This was the third.

Kit’s list had given sixty-four leaves; I had read the line in the church hall. Four were in the false book. That left sixty gone to wherever it was they had gone, and one of them had come out of a Dutchman’s paperback, out of a Dutchman’s pocket, out of the harbour. I took it from under the Concordance and held it to the grey window, and it was what it had been at midnight. It lay on my palm and weighed nothing and had been going about the world for three hundred and fifty-eight years. I distrusted how easily the arithmetic went into a sentence. A Dutchman had held a real leaf. That was all I knew, and it is a very different thing from knowing why.

Kit was on my step at half past seven with his hands hanging, and “Sorry” was out of him before I had the door open.

“They’ve kept Jago.”

“Who has?”

“Garrow. He’s in the cell at Demelza’s. On suspicion of the attack on the Dutchman, they’re saying. Sorry. It’s all over the Co-op.” He swallowed. “The Dutchman’s at Treliske. They say he’ll live. They say it the way they say it about March.”

“Jago pulled him out of the water.”

“That’s what everybody’s said. Mrs Bolitho says it’s the same thing seen from the other side.”

I gave him tea, and he drank it standing, holding the cup in both hands, and looked at the clock three times. I left him in the shop with Tamsin in the yard and told her that if he said “Sorry” more than twice an hour she was to put a sheet of Davey board over his head.

The police station at Trevenna is the front room of the police house at the bottom of Church Lane, between the chapel and the Co-op, and it has the dignity of a bus shelter. There is a counter. There is a wall clock whose tick can be heard from the lane. There is a filing cabinet with its bottom drawer open for ever, a plastic ficus dusted quite recently with a certain loneliness, and a photograph of the Queen hung well away from the damp. At the back a door stood open the width of a hand on the cell, a whitewashed cupboard which had last held a drunk in 1984 and a pig in 1971. Through the gap I saw a bunk and a large grey back turned to the wall. A pair of sea-boots stood on end against the radiator pipe with a newspaper stuffed in each, to draw the water. He did not turn. I think he knew my step.

Demelza sat behind the counter in yesterday’s uniform with a mug in both hands and an expression like wet slate. She had been up for twenty-six hours. I had counted.

“Facts,” she said, without any hope.

I took the leaf out of my cardigan, in its blotting paper, and laid it on the counter between the ficus and the stapler. “I have something. I found it this morning. On the quay steps, caught in the weed, folded up, just about where he went in. I thought it might have come out of his pocket.”

I had worked the lie out in the night, and it was a good one in the sense that every word of it was true but one. It had a hole in it you could have driven the ambulance through. I had worked out, too, what the truth would do to her. A leaf taken from the pocket of a man who might die, before the Inspector came, with the constable in charge of the scene on her knees not four feet off: Garrow would have the badge off her by Monday, and I should have put it in his hand.

Demelza looked at me for as long as it takes a kettle to make up its mind. Then she looked away, at the Queen, and said, “Right. Found on the quay steps. Time?”

“About seven.”

She wrote it in the notebook with the elastic band. It was the worst thing she could have done. She believed me at once. She had been up all night and I was the nearest thing she had to a friend in the parish, and she set down my lie in her careful hand because she trusted me, and I stood on the other side of the counter and saw exactly what it was going to cost, and paid it anyway.

“Don’t touch it,” she said, and then, since I plainly had, “Never mind. What is it?”

“I think it’s the Carne. I want to look at the first leaf.”

“Garrow left the Carne in the safe.” She said it slowly. “For the man from the county record office, Thursday week. He said old paper was in the wrong place wherever it was.”

She took a key on a chain from inside her tunic and went down on one knee to a green safe in the corner behind the ficus, and when she stood up she had a flat evidence bag in her arms and a face that had decided something. She set it under the swan-neck lamp on the desk. Through the plastic I could see the rutter lying open, the cover back, the first leaf on top. I laid mine on the blotter beside it, took the loupe out of my cardigan, and said aloud what I found, because there are things one must say in order to believe them.

“The chain lines are the same distance apart. A quarter of an inch wider than the day-book’s, you can see it, there and there. The same rag, with the same flecks in it, like pepper. The same ink, brown, gone to tea in the thin strokes, with a bite in the downstroke where the quill dug in. The same hand.” I moved the loupe. “Look at the long s, how it leans, like a man walking into a wind. And that is the day-book.” I lowered the glass to the middle of the bag. “There’s the lion in his fence. This leaf has no lion. It’s not that. It’s the book.”

Demelza looked from one to the other. She said nothing for some time, and the ficus listened. Then she said, quite softly, “If I put this in the book, it’s the Dutchman’s.”

“Yes.”

“Garrow gets it, and he writes the whole case round Pieter de Vries and stops looking. I don’t say he’s wrong. I say I’d like another day.”

“You can’t do that.”

“I’m not doing anything. I’m having a cup of tea with a member of the public who has brought in an old bit of paper, and I’m giving it back to her.” She slid it across the counter. “Not the Bindery. He’ll be through it by tomorrow. And not your cardigan.”

“It’s where I keep most things.”

“I’d noticed,” said Demelza, and for a second the corner of her mouth moved.

The door opened at five to twelve without a knock, and the weather changed.

Garrow had not slept either. His raincoat looked as though it had been slept in by a larger man. He had Pascoe, his detective constable, behind him like a hat-stand, and he took in the room, the counter, the ficus, Demelza standing rather suddenly, and me, who had just put a folded square of blotting paper into my cardigan with the air of a woman posting a letter.

“Mrs Pellow, dear. It’s as well you’re here. You’ll have it from the Co-op by dinner, and I’d like it said correctly.”

I sat on the one chair that was not a Windsor, and he stood before the Queen with his hands behind him.

“A Rotterdam dealer comes to Cornwall in June,” said Garrow. “He’s known to the Dutch police, I learned this morning, in a small way, for the tax. He spends a fortnight in a village that has a fine manuscript. He buys nothing at the fair. And when a false book turns up, who tells me, unprompted, that the paper in it is probably Dutch?”

“He was being helpful.”

“People who volunteer are people who are afraid you’ll find it out yourself. Mr de Vries then has a trunk strapped on the quay at eleven at night and a berth on Wilf Hosken’s boat, the Margery Jane, for five in the morning, paid for in cash, after I told him in so many words to stay. That’s a man who made the false book, or paid for it, and was leaving, and quarrelled with his partner on the way out.”

“What partner?”

“Rowe,” said Garrow. “Or your nephew.”

“Kit?”

“He catalogued the book, Mrs Pellow, dear. He knows what it should look like and what it shouldn’t. He has no alibi for Saturday night but a darts match nobody remembers. His uncle taught him to sew. Mr Rowe was Ned Pellow’s closest friend, he has keys to half the village, he held no love for the dead man’s hold on his lease, and he was soaked to the chest at ten to eleven last night on a quay he won’t say why he was on. I have charged men on less.”

“Jago pulled him out.”

“A man who pushes another into a harbour and then pulls him out has excellent grounds for being wet. We see it in drunks. A change of heart; a witness on the Hard.” He glanced at the gap in the cell door and the sea-boots stuffed with newspaper. “Wet boots, Mrs Pellow. Oldest evidence in the book.”

“And the cut behind his ear?”

“The boat.”

“Or,” said Demelza.

“Or,” said Garrow, and nodded as though she had said something perfectly sensible about the weather. “I’m for Truro. The Dutchman’s hotel room, his bank, and the magistrates, who sit at two. When I’ve done I shall have something to say to somebody, and I’d be grateful, Constable, if you’d keep Mr Rowe comfortable. Mrs Pellow. Dear.”

He went. Pascoe went after him, nodding to the ficus on the way out as though it were senior.

The worst of it was that it was good. It had a Dutchman in it, and Dutch paper, and a trunk, and a berth, and a cut head, and wet boots, and a landlord who would not speak. It had two men for the part of the partner. It lacked nothing but the truth, which is a thing inspectors seldom miss. And in the pocket of my cardigan lay the one piece of evidence that would have made it perfect, the single leaf that turned Pieter de Vries from a man who knew about a forgery into a man who held the proceeds. I was sitting on it. I did not believe the theory. I had no better. It is a poor place to stand.

The telephone on the counter rang while Demelza was still looking at the door.

“Trevenna police,” she said. And then, with a change in her back: “Miss Penhallow.”

Even where I sat I could hear it: the faint bark of a woman who has never in her life trusted a telephone to carry her voice, and who sends it to the end of the wire at full strength. “No,” said Demelza. “He’s helping us with our enquiries.” The bark rose. “I see. Since when?” She wrote something down and underlined it. “Your man of business. Yes. Mr Rowe keeps the estate’s books. And on Thursday night he was on his way to you. At eleven. With...” She stopped. “The quarter’s rents. Across the quay, in the dark.” She pulled the receiver an inch from her ear. “No, I’m not suggesting anything, Miss Penhallow. I’m asking. Accounts are best done at night, yes. Because nobody interrupts. I’ll write that down.”

Jago Rowe could not, to the certain knowledge of the village, add up a bar bill without using his fingers, of which he had nine. Loveday had been telling people for some years that he kept her books, and the village had received it as it receives a bishop’s remarks about his housekeeper. It had never believed a word.

From the earpiece, tiny and furious, a high thin whistle began, like a kettle coming to the boil: the hearing aid, a mile of wire away and at full cry. Demelza held the receiver at arm’s length and let it sing. Then she covered the mouthpiece with her palm and looked at me across the counter, and I had never seen so reasonable a person look so uncertain.

“Is she lying,” said Demelza, “or is she in love?”

chapters.title: Kit's Mistake
chapters.html:
Ned taught Kit to sew in the summer of 1965, when Kit was ten and had to sit on a hassock and the family Bible to reach the frame.

The hassock was St Petroc’s. Ned had borrowed it in the spring to mend the pulpit Bible and never taken it back, and the then vicar mourned it to the end of his days. It said PRAY FOR THE NAVY in wool. Kit sat on it with his knees up and his tongue out of the corner of his mouth, and Ned sat opposite, which meant doing everything backwards, since Ned was left-handed and the boy was not. He never once said it was wrong. He said, “Again, but slower,” and at the end of the afternoon he said that Kit had a good needle in him, and Kit went red from the collar to the hair. I was thirty-four, at the window with a basket of mending, and I remember thinking that I had never seen two people so quietly pleased.

I thought of it that Friday afternoon, because Kit was standing in the middle of the shop with his hands hanging at his sides, and he looked, for the second time in my life, like a boy waiting to be told that he had done it wrong.

It was ten past three. I had put a pan of paste on the gas ring in the corner for something to do with my hands, and the smell of clove stood in the room like a guest. Tamsin was at the Co-op for sugar, and I blessed the sugar.

“Sorry,” said Kit. “Auntie Dot. Sorry. I’ve got to tell you something. I’ve been trying since Friday week, and every time I got near it something fell off a shelf.”

I took the spoon out of the paste, and wiped it on the rim, and said, “Sit.”

He sat on the stool at the counter, the one customers never use. He put his hands between his knees.

“The Wednesday,” he said. “Before. I was doing the Carne for the valuation, the collation, you know, you count the leaves and hold each one up to the window. And the chain lines were wrong. Too close, for a book that age. I thought it was a binder’s blank at first, flyleaf stock, you get it. Then I turned a leaf and there was a lion in a fence.”

“And you took it to Aubrey.”

“I took it to Mr Trevithick. He went very quiet. He always called me Christopher. He said, ‘Christopher, you will say nothing about this to anyone. A man can be mistaken, and if I am not mistaken it is a good deal worse. I shall deal with it.’ And I said yes. I said, Yes, Mr Trevithick, because, you know what he was like, and because I thought he’d put it right. He always did.” His thumb went along the edge of the counter, the left one, the nail bitten to the quick. “And he’s dead. And nobody knows I knew.”

“He wrote to the solicitor that same night,” I said. “I’ve read the letter. It’s dated the twelfth.”

His head came up, quite white. “Did he?”

“He did.”

“Then he believed me.” He said it as if it were the first thing anyone had given him in a week. Then his face did something I preferred not to watch, and he looked at the pan.

“You did what your employer told you,” I said. “It is a thing most people are punished for not doing.”

“That’s not the bit.” He drew a breath through his teeth. “Sorry. The Thursday. I came here, Auntie Dot. At six.”

I stirred the paste. It is a thing the hands do.

“I’d borrowed Ned’s Cockerell, for the binding notes. I thought I’d put it back before the quiz. The door was on the latch and Mr Trevithick was at the bench with the lamp on and the rutter open in front of him. And he was happy. You’d have said so. Like a man who’s found his glasses. He said I’d done him a great service and he’d say so in writing. I put the book on the shelf and I put my hand on the bench for something to lean on, because I thought if I stood there he would ask me to say about the paper again, out loud, and I didn’t want to. I moved the lamp. It was in my eyes. And I went out, and I went to the Lantern and sat next to you till closing, and I never said.”

“Did you tell Demelza?”

“She asked me flat, the Friday, in the lane, whether I’d been in the press room. And I said not since Easter last year.” He looked at his hands. “I don’t know why. My mouth said it. Sorry.”

“You told a lie to a police officer who used to take you to the pictures.”

“Used to,” said Kit.

I put the spoon down. I went to the paste shelf, past the ring and the cat, took down Ned’s toffee tin and opened it, and under four bone folders and a seam of cedar dust I found the corner of burned paper. I had meant to do this the other way round, to tell him first what I knew and let him tell me what he knew, and I had let him go first, and it was too late to be tactful. I put the scrap into his hand with the loupe.

“There is something I should have said on Monday.”

He read it twice through the glass. K. – cat. 114 –. And lower down, in the silver of the pencil, Mrs P. in the mor. I watched the colour go out of him by stages, the way it goes out of a sky.

“That’s my number,” he said. “I put 114 on it myself. I typed it on the valuation sheet. Mr Trevithick would have... K. is...” He did not finish.

“It is your number. It isn’t you.”

“Does it matter?”

It does not matter, I thought, to anyone with a jury. “It was in the stove,” I said. “Somebody burned the pastedowns so they should not be read. I found this under the grate on Monday.”

“Monday.” He looked up. “You’ve had it since Monday. And Demelza?”

“She saw it that morning. She said she would come with a bag when she knew what she was going to say, and to whom.”

“She didn’t bag it.” He said it flatly, to the scrap. “She hid it from Garrow.”

“She postponed it.”

“It’s the same thing in a uniform, Auntie Dot.” He put the paper down on the counter as one puts down something hot. “If he finds that out, he’ll have her. You can’t give it to him. You’d be giving him her.”

I looked at him. He had been caught in a lie, and he had a charred scrap of paper in front of him with his own initial on it, and the first thing he had thought of was the woman who had thrown him over. “You might consider yourself for ten seconds,” I said. “I should take it as a favour.”

“Sorry,” said Kit, and very nearly smiled.

I put the scrap in my cardigan pocket, where it joined a pencil, a loupe and a ball of string. The cardigan was by now the most heavily incriminated garment in Cornwall.

The bell went, and nobody pretended it was a customer.

Garrow came in first, in the raincoat, with a folded sheet of foolscap in his hand. Pascoe came behind him, and a uniformed constable I did not know with a face like a shut gate, and behind them in the doorway, in her helmet, with the notebook held against her chest in both hands, stood Demelza. The lane at her back was full of the Friday light, and Mrs Bolitho’s geraniums, and, a decent distance down, a white Ford the colour of a bandage with two more men in it.

“Mrs Pellow, dear,” said Garrow. “Mr Pellow. I’m obliged to you both for staying put.” He unfolded the foolscap and cleared his throat and read aloud in the voice of a man giving the minutes of a meeting about drains.

“Whereas it has been made to appear on oath before the justices sitting at Truro this afternoon that there are reasonable grounds for believing that evidence relating to the death of Aubrey Charles Trevithick, on or about the thirteenth day of July, is to be found on the premises known as the Marigold Bindery, Fish Cellar Lane, Trevenna, comprising the shop, the press room and the net loft...”

I went on stirring. The paste had begun to catch at the bottom. I could not stop and I did not want to; the smell of clove came up out of the pan, warm and sweet, Christmas in a shop in July where a man was being read a warrant. The pots stood in their row along the counter, and I watched Garrow’s mouth over the top of them. I heard “seize and remove,” and “the person of Christopher John Pellow.” I thought of the girl who would be coming up the lane with a bag of sugar, and blessed the sugar again.

“Christopher Pellow,” said Garrow, folding the paper, “I am arresting you on suspicion of the murder of Aubrey Trevithick. You do not have to say anything unless you wish to do so, but what you say may be given in evidence.”

Kit stood up. He did it carefully, as if the floor might not take his weight. He said “Sorry” to the boards, in the voice of a boy of ten with a needle through his thumb.

“Your left thumb, Mr Pellow,” said Garrow, “is on the underside of the lamp that stood over the dead man’s work. You told Constable Kitto on the fourteenth of July that you had not set foot in that room since Easter last year. One of those statements is untrue, and the lamp can’t tell lies.”

“I was going to say. I came here to say it to my aunt first.”

“I’m sure you did.”

“He did,” I said. “He has been in this shop since ten past three. I can give you the time to the minute.”

“I’m sure you can, Mrs Pellow, dear. You may give it to me again at Truro.” Garrow looked at the pan. “You may put that down.”

“If I stop stirring it, Inspector, it will be glue.”

“Then stir,” said Garrow, and, to do him justice, for an instant he looked very tired.

From the press room came the sound of drawers being opened by a man who did not know which of them stuck. Kit turned at the door. He looked at nobody; he looked at the row of pots.

“Auntie Dot.”

“Yes.”

“Sorry. The cat. I’ve been giving her the good tin at six, the pilchards. She won’t touch the other. She hisses at me. It’s how you know she’s fond.”

“I shall give her the good tin.”

“And not the...”

“Not the other.”

“Thank you,” said Kit, to the doorframe, and went out between Pascoe and the man with the shut face. I heard his shoes go down the step, one, two, as they had gone down it at ten, on errands for Ned.

Demelza stood against the jamb to let them by. She looked at the lintel. She did not look at Kit, and she did not look at me, and I had never seen her so closely occupied with a piece of wood.

“Constable,” said Garrow, going past. “The second car.”

“Sir.”

They put Garrow in the first car, alone, and Kit in the back of the second between two men who did not know him, and Demelza in the front beside the driver with the notebook on her knee. The blue lamp stayed dark. It went down Fish Cellar Lane at the pace of a hearse, past the geraniums and the net lofts and the corner by the old pilchard cellar, and the tail-lights turned the colour of Mrs Bolitho’s flowers, and went round the bend, and out.

Quire had come to the step. She sat in the last of the sun with her torn ear to the lane and her bib very white, and she watched them to the end of it, as she watches a hole in the skirting, and did not hiss. Then she turned her head and looked at me, and at the pan, and at the empty stool, and with the air of a person who has been kept waiting asked for her tin.

I found I did not know which was the good one.

chapters.title: Nothing Left on the Bench
chapters.html:
It turned out that the good tin was the one with the fish on the label. I learned this by opening both and setting them on the step side by side, like a woman laying two hats on a bed, and letting Quire choose. She sniffed the tin with the cat in a basket on it, which I had bought, and gave me a look I shall carry to my grave. Then she ate the pilchards with her back to me, steadily, as though the afternoon had been arranged for her convenience.

It was a quarter past six. The constable with the face like a shut gate had allowed me to fetch the tins from under the shop counter on condition that he looked in my bag, and he had looked in it with an interest that was not unkind. “Cat food, Mrs Pellow,” he said. I said yes. He wrote it down.

Garrow’s Rover came up the lane at half past, in second gear, and he got out of it like a man who has spent three hours in the company of the county’s idea of a sandwich. He had left Kit in Truro, he said, with people who were very good at it. He did not say at what, and I did not ask.

“We shall want a second sweep, Mrs Pellow, dear. The gentleman from Scenes of Crime will be here at eight tomorrow, and he doesn’t care to find things moved.”

“I haven’t moved anything.”

“No,” said Garrow. “And you won’t.”

Pascoe had a roll of white gummed tape, a rubber stamp, and the face of a boy given the best job at the school fête. He laid a strip across the join of my yellow door and its frame at the height of my hip and smoothed it with the side of his thumb, as I should have smoothed a hinge. He did it well. I told him so, which I regretted, because he went pink and said thank you, ma’am. Then he did the sash window, and then he went round the back and did the yard door, and I heard him whistling through his teeth among the bins.

“I have a pan of paste on the gas ring,” I said.

“It was turned off at ten to five.”

“Then it is rubber by now.”

“I’m sorry for it,” said Garrow, and the dreadful thing is that I think he was.

“I should like my bone folder.”

“I’m afraid everything on the premises is an exhibit.”

“It is a piece of cow, Inspector. I have had it thirty years.”

“Then it will have a very full history,” said Garrow, “and be returned to you with a label.”

“There is the Chapel’s pulpit Bible on the bench. It has come away at Leviticus.”

“It will be perfectly safe.”

“It is a Methodist Bible, Inspector. It was safer with less company.”

He pretended not to hear. He touched the brim of his hat to me, which no policeman had ever done, and I had the impression that somebody had told him to. The Rover reversed down the lane with a great deal of noise, and a young constable I did not know was left on an upturned fish crate beside Mrs Bolitho’s geraniums, with the look of a boy waiting for a bus that has been abolished.

The seal was a narrow strip of paper with a red stamp. Any child could have peeled it off in a minute, and it kept nothing in and nothing out. But it said that someone had noticed, as a plaster says so on a graze, and the door beneath it, which is Marigold yellow for Ned’s mother’s favourite flower, looked like something that had been hurt. Since I came to Trevenna in 1962 there had not been a bench within twenty yards of my bed that I was forbidden to stand at. I stood at the foot of the step for some time, to see how it felt, and it felt like standing at the foot of a step.

I had a trestle in St Petroc’s hall and a canvas tool roll under it, left behind on Sunday when the fair broke up, and nobody had told me I might not fetch them. I went because it was somewhere to go with my hands empty.

The fair had ended on Sunday, officially. Three dealers had stayed on all week in the hall, because the chairman had held the float and the chairman’s cash box was in the vestry under his daughter’s eye and a bank manager’s, and nobody could be paid until the one and the other agreed. That afternoon they had agreed. When I came in at seven the last stalls were coming down. A man who sold sea charts was rolling his stock into tubes. A woman with cookery books and lace bobbins was folding a banner into smaller and smaller squares. At the far end, where Pieter de Vries had kept his maps, a dust sheet hung over the trestles with a card pinned to it in his firm square hand, BACK SHORTLY, and nobody had had the heart to take it down.

The Institute was there as well, having come to borrow the long tables for the regatta tea. The hall did what a roomful of people does when the woman they have been discussing walks in: it became extremely busy. Doris Rosevear carried a chair to the far wall, where there were already eleven. Edna Chegwidden measured a trestle with a tape, twice. Miss Hocking counted teaspoons aloud, in tens, with the fixed attention of a woman defusing something.

Only Gwen Trewhella, who is deaf, looked up with her whole face and said at the pitch of a woman hailing a boat across a bay, “DOT! IS IT TRUE THEY’VE TOOK YOUR KIT FOR IT?”

A teaspoon fell. Miss Hocking lost her place and began again from nought.

“Ned’s nephew,” I said.

“WHAT?”

“Yes, Gwen.”

“WELL, I NEVER. AND HIM SUCH A POLITE BOY.”

It was the kindest thing anyone said to me that day, and it made matters worse. Doris steered her off by the elbow towards the urn, and over her shoulder, not quite to me and not quite to the urn, said that Morwenna had been asking after me, and was thinking of me, and would have come up with something hot only for her knees. I said that was kind of her. It was kind. I turned it over later, with the rest.

My trestle stood where I had left it by the tea urn. Somebody had wiped it down. The roll lay underneath, tied the way I tie it, and I knelt and went over it by touch, as you go through a child’s pockets: two folders, the dividers, the awl, a lump of tallow wax in a twist of paper, the needle book, the little brass gauge with the worn thumbwheel. Nothing the police wanted, because the police had not known it was there. It was not much. I held it against my chest like a woman on a station platform.

Reverend Nance was in the porch with an armful of hymn books, bicycle clips on, a cough drop travelling from one cheek to the other. He stood aside to let me out. “Forgive me, Mrs Pellow,” he said, “if there is anything...” His arms were so full that he could not offer me his hands, and the sentence had nowhere to go, so he shut his mouth on the cough drop. I said thank you, Mr Nance. I think we were both relieved.

Demelza was waiting at the foot of Fish Cellar Lane under the one lamp that works, in uniform, with her helmet under her arm, like a woman who has walked as far as the gate and found she cannot go through. The grey cuff of Kit’s jumper showed at her wrist.

“He’s had his tea,” she said, in case I was going to ask. “Sausage and chips from the canteen. He ate the chips.”

“And the sausage?”

“Said he’d leave it for the next man.” She made a noise through her nose that was not a laugh. “They’ve given him a blanket, Dot. It’s grey. It’s got a stripe.”

I said nothing, which was the right thing, and we stood there.

“I’ve been spoken to,” she said. “Garrow did it in the corridor at Truro with a sergeant going past for the effect. ‘Constable Kitto’s judgement in this matter has been compromised by an undeclared personal association.’ Fourteen months, and he calls it an association. It goes on my file on Monday.”

“Everyone in Trevenna knows about you and Kit. The gulls know.”

“The gulls aren’t Truro.” She turned the helmet round in her hands. “I’m to mind the police house. I’m to mind Jago Rowe in the front room. I’m to keep out of the Bindery and away from civilians connected with the inquiry, which is you. He put you last, I noticed, as if you were the easy one.”

“Then we shan’t discuss it.”

“No.”

We both looked up the lane at the door with its strip across it. “That’s Pascoe’s,” said Demelza. “He did seals at the Academy with a ruler.”

“He did it nicely.”

“He would.”

She unbuttoned the breast pocket of her tunic and took out the black leather wallet with her warrant card in it. “He said that if I felt I couldn’t keep to the rules of the service I knew where to put this. On his desk, in the morning.” She opened it under the lamp. The photograph showed a girl of twenty-six with her plait pinned up for the occasion and the expression of someone who has been told to stop smiling. We looked at it between us. On the chimney opposite a gull said something rude.

Then she shut the wallet, put it back, buttoned the flap and patted it flat, the way you put back a coin you have decided not to spend.

“Jago Rowe has said eleven words since two o’clock this morning,” she said. “Nine of them were ‘tea, please’. I’m going back to hear the other two.”

“Demelza.”

The scrap was in my cardigan pocket, with the loupe and the string, and for a moment it felt as warm as the stove had on Friday morning. I had promised to tell her first. I had told her first, on Monday, and she had said she would come with a bag, and had not. There was nothing I could give her that night but my fear, and she had enough of her own.

“Nothing,” I said. “Eat something.”

“Right,” said Demelza. “Facts.” She went down the lane, a short, wide woman with a helmet under her arm and her back very straight, and did not look round.

The search had put my paste pots out on the step. There were eight of them in a row with their lids on the ground beside them, because the constable who wanted the counter clear had not known where else a paste pot goes, and they looked like patients in a corridor. I sat down among them. Quire got on my knee, which she does not do, thought better of it, and moved to the pot with the least paste in it.

I counted what I had, as you count the till on a bad Friday. A pin-prick at the foot of a gathering, which proved that my husband had been fond of something he never mentioned. A charred corner of paper that said K. and Mrs P., which a man who wished to could read as Kit and Mrs Pellow, two people on one step. A leaf of a pilot’s book lying between blotters under a concordance. A cat. I noticed that I was holding the cat in particular, as though she were evidence.

Then I counted the other things, which are the ones that wake you. The Michaelmas rent, ninety-two pounds to the Harbour Trustees, who had let the building to the Pellows since 1951 and had never once been paid late. The electricity, with the new strip light in it. Takings since the fair, eleven pounds forty. Nine jobs pinned to the cork board behind the seal, each with a name and a date, and each name belonging to somebody who would hear by Sunday that the Bindery had a police strip across its door. In a village of six hundred a bookbinder is not a woman you send your grandmother’s hymnal to if she has been shut out of her own bench on suspicion of murder. One need not be unkind to be careful.

The good tin was forty-two pence. I worked that out too, sitting there, and it was the most cheerful sum of the evening.

Down on the Hard the children were playing sardines. One child hides, and everybody else hunts, and whoever finds her squeezes in beside her without a word, until the last seeker is left alone, hunting for a hiding place packed with giggling children. They had chosen the old lifeboat shed, whose door has not shut since Suez. I could see it from the step. The last seeker, a small boy in a pullover, went past the door with his hands out in front of him, the way you feel for a switch in the dark, while behind it nine of his friends held their breath. Then he went past it again.

I had done that.

The church clock was striking eleven as I reached the corner of the old pilchard cellar on Thursday night, and I counted the strokes, as one does, and by the last of them I was level with the press-room window. I was humming something from the music round, I could not tell you now what. The window was a square of black slate. I thought: he has gone home with my key in his pocket, and tomorrow he will bring it back with an accurate remark, and I shall be obliged to say thank you. I thought of my bed. I did not put my hand on the sash and say his name, and I did not so much as turn my head.

The doctor from Truro had said between ten and midnight, which is a doctor’s way of saying he would rather not. If it was before eleven, I had walked past Aubrey in the dark. If it was after, I had walked past whoever did it, and been walked past in return. I have never been able to decide which I should rather have. Garrow would say that if I had gone in there would have been two of us on the boards, and he would be right, and I have said as much to myself in the voice of a sensible woman at three in the morning a great many times. It makes no difference whatever. He was on one side of a pane of glass and I was on the other, thinking about my bed.

It was quite dark when Tamsin came. I had not heard her on the lane because she had come down from my cottage, with my brown teapot in its knitted cosy held in both hands like an offering, two mugs hooked on her fingers and the bag of sugar still under her arm. She had been carrying it about since ten past three. She had stood at the corner of the cellar for the whole of the warrant, she told me afterwards, and then gone to her mother’s for her tea so as not to be asked, and the policemen had taken her sleeping bag out of the loft and put it back with the zip the wrong way round, which she took personally.

At the time she said nothing at all. She sat down on the step below mine, among the pots, and poured, and put two sugars in my mug without asking, which is how I take it and which I had not known she knew. She gave it to me. We drank.

I know how long it was because the church clock struck the quarter and then the half. The children came up from the Hard in a straggle, and fathers whistled them in from doorways. The tide went on out under the quay, leaving its weed and its smell. Tamsin’s fingers were blue to the second knuckle, from some pen. She held the mug in both hands and looked at the harbour like a person reading small print. Quire left her pot and sat between us with her back to the pair of us, which is as near as she comes to a blessing.

Nobody had said a word to me for twenty minutes, and it was the most useful twenty minutes of the day. Everyone else that evening had talked to me from somewhere else, from the far side of a trestle or a lamp or a rule. Tamsin did it from the same step.

When the last of the tea was gone she set her mug down on a paste pot, wiped her hands on her jeans, and said, like a girl reading from a list in her head, “I’ve got a copy of Ned’s notebook. Some of it.”

chapters.title: Tamsin's Exercise Book
chapters.html:
“It got a B plus,” said Tamsin, and laid the exercise book on my kitchen table the way a woman lays down a hand of cards she knows is better than yours.

It was a quarter past ten. I had put the kettle on, because it is what one does, and moved Quire to the dresser among the blue-rimmed plates, which takes five minutes and a certain amount of language. The single bulb over the table made the room look as though it were being interviewed. Through the window above the sink the riding lights of the moored boats lay along the harbour in a short row, yellow as commas.

The book was red, school issue, with a label stuck on the front in a hand I knew from the shop order forms: TREVENNA, VANISHING TRADES. T. BRAY, 4B. Underneath, in green ink, someone had written Neat. More sea next time. L.

“That’s Mr Lanyon,” said Tamsin. “He set it in May. A trade that has gone or is going in your own parish. Everybody else did pilchard curing. Tommy Rosevear did pilchard curing twice and got a C. So I did bookbinding, because it was in the lane and I could watch.”

“You didn’t tell me.”

“You were busy being cross about the electricity bill.” She turned a page without looking at it. “You lent me the notebook on a Saturday. You said mind it, and you said you couldn’t read it yourself because you couldn’t stand to see his hand. I sat at the shop desk and you did the ledger. I’d done two pages and you said that’ll do, I’ve got to lock up, so I did two.”

I did remember. I remembered a green notebook going across the counter in my own hand, and thinking what a relief it was to have it out of the cupboard, and that I should never have to think of it again.

“I copied them exact,” said Tamsin. “The words, I mean. I tidied the rest.”

She had. I should like to say that I was too much moved to notice, but I am a bookbinder, and what I noticed was the hand. Ned wrote like a spider walking home from a wedding.
