Tamsin had taken what he wrote and set it down in a clear upright script like a row of well-sewn stitches, every seven crossed, every loop closed, with notes in square brackets in the margin where she had been unable to read him and said so. [pen changes here, green to blue-black.] [crossed out, can’t read, begins with H?] It was a better hand than mine. She watched me see that, and she did not look modest.

“You’ve tidied his sevens.”

“Everyone’s sevens. Mr Lanyon said it was an A for the handwriting and it didn’t count.”

“It counts with me.”

“Right,” said Tamsin. “So.” She flattened the book with the side of her hand, and I put on my glasses and read the first page.

PUPILS. Saturdays, and any evening I can stand it.

J.R., from 1951. Holds the paste. Will not sew. Says his fingers are for rope.

M. Hext (left-handed, forced right at school). 1955 to 58. Best I’ve had. Hook key to her for Saturdays. Fetch back.

Second frame to M.H., wedding present, 1958. She will use it.

C.J.P., my brother’s boy, 1965, aged ten. Sews like a wet Tuesday. Will come.

I laughed at the last. I could not help it; I had watched Kit sew, and Ned was exact. Then I read the third line, and the laugh went out of me like air from a bellows, and I read it again.

“Hext is a common name,” I said.

“In Trevenna?”

“There is Hedley Hext on the Chapel side. He is eighty-one and blind.”

“Was he a girl in 1955?”

“She wasn’t a Hext in 1955. She married Ronald in the spring of ‘fifty-eight.”

“The ink changes there. I put it in brackets.” Tamsin leaned over and put a finger on the margin. “I thought he’d written the list out fair afterwards. At the wedding, maybe. When he gave the frame.”

“I never knew there was a second frame.”

“Why would you? You didn’t read it.”

She was right, and she said it without any cruelty, which was worse. I took off my glasses and put them on again. The kettle had begun to tick on the ring behind me.

“Page two,” said Tamsin, and turned it for me.

1964. REGATTA BOOK for the committee. Foolscap ledger, 200 leaves, sewn on five cords, half calf, marbled sides, red label. Boards 2 mm millboard and not a hair more. It is carried down the quay in a wind by the chairman, and in 1931 Hocking’s father dropped the old one in the harbour and it took a boy in a punt, the tide table and most of an afternoon to get it back. Light enough to drop.

Charge: nine pounds and a pint (J.R.).

“Ned and his two millimetres,” I said, and something in the figure caught, as a nail catches in a cardigan sleeve. I could not see what. It was ten at night and I had been in a state of siege since half past three, and I let it go. “He always did know exactly what he wanted a book to weigh.”

“It’s the one she showed round at the WI,” said Tamsin. “Mum says. The one with the hinge she mended.”

“Yes.”

“Dot.”

“I know what you’re going to say.”

“I’m going to say it anyway.”

“Then I am going to say that it is an old man’s list, written in a good mood. Morwenna cleaned his brushes. She brought him pasties. She was a girl in a bright coat in a workshop and he was kind to her.” My voice had gone up, I noticed, into the register in which I speak to men from the gas board. “Morwenna Hext cannot bind a hymnbook. She has never mended anything in her life but a hem, and she did that badly.”

“She mended the Regatta Book’s back joint,” said Tamsin. “You said yourself you couldn’t see the join.”

I had no answer to that. I got up and made the tea, which was a thing to do with my hands, and filled the kettle again and set it back on the flame for a second pot, and sat down.

The funeral was a Tuesday in March, and the wind took the hymn sheets out of the porch and sent them over the churchyard wall like gulls. I had forgotten my hat. I stood in the front pew of St Petroc’s with my gloved hands folded and everyone’s good opinion of Ned coming at me from behind, a lovely man, a lovely man, and at “Abide With Me” someone took hold of my left hand. I had thought it would be Kit. It was Morwenna, with a glove on one hand and not the other, singing the alto line in her small steady voice and holding on through “change and decay” so hard that my wedding ring left a mark on the next finger for two days. When we sat down she did not let go, and neither did I. In the porch afterwards, when people were saying lovely, she was the only one who said, “He was a careful one, Dot.” It was the best thing that was said that day. I had kept it in my pocket for three years like a stone with a hole in it.

“She held my hand,” I said. “Through the hymn.”

“I know. Mum told me. She said she was lovely to you.”

“She was.”

“I’m not saying she wasn’t.” Tamsin’s voice was careful, and it came to me that she was sixteen and had never had to say this to anyone. “I’m saying write it all down and see where it goes. Mr Lanyon says that about essays.”

“I am not writing a case against Morwenna Hext in my kitchen at half past ten at night.”

“Then I will.” She held up her fingers, the blue ones, and began to turn them down. “Right. So. One. The woman in the mac smelled of church. Polish and candles. I thought vestry, I thought Mr Nance, so I went and sniffed things on Wednesday, in the hall. Everything churchy’s got beeswax. The polish and the tapers. And the only person in Trevenna who smells of both at once is the one that sells the tapers and does the brass.”

“Half the Institute does the brass on Wednesdays.”

“Half the Institute doesn’t keep eight hives.”

I thought of a golden tail of thread lying in a seam of my cutting board, and an envelope in my drawer, and I said nothing about it, which Tamsin noticed.

“Two. She pours with her left. At the fair, with the honey, and at the quiz when she did the tea for our table. She cuts cake with her left. And she signs the lifeboat tin with her right, I watched, and she writes the answers with her right, and I thought: people do both. But they don’t. Not like that. Not smooth.”

“I saw her do it at Penhallow Court,” I said. “She poured with her left and then saw me looking and changed hands. I took it for nerves.”

“Three.” Tamsin turned her head and looked at the dresser, where Quire sat among the plates with her bib very white and her ear very torn, watching us both with contempt. “That one hisses at everybody. At the police, at you when you’re late, at Kit, and he’s fed her for three years. She went into Morwenna’s lap like she’d been doing it all her life. I was on the loft steps. I saw.”

“A cat is not a witness.”

“She’s the only one of us with no reason to be polite.”

The bulb hummed. Down on the harbour a halyard was knocking against a mast, slowly, as if somebody were being asked to come in.

“She left the quiz at ten to ten,” I said. I had not meant to say it. “The Thursday. I found the sheet in Jago’s biscuit tin, in two hands, with the time written at the foot of the music round. I asked her at the Lantern, lightly, and she said half past ten. I showed her the sheet, and she said her memory wasn’t what it was, and Ronald had asked her if she was the new nurse, and she offered me cake out of her bag.” I stopped. “I let it go.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted her to be forgetful.” It was the truest thing I had said to anyone that week, and I said it to the tablecloth. “And Loveday Penhallow told me, unasked, in front of both of us, that Morwenna had sat up with her till midnight that night playing piquet. Her hearing aid squealed all the way through. She has that aid, Tamsin, it whistles when she tells a lie, and in the whole of that afternoon nobody noticed how often.”

“Two lies,” said Tamsin, “from two women who aren’t liars.”

“Yes.”

I sat down again and pulled the exercise book towards me, and I did something I had not done in three years, which was to read my husband’s words as though he were in the room and I were obliged to listen. Not the list. Not yet. I looked instead at the drawing on the facing page, which Tamsin had put in because Mr Lanyon liked diagrams: a sewing frame, Ned’s, the oak one in the press room with its four pegs and its worn cross-bar, in pencil, every peg labelled. [oak, one peg newer wood.] And down the side, in her round-backed brackets: [there were TWO of these? Ned says 2 in the book. Where is the other one?]

I had been asking the wrong question for a week. I had asked who, and refused the answer, and gone on asking it. But the question was not who. Somebody had been in my shop, Demelza had said, on the first morning, and I had taken it for a thief with a key, because I had needed it to be. It was the other way about. The shop had never been used. It was the book that had been brought to the cover. Whoever it was had needed a frame, a month of evenings, a bench, a press of some sort and a pot of clove paste, in a village of six hundred where a woman cannot buy a stamp without the Post Office knowing what she means to write, and had done it all without anyone smelling Christmas in July.

“How,” I said. “Not who. How. Where in Trevenna would you sew sixty leaves of a seventeenth-century pilot’s book, left-handed, on a frame nobody knows you have?”

Tamsin said nothing. For once she had the sense to say nothing.

I pulled the notebook copy round and put my finger under the third line. “M. Hext,” I read aloud. “Left-handed, forced right at school. Best I’ve had.” I heard it as Ned would have said it, to the back of the stove, not looking up, in the voice in which he gave out his highest praise, which was a sort of grunt. I read it a second time, more quietly. “Best I’ve had.”

He had never written that about anyone. I knew it as I knew the stairs. He had said of me, in his kindest mood, that I would do, and I had treasured it for twenty-seven years.

“Morwenna Hext was a better binder than I am,” I said, and behind me the kettle, which I had set back on the flame for a second pot and forgotten, boiled over onto the hob with a noise like an audience.

chapters.title: What Jago Couldn't Say
chapters.html:
Jago Rowe ducked under the lintel of the police house at ten past midnight as he ducks under every lintel in Trevenna, but this time he did it as though the wood had said something personal.

Demelza had knocked at my door at twenty to twelve. I was standing at the sink with a cloth, wiping up a kettle’s worth of water from the hob, and Tamsin was asleep upstairs in the box room under Ned’s eiderdown with her boots on, because I had not had the heart to take them off. “I’m letting Jago out,” said Demelza. “He’s on your way home.”

“I am home.”

“Then he’s on your way to Jago’s. Get your cardigan.”

We walked down together. Church Lane was empty and smelled of the Co-op’s bins and somebody’s late roses. She did not talk. At the chapel wall she said, without turning her head, “You’ve got something. It’s on your face like paste.”

“It’s not something yet.”

“Dot.”

“Five o’clock tomorrow, in my kitchen,” I said. “If I’m right I shall tell you first, before Garrow, before Kit’s solicitor, before the Pope. If I’m wrong I would prefer to be wrong in front of nobody.”

She considered it as far as the Co-op. “First,” she said.

“First.”

“Don’t be wrong, then,” said Demelza.

The police house is the front room of a semi-detached cottage at the foot of the lane, with a blue lamp over the door that has not been lit since 1981, and a cell behind a door that used to be the pantry’s. The ficus was drooping. The Queen looked down from her photograph with the expression of a woman who has seen a great many men released and was prepared to wait for the next. Jago sat on the bench with his boots between his knees, pulling the newspaper out of them in long grey handfuls, and the room smelled of old sea and older newsprint.

“There’s a form,” said Demelza, who stood by the door with her notebook. “I’ve filled in the form. Everything we have against you, Mr Rowe, is that you got wet. A man you pulled out of the harbour is alive and will go on being alive, with his own money in his pocket and nobody’s fist on his head. Being unwilling to say why you were there is not an offence in this country. So I’m not holding you. For lack of evidence. It isn’t an apology.”

“Constable,” said Jago.

“I’d go home, Mr Rowe.”

He stood up. The room got smaller. He put his coat on, and sat again to work his foot into the second boot, and it was then, as he bent, that the lamp caught the heel and I saw the painted figure on it, a white 12, slapped on with a brush and gone grey at the edges. Fishermen do it so their boots do not walk off the quay. A white twelve and a rim of salt.

I said nothing. I thought of six pale macs on six pegs, and under them, standing in a line like a polite congregation, a pair of black rubber sea-boots in a damp passage in a granite house.

“I’ll walk you home,” I said.

“I know the way, Dot.”

“Yes. But I know the boots.”

Jago lives at the harbour end of Net Loft Row, in a cottage so full of other people’s lobster pots that the kitchen is a sort of wicker cathedral. They go up the walls in stacks, to the ceiling, with the laths in their ribs and the old green twine hanging off, because there is nowhere else in Trevenna to put them and he is not a man who says no to a neighbour. He lit the stove with a sheet of the same newspaper and filled the kettle and put it on the wrong ring, and moved like a big man who has been told off.

I had sat in that kitchen a hundred times. I had sat there with Ned, with a pint, on the night of the Jubilee. I looked at the wall by the dresser where a photograph hung in a plain frame, and I saw it, for the first time in twenty-seven years, instead of the picture of it that I had carried about. A girl of nineteen in a riding hat set at an angle, on a grey horse with its ears back, laughing at whoever held the camera. She had the Penhallow nose. She looked as if the camera belonged to her, which I imagine it did. I had always taken it for a calendar page.

“Leave it, Dot,” said Jago, behind me.

“I did leave it,” I said. “For eight days. I am told it is a fault.”

He said nothing. The kettle began to tick.

“Size twelve boots with a white twelve on the heel,” I said. “They stand in the back passage at Penhallow Court under six pale macs. Loveday said they were the gardener’s. Loveday has not had a gardener since Suez.”

He set down the caddy very carefully.

“That’s the size of it,” said Jago.

It came out of him as the tide comes up the Hard, slowly, and then all of it. “Thursdays,” he said. “I leave Jory the key to the box and the plug on the jukebox at half past nine, and I tell them it’s the books. It is the books, for ten minutes. I do the quarter’s rents on her kitchen table. Then she makes tea, and we play piquet for coppers, and she cheats, and I do the buckets. There are eleven. They’ve gone up since March.” He moved a hand the size of a frying pan. “Three years, since the winter Ned went. She came into the Lantern in her gumboots, which she hadn’t done since 1956, and ordered a small sherry, and said I looked as if I could do with an evening.”

“Nineteen fifty-six.”

“Aye, you’d not know. You came in ‘sixty-two.” He looked at the photograph, not at me. “I was twenty-eight, on the pilchard boats. She was forty-one and the daughter of the house, and there was a hay barn, and it got out, because in Trevenna it does. The Chapel took it up. Her father sent me a fortnight’s wages in an envelope and a berth on a coaster out of Falmouth, and I went, because I was twenty-eight and thought it was what you did. Three years. When I came back she was Miss Penhallow and I was Jago Rowe and we nodded in the street. Thirty years. Like two ships.” He breathed out. “Ned never said one word. He bought me a pint. He was good that way.”

“Nobody would mind now, Jago.”

“Everybody would mind,” said Jago, “and then they’d be kind to us, and I couldn’t stand that.” He took the kettle off. “She’s seventy-four. Let a man keep one thing in this village. Garrow’d have her name in the Truro paper by Sunday with the old story dragged out behind it like a dead dog.”

“On the thirteenth,” I said.

“Half past nine till midnight. I left by the kitchen door and was home by half past, and nobody saw me, which was the idea.”

“Did Morwenna Hext come to the house that night?”

He looked at me then. “Morwenna? No. She does Tuesdays.”

“Loveday told me, on Tuesday, in front of Morwenna, that Morwenna sat up with her till midnight on the Thursday. Playing piquet.”

Jago’s hand stopped halfway to the shelf with the tea in it. “Piquet,” he said.

“Yes.”

“That was me. I lost sixty pence.” He put the caddy down. “Nobody came to that door but me. The bell’s the size of a bucket. I’d have heard it in the cellar.” The big face under the bald dome worked, slowly, as a winch works, and he said, very quietly, “She put Morwenna in my chair.”

“Her hearing aid squealed all through it. I thought it was the aid.”

“It’s not the aid,” said Jago. “It’s her. She’ll do it lying in the dark with her mouth shut.”

I did not say why I thought it mattered, and he did not ask. He is not a stupid man, only a silent one, and there is a way of being silent that is a form of listening. I got my cardigan from the back of the chair.

“It’s half past twelve.”

“She doesn’t sleep. She told me so, in July, with the buckets.”

“I’ll come.”

“You’d frighten her.”

“She’s not frightened of me. She’s never been.”

“Then you’d frighten me,” I said. “You have been in a cell for twenty-two hours. I should like one of us to arrive.”

He took a black rubber torch from a nail by the door, as long as my forearm, and put it in my hand. “She’ll be in her gumboots,” said Jago. “Don’t say.”

It is twenty minutes from the Hard to Penhallow Court if you take the cliff path, and in the dark it is twenty-five, with the sea going on at your left hand like a person breathing in the next room. There was no moon to speak of. The gorse gave out its coconut smell, and something in the hedge went away from me with a rustle. I kept the torch low. I did not rehearse. I have found that if I rehearse a conversation, the other party comes in with different lines, and I am left holding mine like a woman with the wrong key.

There was a light in the kitchen. When I banged the knocker it was not a minute before the bolts went back, and Loveday Penhallow stood in her own doorway with a hurricane lamp held up beside her face, in a flannel nightdress down to her shins, a man’s cardigan, and gumboots.

They were on the wrong feet. Each toe pointed away from the other like the hands of a clock at ten to two. I had been told not to say, and I said nothing, and she watched me say nothing with her head on one side.

“Pellow,” she said. “It is one o’clock in the morning, you have lost your senses, and I have no sherry.”

“Jago is out.”

The hearing aid in her ear gave a small, delighted sort of cheep. “Is he? Good. He is a fool, and I am obliged to him.” She stood aside. “Come into the kitchen, then, I have the range lit. I do not sleep. Eleven buckets is a very good alarm.”

It was the warmest room in the house and the only one with its lamps on. We sat across a scrubbed table with a pack of cards on it, a fan of them half-dealt, as if someone had been called away in the middle of a hand, and I did not look at them.

“He says he was here from half past nine until midnight on the thirteenth,” I said. “He says he lost sixty pence at piquet. He says nobody rang the bell.”

“He’s a gentleman. He will say what is convenient.”

The aid screamed. It went up through the scale and stopped. Loveday put a long hand, the beautiful one, flat across her ear, as one would to a child who has told a story at table, and for a time neither of us spoke.

“Oh, Pellow,” she said.

“Who asked you?”

“On the Friday. Before nine in the morning, before Aubrey was out of your press room. She stood in my hall in her mac with a cake in a tin, and she said, ‘Loveday, dear, if anyone should ask, I sat up with you last night.’ She did not say why. I did not ask why.” The long hand went down, and she looked at me, and I saw that she was frightened, and had been frightened for a week, in a way that made her look younger than Jago’s photograph. “I am a coward, Pellow. You may tell the Chapel.”

“Why did you say yes?”

“Because she reads to me. Eleven years on a Tuesday, in all weathers, with Ronald going the way he is. Friendship. And shame.” She turned a card face up and turned it down again. “I have known for years that things go out of this house. A snuffbox. The plates from the Hakluyt. A Book of Hours I never liked. Small things. She would borrow them. She always said so. Sometimes they came back, and sometimes not, and I told myself it was her way of being useful, because she had so little else to be useful with. I did not look at it. If I said no to her now I should have to say I had known, and for how long, and that I had sat in my own house and watched the Penhallows go out of it by the teaspoon so as not to be disagreeable.”

“Did you know about the Carne?”

“I know that Garrow said ‘interfered with.’ Nobody says that about a book that has merely been stolen.” The aid said nothing at all. “I’m not a fool. I only practise.”

I got up. It seemed discourteous to sit. The range ticked, and in the passage, through the open door, I could see the macs on their pegs, and the place where a pair of boots had stood.

“Is it Morwenna?” said Loveday.

“I don’t know yet.”

“You do, Pellow. Your face is doing what the Chapel’s did in 1956.” She had got up too, a thin old woman in a nightdress with her feet in the wrong boots, holding the lamp, so that her shadow went up the wall behind her and over the ceiling to meet the rest of the house. “Will they put her in prison?”

She did not wait. She turned and went away down the passage with the lamp, the boots clumping, left on right and right on left, and I was left in her kitchen with the cards and the question and nothing to put it in.

chapters.title: Measuring the Boards
chapters.html:
The bunting went up in the night. I watched the last of it from my kitchen window as the light came: forty yards along the harbour wall, from the corner of the Lantern to the lifeboat house, hung by men who had been up since three and did not wish to be thanked. Red and white, a yellow that was meant for Cornwall, a run of blue triangles borrowed from some signal locker, all in the order Jago likes and no other. He had been at it since he left his own kitchen. I did not need to be told. When a big man cannot sleep he finds something with a rope on it.

By five o’clock there were four cups on my table with the tea going cold in them, in the order they had been poured.

Imogen Mayne had come because my note said her father’s name and nothing else. It was in Tamsin’s hand, since mine would have taken longer to read, and Tamsin had pushed it under the door of Room 3 at the Lantern at half past four and come back up the lane at a run. Imogen followed in the leather jacket, her cropped head bare, smelling of cigarettes and the Lantern’s carpet, and sat down at my table without being asked. “If this is about the piano,” she said, “I’ve said all I’m going to say.” It was not about the piano.

Demelza had arrived ten minutes before, from the police house, with her tunic buttoned one hole out. Whatever she had done with Jago’s cell and her conscience in the interval she did not offer, and I did not ask. Tamsin sat on the dresser stool with the exercise book on her knee and Quire beside her like a bookend, and watched the three of us as a girl watches a lesson for which she has already done the homework.

I told it in order. If you tell a thing in order to tired people, it is believed as a matter of rhythm. Tamsin’s copy; the pupil list; Jago’s boots, and Loveday’s piquet, and a cake in a tin on a Friday morning in a hall. I gave it flatly, the way I would give the dimensions of a book, and while I talked Demelza read the two pages with her finger under the lines like a child, and Imogen smoked.

“The woman with the cake,” said Imogen, when I came to the name. “The one who put her arm round me at the bar last Thursday.” She laughed once, down her nose. “She said Daddy was the most exact man she’d ever met, and that exactness was a kind of love. I was so grateful I said thank you to her sleeve.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be. It was a good line. I’d have used it myself.” She tapped ash into the saucer I had given her. I had never in my life given anybody a saucer for that purpose, and Ned, who smoked his pipe in the yard like a man doing penance, would have fainted.

“Right,” said Demelza, and shut the book. “Facts.” She said them to the table. “A schoolgirl’s copy of a notebook that’s been stolen, so it’s a copy of nothing I can produce. A dead man’s scrap with half a name on it. A pensioner’s hearing aid. A landlord I let out last night on my own say-so, who’ll tell you where he was only in a dark kitchen. And a cat.”

“And the beeswax,” said Tamsin.

“And the Jam Tarts’ sheet,” I said.

“Is the light any use?” said Imogen.

We looked at her. She had her chin in her hand and the cigarette burning down between two fingers, and she was looking at nothing, like a person who has been trying to remember something for several minutes and has at last decided to say it badly. “At your meeting, on Tuesday. The bunting, the sandwiches. I was trying to be invisible with an egg roll. She went on about a headache. She said the light at your place had given her one. In your workroom, over the big iron press. She’d stuck her head in at Easter.”

The kitchen did not change. Down on the harbour a halyard knocked against a mast. “Which light?” I said.

“A long one. A tube. It flickers.”

“It was fitted last October,” I said. “It comes on in three stages: a flicker, a stammer, then the light. A person would have to stand under it and wait for the third to be given a headache. And on the morning Aubrey was found, with a teapot in her hand and half the lane listening, she told Demelza and Garrow and me that she had not set foot in that room since Ned died.”

“March ‘eighty-six,” said Demelza. She wrote it down and underlined it twice, and I saw a muscle move at the hinge of her jaw.

“I did not sleep,” I said. “At three o’clock I got Pieter’s leaf out from under the Concordance and measured it with my gauge. Laid rag, sized, a hair under a sixth of a millimetre. Say point one five.” I took the little brass thing out of my cardigan and set it on the table among the cups. “On Tuesday night at the Institute, to be funny, I put this on the front board of the Regatta Book while Jago and Mr Nance quarrelled about who should carry it to the finish. Three and a half.”

Tamsin did not need to be asked. She opened the exercise book to the second page and put her finger on the line. “Two,” she said. “’And not a hair more.’”

“I picked it up that night and thought it too heavy for a ledger. I put it down to Ned. I put everything down to Ned that week; it’s a habit.” I looked at my hands. “He wrote two millimetres because he wanted a book an old man could hold up in a wind. And the one I weighed in the hall could have been used to prop a door.”

Tamsin had found a pen and was writing on the back of her left hand, in the clear upright script, with her tongue between her teeth. “Three and a half take off two,” she said. “One and a half. That’s one board. There’s two boards, so three.” She looked up at the ceiling and her lips moved. “Three divided by nought point one five.”

We waited. In the grate behind her a cinder settled.

“Twenty,” said Tamsin.

Nobody said anything. Imogen put out her cigarette in the saucer, slowly, and went on pressing it after it was out.

“Twenty what?” she said.

“Leaves.” I heard my voice come out level, and was ashamed of how well I had learned it. “A millboard can be split down its thickness, like a sandwich, and something flat and old laid in, and the layers pasted back round it. A good hand does it so that you couldn’t find the join with a thumbnail. Then you cover it in calf and marbled paper, and put a red label on the front, and offer to take the Institute’s treasurer’s job.”

“Sixty leaves are missing,” said Demelza.

“Four are in the false book. Sixty are gone. A dealer has some, I should think; that is what a dealer is for, and the Dutchman’s one folded leaf says he does. But twenty, I say, are in a ledger that has been carried round Trevenna for a month in a flour sack, being admired.”

Demelza got up. She is not a woman who walks about when she thinks, but she went the length of my kitchen, which is eleven feet, and back, with her hands behind her like a constable on a beat.

“I can’t get a warrant on thick boards,” she said. “I’d put it to the justices at Truro with Garrow’s name or mine, and they’d ask who measured, and I’d say the aunt of the man we’re holding for the murder, and the clerk would look at me the way you look at a woman who tells you the bus is late because of the Pope. Garrow won’t hear it. He has a thumbprint on a lamp, a Dutchman, and a theory with a train timetable in it. And I can’t so much as mention the leaf without giving him you and me together.” She stopped. “And if I walk up to the president of the Institute on regatta morning and ask for the club ledger, she says, ‘Of course, my handsome, I’ll bring it round after the cup,’ and she doesn’t.”

“No,” I said. “You don’t ask in private.”

“Dot.”

“She has never in her life refused anyone anything in public. She would hand over her handbag first. If I ask her in front of forty people, with the cup on the table, to let me look at a hinge I admired in the Institute’s hall on Tuesday, she will say yes and smile, because the alternative would be to be seen to say no.”

“The prize-giving,” said Tamsin.

“The prize-giving. She’ll lay the Book open on the table for the cox to sign. I shall ask to see it. And I shall have my dividers.”

It was a good plan. I mention that because it was also the worst plan I have ever made, and I watched the three of them find that out in the order in which their faces permitted it. Imogen was first.

“And if you’re wrong?”

“Then I shall have measured the Institute’s ledger with a pair of dividers in a tea tent, in front of the whole parish, and accused its president of murder over a plate of egg sandwiches.” The words were quite steady, as if they belonged to someone I had met at a funeral. “I shall not be asked to mend so much as a library ticket in this county again. Well.”

“That isn’t how it’s done,” said Demelza. “If she takes fright. If she puts it in the harbour.”

“It floats, mostly,” said Tamsin. “In 1931 it took a boy in a punt.” Everyone looked at her. “It’s in the notebook.”

“Ten past three,” I said.

“Ten past,” Tamsin agreed, and she crossed her ankles on the stool and became, for a moment, a woman of forty. “Not before the race, or she’ll say she’s bringing it to you after. Not after the prize-giving, because the Book goes back in its sack and she goes home. You do it when the cox is waiting to sign, with the pen out and the cup on the cloth. That’s ten past three if Trevenna time holds, and it will. Twenty minutes late is what it does.”

“I am to stand where?” said Demelza.

“At the back.”

“I’m not agreeing to anything.”

“No.”

“I want that heard.”

“It’s heard.”

It was Imogen who broke it. She reached down beside her chair for the leather bag, a big creased thing with a broken buckle, and brought out a buff folder, and put it on the table without opening it. “I don’t know why I brought this,” she said. “It was in the case with the letter. I thought, it’s in his hand, and I don’t know what to do with a thing that’s in his hand.”

The folder held Kit’s typed schedule of the Penhallow shelves, forty-one sheets, with a pencil going up and down the margins like a man walking a cliff. I knew the pencil before I saw the words. Two B, soft, and every seven crossed in the continental fashion, as I had seen them in silver on a scrap in a stove. Against lot 31, a Hakluyt: M.H. to mend, L.P. consents, Feb. Against lot 57, a Book of Hours: M.H., mending. Not on shelf, Apr. Against two almanacs and a snuffbox in a drawer: M.H. again, and a question mark, and on the last sheet in the bottom corner, small, as an old man notes a thing for himself and does not mean the world to see it, Mrs H. is kind, & careful. Cf. all of the above. Ask Mrs P.

Demelza read the last line twice. Then she turned the sheet to the window, where the light was coming up the colour of weak tea, and breathed out through her nose. “That,” she said, “Garrow can’t ignore.”

“It doesn’t say she’s a thief.”

“It says she was handed seven things by a house where a murdered man was sent to value the contents, and that he wrote her initials against every one and ended with a note to you. It’s dated. It’s in the hand of a man whose letter Garrow has had in his own pocket for three days. He’ll hate it.” She put the sheet down on the table very gently, as a person lays something hot on a cloth. “I can put this in his hand before the cup.”

I took the scrap out of my cardigan, in its fold of blotting paper, and put it into her palm. She looked at it. Then she took an evidence bag from inside her tunic, where it seemed she had been carrying one for some days, and sealed the scrap into it herself and signed the label on her knee. “That’s the first thing I’ve done by the book all week,” she said, “and I’d like it noted that it doesn’t feel any better.”

“Put down that I held it five days.”

“I’ll put down what happened.”

“Then put down that too.”

“And at the back?”

“I’ll be at the back. At the back where I can see the Book and the door.” She buttoned her tunic correctly for the first time that morning. “If you’re wrong I was at the lavatories.”

“The Institute’s lavatory,” said Tamsin, “is a bucket behind a hessian screen.”

“Then I shall be very discreet.”

They went, one after another, as the light climbed the dresser. Imogen went to find a clean shirt and a face to put on her father’s cup. Tamsin went to find the quay and the programme and the exact minute of everything, which she can do with one look at a blackboard. Demelza went, I suppose, to find whichever of her several consciences was senior.

When they had gone I took the tool roll off the dresser and untied it on the table. I laid out my dividers, my second-best bone folder, and the little brass gauge, squared to the edge of the table with the last cold cup, like a woman setting a table for a guest who will not leave. Quire got up and sat among them. She does not usually care for dividers.

Outside, the harbour had filled with flags.

chapters.title: Regatta Morning
chapters.html:
Nobody looked at me on the morning of the regatta, and I have never been so grateful.

By eight the harbour looked like a quilt dropped from a height. The tide had gone out by then in its slow way and left the moorings leaning on the mud at all angles, each hull with a flag at its mast, so that the whole basin was a mosaic of triangles, reds and blues and Jago’s one yellow, and the water in the channel the colour of pewter. Stalls ran the length of the quay: pasties, crab sandwiches, a coconut shy, the lifeboat tin rattling on its string. Ada Bolitho had a table by the Post Office wall for her raffle, and on it, in the raspberry felt hat, with its amber glass eyes blazing at the sea, stood the otter. Nobody dared to ask her whether it was the prize.

The five gigs had been brought round overnight and lay on the Hard in their long black-and-yellow hulls like sleeping pike, with six oars each laid inboard along the thwarts and a crew in white jerseys sitting about them eating pasties with the particular calm of men who are going to be sick later. The Trevenna boat was the Provident. Wilf Hosken, who had rowed her stroke thirty years before, stood at her stem with his hand on the wood, saying nothing, which for Wilf is a speech.

The band was tuning up on the quay. I stood at the back of the crowd where the wall steps down to the Slip and let it carry me, in my second-best cardigan, with the tool roll in my canvas bag. The Trevenna Silver Band tunes up as other bodies of men go to war: everybody at once, in every key, in the conviction that the others will see sense.

“Mrs Pellow!” Jory the potman was at the Lantern door with a cloth over his shoulder and his hands cupped. “Phone! It’s the constable!”

I should say that the Lantern’s payphone hangs in an alcove at the end of the bar, between the dartboard and the gents, and that I had not been near it since Aubrey stood there on the thirteenth with his back to the room and said, Half ten, then. The floats overhead had their lamps lit, 140 of them, a ceiling of small green moons. Jago’s regatta breakfasts were in progress, four crews at the long table and a smell of bacon. Jago himself was at the back with his sleeves rolled, lifting a tray, and when he saw me he put it down, and I knew from the way that he did it that he was not going to be in the room for what came next.

“Dot,” said Demelza’s voice, very small and a long way off, with a hospital’s echo behind it. “I’m at Treliske. I came at seven. Nobody stopped me. I’d the uniform.”

“Is he awake?”

“He’s been awake since yesterday. He didn’t speak till half an hour ago. The sister says he looked at the ceiling for a time and said it, and then said it again, as if to check. Twice.” She stopped. I could hear her breathing, and the squeak of a trolley. “’The lady with honey.’”

I held on to the receiver. At my elbow, on the bar, between a bowl of pickled eggs and a dish of dry roast peanuts, someone had set a jar of heather and gorse honey for the lifeboat tin, with a handwritten label in a neat upright hand: HONEY FOR THE LIFEBOAT. M.H. It was the jar Pieter de Vries had looked at from the door on the Thursday night, standing as if undecided, with his collar not yet turned up. I put my hand over the label as one covers a child’s ears.

“What else did he say?”

“He asked what day it was. He asked for his glasses, and the sister says he can’t have them till the doctor’s been.” A pause. “It’s a man with a bang on the head, Dot. It’s one phrase. It’s not a name.”

“I know.”

“I thought you’d want to hear it first.”

“First,” I said. “Thank you.”

When I had put the receiver back I stood for some time with my hand on the jar. I had known it since the kitchen, but knowing is for kitchens. This was a phrase with weather in it, spoken by a man who had floated face-down in the dark, and it came to me not as an idea but as a taste. I did not look round. Behind me in the Lantern someone had begun to sing, and four crews joined in with their mouths full.

Loveday Penhallow arrived at half past ten in a bath chair.

It was a wicker chair on iron-tyred wheels that had stood in the Court’s coach house since her mother’s last illness, and Reverend Nance was pushing it down the lane from the church in his bicycle clips, with a rug over the old lady’s knees and the face of a man steering a hearse. Every cobble produced from him a small cry. “Forgive me,” he said. “Forgive me. I’m so sorry. It is nothing.”

“Do not apologise to the cobbles, Arthur,” said Loveday. “They were laid in 1740 and will outlast the pair of us.”

She wore her good tweed and a hat with a pheasant feather, and she had her blackthorn across her lap like a lance. When the chair drew level with me she lifted one gumbooted foot a quarter of an inch from the footplate and put it down again.

“Pellow. Right feet. Say nothing.”

“I wouldn’t dream.”

“Hm.” She looked at me with her whole narrow face, and the hearing aid in her ear gave a thin whistle, though I had not said a word that could be called untrue. “I’ve come to see whatever it is you’re going to do. The aid is on. It will tell me.”

“I haven’t told you I’m going to do anything.”

“You have a face like the Chapel in 1956,” said Loveday. “Take me to the tent, Arthur.”

The marquee stood at the head of the quay, a great white affair that had been put up at six in a sea mist and was still steaming faintly in the sun like a horse. Inside it was cool, and smelled of damp canvas and urn. The Institute’s long tables ran down the middle with their cloths, set for the regatta tea; at the far end, where the canvas gave on to the Slip and the harbour mouth, a smaller table had been dressed in white, with a silver cup, a pen on a saucer, a bowl of orange montbretia from some hedge, and in the centre, laid flat on a folded cloth, with its red label turned to the roof, the Regatta Book.

Morwenna was squaring it to the edge of the table with two fingers of her left hand.

She wore the Institute’s green sash over her best blue dress, and her pearl studs, and the silver perm was newly set. She saw the chair before she saw me and came across with her arms out, and the apple cheeks were flushed with pleasure. “Loveday, my dear! Out in the air! Whatever will Dr Tregellas say?” She stooped and kissed the old woman’s cheek. “How lovely to see you so well.”

The aid screamed. It was not a whistle; it was a shriek that went up the scale and cracked the air like a dropped tray, and half the tent turned to look.

“That wants a new battery, my handsome,” said Morwenna comfortably.

“It wants nothing of the kind,” said Loveday.

Morwenna laughed, a warm small laugh. She straightened and turned that bright, kind face on me, and I saw her take in the cardigan, and the shadows under my eyes, and the bag over my shoulder, all in a second. “And you look like a wet week. You’ve not slept. Sit. Eat.” A saffron bun came out of the bag on her arm in a paper napkin, and was in my hand before I had formed an opinion. “They’ve let Jago go, I hear. Edna’s sister at the Co-op. I am glad. I never thought it of him, not for a minute.” Her left hand went back to the Book, and smoothed the cloth beneath it. “And that poor Dutchman. Is he mending?”

I have thought about what I said next a good many times. I could have said that he was awake. I could have said he had spoken. There was a woman a yard from me whose hands I had known for thirty years, smelling of woodsmoke and wax, and in a moment I should have to say it to her face, and it seemed the least of what I owed her to say it first.

“Still asleep,” I said. “They say he may be days.”

“Poor man,” said Morwenna.

I ate the bun. I will say that. It was a very good bun. I ate it because to refuse it would have been information, and I stood in the tent among the damp canvas and the montbretia with the yellow crumbs on my fingers, eating her cake, with my eyes on the red label on the Book, which did not seem to me to be very much heavier than a ledger. Behind me Reverend Nance had stopped saying sorry. I noticed that. It was the first time in my life I had known him silent.

Garrow was at the foot of the lifeboat house steps at a quarter to twelve, in the raincoat, in full sun, with the face of a man who has been told he must enjoy himself. Demelza stood a yard behind his left shoulder with the notebook against her chest and her eyes on the middle distance. She had given him the folder, I could see. His hand was resting on it, on top of the raincoat’s pocket, as one rests a hand on a dog one doesn’t trust.

“Mrs Pellow, dear.”

“Inspector. I should like to ask you to be in the tea tent at three.”

“And why would that be?”

“Because the constable has given you something to read, and I am going to ask a question in public, and you will want to be somewhere you can hear the answer.” I did not say any more. I had an idea that if I said more, the idea would come to pieces in my hands.

He was silent a moment. A gull walked along the rail beside us with an air of conducting an inspection. “I have read Mr Trevithick’s list,” said Garrow. “I have also been handed a scrap of burned paper which I shall have something to say about on Monday, to more than one person. I do not say the list means anything. I say it is a catalogue of books that a lady was kind enough to repair. I do not say that you are right. If you are wrong, Mrs Pellow, I shall find it hard to be gentle.”

“I should not expect it.”

“I’ll stand at the back,” said Garrow.

“That is all I ask.”

“It is all I shall do.” He took out a handkerchief and mopped his forehead, and for the second time in two days he looked, briefly, very tired.

At noon Jago fired the gun.

He stood on the harbour wall above the Slip in his shirtsleeves with the starter’s pistol raised in his right hand, the one with nine fingers, and the whole quay hushed, the band halfway through a bar and the otter staring at the sea. The five gigs lay across the harbour mouth in line abreast, oars up like the legs of a row of beetles, on a young flood that had been making for an hour and twenty minutes. Jago looked at the water, and at the men, and at nothing, and I thought: he has not slept, and he has hung forty yards of flags, and he is doing his job. He lowered his arm and the gun cracked and the gulls went up off every roof in Trevenna like thrown paper.

The race went out past the Point to the buoy and back, a mile each way, and the crowd ran along the quay wall as the boats shrank, and we saw them only as a flicker of oars. They turned at the buoy in a scrum. The Provident came out of it second. Tamsin, beside me, had hold of my arm in a grip that would leave bruises, and she did not breathe, and Wilf Hosken on the wall above us shouted advice in a voice I had not heard from him before, a rusted old pilot’s-boy voice that cracked at the high notes. Halfway home they went into the lead. A length. Two lengths. Then the band struck up.

It struck up three tunes at once. The cornets began “Trelawny”; the trombones, who had not been told, began “The Floral Dance”; and a single euphonium, somewhere at the back, struck up “Eternal Father” in the manner of a man who has been given the wrong music and is determined to see it through. They met in the middle of the second verse of “Trelawny” as a family meets a quarrel at Christmas, and settled it, and ended on it, and were cheered as if they had meant to.

The Trevenna gig crossed the line a length clear, with the white jerseys heaving and the oars shipped in a single movement as clean as a page turning, and Jago fired the gun a second time, and the whole of the harbour roared. The boats leaned on their moorings. The otter looked on. I had never seen anything so loud come out of so many people who were so seldom permitted to shout.

I turned from the water, for no reason I can name, and looked at the tent.

It stood at the head of the quay with its flap tied back. Reverend Nance had wheeled Loveday’s chair to the open side to watch, and at his elbow, in her green sash, a tray of egg sandwiches balanced on one arm, was Morwenna, who was pressing one on the Reverend with her free hand. He said he really couldn’t. She said, “Sit. Eat,” and he sat on a folded chair, as people do, and ate. And in the moment in which the second gun went off and the crowd rose and every face in Trevenna turned to the water, I looked at the tent, and Morwenna Hext, over the head of the man she was feeding, was already looking back at me.

chapters.title: The Tea Tent
chapters.html:
The sandwiches were cleared at ten past three. That was the first thing, and it nearly ruined everything.

By then the tent was as full as the Chapel at its anniversary tea. The crews had come up from the Hard in their white jerseys, steaming, and sat along the benches with the cox, a stout twelve-year-old called Kerensa Rosevear in a lifejacket two sizes too large, holding the Institute’s pen in both hands like a candle. The Chapel had come, and the Lantern, and the Co-op, and Ada Bolitho in the raspberry hat she had taken back from the otter for the occasion. Gwen Trewhella sat at the front with her hand cupped behind her ear. I counted forty-odd faces, and the canvas over them dripped slowly, like an old clock, on the long tables. Imogen stood at the dressed table with the silver cup in her hands and her chin up, looking more like her father than she knew. Demelza was against the back pole. Beside her, behind a trestle, with an expression of the deepest forbearance, stood Garrow.

Edna Chegwidden had begun to clear. The Institute clears the sandwiches at ten past three; it has done so every regatta since 1971 and does not mean to change for murder. She took up a tray of egg and cress, and Doris Rosevear took up the tongs, and Garrow came off the pole like a man stung.

“Nobody is to move anything!”

“I’m moving the sandwiches, Inspector,” said Edna, “not leaving the country.”

“Nothing is to be removed from this tent.”

“They’ve been out since two. They’ll turn.”

“Madam, I am not concerned for the sandwiches.”

“Somebody had better be,” said Doris, and for a moment the whole Institute stood with its trays like a row of waitresses at a siege, and forty people laughed, and in the laugh I walked up the length of the tent to the table at the end.

My hands had begun to shake, a fine tremor like a spring in a clock. At the third trestle I put them on the table’s edge and held on, the way I do at the bench when a gathering resists, and found it steadier than I had expected.

“Morwenna,” I said.

She was standing behind the white cloth with her hands folded on the sash, the apple cheeks pink, the pearl studs in. The Regatta Book lay open before her at the last written page, where the winners’ names go in the treasurer’s hand: Trevenna, Provident, 1988, and under it a blank. She smiled at me with great warmth. “My handsome. Has it come to you to say a few words? I didn’t think you’d the heart. Sit down, I’ve saved you a slice.”

“May I look at the Book?”

“The Book?”

“The hinge,” I said. “The one you mended. I said on Tuesday I couldn’t find the join. I should like to look at it properly before the cox signs, if nobody minds. It’s an old woman’s whim.”

There was a rustle down the tent, a polite settling, of people deciding that this was the sort of thing I would do. I felt them lose interest in me. It is a sensation I have known all my life, and for the first time I put it to use. Morwenna looked at me for the length of one breath. Then she lifted the Regatta Book in both hands and held it out across the table, smiling, and laid it in my arms like a child at a christening.

“Of course,” she said. “Mind the corners. And you’ll have a bit of cake, Dot, before you start, you’re white as a sheet.”

“Afterwards.”

“Mind you do.”

It was heavier than a ledger. I held it against my chest and my heart went, once, hard, against its boards.

“I want to tell you about a hammer,” I said.

I did not raise my voice. I have found that when you have never been listened to in a room, the one thing you must not do is shout, because they have a rehearsed answer to a woman who shouts. I spoke as I speak to a customer over the counter about the condition of a spine, and the tent, being a tent full of people who had come for sandwiches and found themselves at the end of a sentence, bent forward to hear.

“On the morning Aubrey Trevithick was found,” I said, “the backing hammer in my press room hung face-out on its nail. That is how my husband hung it. Ned was left-handed, and it falls to his hand that way. I have hung it face to the wall for twenty-seven years, and so does every right-handed person who ever worked at that bench. Whoever hung it after Aubrey was dead was somebody who had watched Ned, or been taught by him, so long ago that the habit had gone into the wrist.”

“Dot, my handsome,” said Morwenna gently, “half the village watched Ned hang that hammer. I came in and out with the buns for thirty years. A person sees a hammer.”

“Quite right,” I said. “A person does.”

“Whoever sewed the Carne Rutter this spring,” I went on, “turned the kettle stitch to the left. Ned’s stitch. He taught it to his pupils because he never thought there was another way. It was sewn fast and even, by a hand that did not stop to think, and Kit, who learned it on a hassock at ten years old, has sewn like a wet Tuesday ever since.”

A noise went through the tent at “wet Tuesday”, something between a laugh and a sob, and Demelza at the back looked at the roof.

“You’ll have to forgive Ned his sayings,” said Morwenna.

“The paste on the hinge was Ned’s paste. Wheat starch, a pinch of alum, a drop of clove oil. It smells of Christmas. Only Kit, Jago and I ever made it, and Ned.”

“My dear, I’ve put cloves in my plum cake for forty years. Half the lane has had a jar of that paste off Ned for their wallpaper.”

“There was beeswax on the thread. I use tallow; so did Ned. Beeswax is a hobbyist’s choice.”

“I sewed the Institute’s banner with beeswax,” said Morwenna, “and you told me so yourself, and you said it was a lovely job.”

“I did.” My hands were beginning to shake against the cloth of the Book, and I laid them flat on the red label, to feel the boards. “On the Saturday night someone broke into the Bindery and took Ned’s notebook out of the paste cupboard. They forced the window. They did not force the cupboard. And they shut my cat in it with a saucer of milk, one of my own blue-rimmed saucers, and laid a teaspoon beside it with the handle to the door.”

Somebody breathed in. It was Ada Bolitho.

“Quire bites everyone,” I said. “She has bitten the police and me when I was late. She was carried to the cupboard and fed without a mark on anyone. That was done by a person she knew.”

“She is a lovely cat,” said Morwenna, “when she’s not hungry.”

“And the key.” I had not known I was going to come to it. “Ned’s notebook, which a girl of sixteen copied two pages of in May, says there was a key to that cupboard on a hook in the press room, lent on Saturdays to a pupil, and that it was to be fetched back. The hook has been bare as long as I have known it. A key like that stays in the pocket of a coat for thirty years and more, because nobody ever asks for it.”

“Ned gave keys to half the lane,” said Morwenna. “He’d have given away his boots if you’d stood still.”

There was not an unkind note in her voice. That was what I could not bear. She answered every point with courtesy, as one answers a mistaken but dear person at a meeting, and the more courteous she was the more of that large wet tent turned its face towards her, on her side. Garrow’s hand had crept to the trestle in front of him and lay flat there, quite still.

“On Tuesday evening at the Institute, with the urn running, you told the committee that the strip light over my nipping press gave you a headache. You had stuck your head in at Easter.” I made myself look at her. “That light was fitted in October. It comes on in three stages: a flicker, a stammer, a light. A person has to stand there and wait. On the morning Aubrey was found you told me, and Demelza, and Inspector Garrow, that you had not set foot in that room since my husband died.”

“I might have looked in at the shop door with the Easter buns,” said Morwenna. “A figure of speech, Dot. I couldn’t tell you now.” For the first time, a very small line appeared between the grey brows, as a pencil mark appears when you press a little too hard. “I do see how it looks.”

“And lastly there is the K.” I turned. Demelza, at the back pole, without a word, lifted a small clear bag by one corner so that the front benches could see it: a charred scrap with a silver trace of pencil that the light just found. “That was under the grate of the press-room stove. It is in her hands today, and in the Inspector’s, because I kept it five days when I ought not to have, and any blame for those days is mine. Aubrey wrote on the pastedowns of the Carne before they were burned. K., cat. 114. That is Kit’s catalogue number for the rutter. Aubrey noted that Kit had flagged the paper. It was a footnote, and nobody ever meant it as an accusation. The line under it says Mrs P. in the mor, because he was waiting for me in the morning. And at eleven the night before I walked past his window and did not look in.”

My voice did something at the end of that, and I let it. At the back pole Garrow said nothing at all, which in him was a kind of speech.

“Now I should like to measure the Book,” I said.

Nobody said anything. The canvas dripped.

I laid the Regatta Book on the white cloth, open at the back board, and took the dividers from my bag. I opened them across the edge of the board until the two points just kissed the front and the back of the thickness, and held them up, and carried them to the brass gauge Tamsin held out flat on her palm, and read the figure aloud. “Three and a half.” I did the same for the front board. “Three and a half.” I took Tamsin’s red book. “In 1964 my husband wrote in his job book, ‘Boards two millimetres and not a hair more.’ I measured them on Tuesday night with this gauge, as a joke, and you have all just watched me measure them again.”

Garrow had come off his trestle. He stood at the third table, not quite beside me, and his eyes were on the dividers.

“Ned bound them thick,” said Morwenna.

“He wrote two.”

“He was always one for changing his mind, my dear. I recall him saying, after, that he’d gone up a touch because of the wind.”

“I do not think so.” I turned the pages of Tamsin’s book to the first, and I read aloud, as steadily as I could, with a hand on the table’s edge to hold it, the line that she had copied in her clear upright script from my husband’s green notebook. “’M. Hext. Left-handed, forced right at school. Nineteen fifty-five to fifty-eight. Best I’ve had.’”

“WHAT’S SHE SAYING?” said Gwen Trewhella.

“That Morwenna can bind,” whispered Doris Rosevear, loudly.

“OF COURSE SHE CAN,” said Gwen, with great contentment. “SHE DID THE BANNER.”

Nobody laughed. It was a different silence from the other, and it went up through the tent like water up a wick. Forty people looked at me. I had not been looked at by so many people at once since Ned’s funeral, and then I had been looked at as a widow, an object of tact. This was the other thing. They were looking at me with the faces of people who have been shown that the page is not blank, and Ada Bolitho’s hand had gone to her hat.

“I loved you, Morwenna,” I said.

I said it in an ordinary voice. It was the hardest sentence of my life, and it took no longer to say than ‘pass the teapot’.

“I think I still do. You held my hand through ‘Abide With Me.’ You have put saffron cake on my step at every bad time since 1962. I would have given you anything you asked, and you never asked. I only wanted you to know that before the rest.”

Morwenna’s face did not change. The mild blue eyes met mine across the table, level and warm, and the lines about them gathered, a little, as if at a joke she was too well-mannered to share. “That is very kind of you, Dot,” she said. “And you’ve done a great deal of thinking, and you haven’t eaten. You must sit.”

She sat down herself, in the folding chair behind the white cloth, as one sits at the end of a long committee, with her hands in her lap.

That was when Quire jumped.

I do not know how she came to the tent. I had left her in the kitchen at noon, among the dividers, with the door shut. Perhaps she had gone through the window; perhaps she had walked down behind the crowd at the heel of the gig race, as she does, in the unconcern of a person for whom the world has been arranged. She came across the grass from the Slip end where the canvas lifted, black and white and one-eared, past forty pairs of feet, and went up onto Morwenna’s knees in a single movement, turned round once, and settled, with her bib to the roof and her eyes half shut, like a bun into a tin.

Nobody moved. In the back of my head, as clear as a bell in a cold room, I heard myself say it on a Friday morning in July to nobody at all: Quire, who hisses at everyone.

Morwenna looked down at the cat. She put out her left hand and stroked the torn ear, once, with a finger, as one touches a thing to check it is still there. Then she lifted Quire in both hands, very gently, and set her down on the grass.

She stood up. She took the Regatta Book from the white cloth, with the dividers lying open across the boards where I had left them, and the dividers slid on to the cloth with a small bright sound. She tucked the Book against the sash, as a woman puts her handbag under her arm to leave a meeting at the end of the agenda. Then she walked down the length of the tent, between the benches, nodding to Edna and to Mrs Trewhella, to the open flap, where Jago Rowe stood against the daylight with his big hands hanging. He stepped aside. He held the canvas back for her, as a man does for a lady, and she went out into the sun.

Nobody stopped her. I have gone over that a good many times, and the nearest I can come to it is that nobody present could think what the form of words was.

chapters.title: High Water on the Slip
chapters.html:
Ada Bolitho said afterwards that I left the tent like a woman who has seen her bus, and I daresay that is fair. I did not run. I have never run for anything but a kettle. But I handed Tamsin her red book and went down the benches between forty people who leaned out of my way as if I were a draught, and nobody spoke until the flap, where Demelza stood with her notebook shut in her fist and a face like a closed shop.

“Ten minutes,” I said.

“Dot.”

“She hasn’t anywhere to go. The harbour mouth is the far end of Trevenna from the road, and the only other way out is wet.”

Demelza looked over my head at the harbour. Behind us Garrow’s voice had risen on the subject of sandwiches. Edna Chegwidden had put an egg-and-cress into his hand to stop him pointing, and was telling him it was rude to waste it.

“Whatever she says to you isn’t evidence,” said Demelza. “I want you to know that I know that.”

“I know it too.”

“I’ll be at the top of the Slip. I’ll see you and I shan’t hear you. Ten minutes, and once he’s finished that sandwich I can’t promise.” “It’s the only favour I’ve got left, Dot. I’d like it back one day.”

The Slip is a ramp of concrete laid in 1923 at an angle chosen by a man who had never walked down it in court shoes, with a galvanised rail along its eastern side and the lifeboat house at the head, its green doors shut. The shower that had turned the tea tent into a drum had gone through at three. The sun had come out low and yellow, and the tide had climbed the ramp until only the upper half showed, streaked with green weed, lapping the concrete with the small domestic sound of a cat at a saucer.

Morwenna sat on the rail, side-saddle, with the Regatta Book across her knees and her handbag at her hip, swinging one foot like a girl on a gate. Along the flank of the Slip below her the gig Provident lay afloat on two ropes, oars shipped, her crew all gone to the tea. As I started down, Jago Rowe went past me, hands hanging, without a word, and stepped into her and sat on the stern thwart like a man told to mind a boat. I did not take that in. I set it down because I had spent the afternoon taking in everything else.

“Mind the weed,” said Morwenna, without turning her head. “Sit down, my handsome, you’ve been on your feet since half past two.”

There was an iron mooring post at the foot of the rail, and I sat on it.

“Is Demelza going to arrest me?”

“When we’ve finished.”

“Good. I should like to finish.” She opened the handbag, took out the tin, and lifted the lid: half a saffron cake, yellow as a duckling, the horn-handled knife laid along the top. “Sit. Eat.”

“No, thank you.”

“Well.” She looked at the cake and shut the lid on it. “That’s the first time since 1962.”

She meant it for a joke, and it was one, and neither of us laughed.

“You’ve told them all of it, Dot, bar what it was for,” she said. “I find I’d like someone to have that right. Then I shall have said it once, and it’s very restful, having said a thing once.”

“Three hundred and eighty pounds a week.” She said it as one gives the quantity of flour. “That’s Gwithian House, with the garden and the nurse who doesn’t raise her voice. The County would have him at Bodmin for nothing, in a day-room with twenty chairs. I went and stood in the door of it. He likes things in their drawers, Ronald. On a Tuesday he doesn’t know me, and I’m the nurse. On a Sunday I’m his wife. I take the bus and take my chance.”

“You could have told me.”

“And you’d have found something out of the rent, and starved the cat. I am the one who brings the cake, Dot. It isn’t a position you can reverse halfway through. I’ve counted the regatta’s money since 1971, and you’ll find every penny of it. It was only my own that ran out.”

“I read to Loveday on Tuesdays and had the run of the shelves, as you saw. Small things first. A snuffbox. Three plates out of a Hakluyt. I called it borrowing, and I think she called it that for me; she’s no fool, Loveday, only gifted at not asking. Then came the second winter of fees, and the Carne at the end of the long shelf in Ned’s cover. Ned had told me what it was worth once, on this harbour wall, over a pasty.”

“I took it home in March under the shortbread, and put the day-book in its cover the Tuesday before Easter. The 1763 estate day-book; nobody had opened it since the old Squire. I sewed it in the honey-house, on the second frame. Ned carried that frame up Church Lane himself in 1958, on a handcart under a blanket, and said Ronald wasn’t to be told what it was for. Ronald never asked.”

“It was the best sewing I have ever seen in a forgery,” I said.

I had not meant to say it. Morwenna looked pleased. God forgive her, she looked pleased, and for a moment so did I, and neither of us referred to it again.

“I met Mr de Vries at the Lemon Street book sale in Truro. I said a lady I knew had some old leaves. He didn’t ask where from. They don’t, my handsome, if the price is right and the lady has a pleasant face. Forty, in three goes. Twenty I kept back, because I was frightened, and the safest place for anything you’re frightened of is the one book in Trevenna nobody would think to open.”

“The treasurer’s.”

“Ned made those boards too thin for what I wanted. So I split them and laid the leaves between with wheat paste and shut them up again. I’ve carried that book about the village for three months like a hen with a china egg.”

I had held it in my two hands in the WI hall, found it heavy for a ledger, and put that down to Ned. Well.

“I want to tell you about Aubrey,” said Morwenna, “because they will say he was in it, and he wasn’t.”

“I know he wasn’t.”

“Jago will have told you about the telephone in the passage. He spoke into it with his back to me, and nobody on the end. ‘Half ten, then.’ He couldn’t say it to a woman’s face. That was Aubrey, he took other people’s shame and wore it like a spare coat. I said, ‘Half ten, Aubrey,’ to his back, and went to my table and wrote 8.40 at the foot of the first round in my best hand.”

“I left at ten to ten, for my mac. Then I stood in the old pilchard cellar doorway at the foot of your lane and watched Imogen Mayne go up and come down again with her face wet, and I thought, well, he’ll be softened. I walked up at half past. The door was on the latch. He was at the bench in his shirtsleeves with the lamp on and the rutter open, writing on the pastedowns in pencil. He did not turn round. He said, ‘Mrs Hext, I am glad you came. I have thought what I should say, and I find it is the plain thing.’”

“He wanted them back, Dot. Every leaf. Then he would tell Loveday the book had been injured by an incompetent binder, and that would be the end of it. He gave me his word, and he was a man who kept it. I said I couldn’t, they were sold, the money was Ronald. And he said, ‘Then you must say so in the morning, to Loveday and to Mrs Pellow, and I shall stand beside you.’”

She was quiet.

“He would have stood beside me. I have been over it a good many times, and I think it is the most dreadful thing anyone has ever offered me.”

“And then?”

“Then he turned back to the bench to write it down. ‘Accuracy,’ he said, ‘is a form of courtesy,’ and he put his pencil to the paper. The hammer was on its nail at my left shoulder; I’d put my hand on it when I came in, as you steady yourself on a gate. I should like to tell you I decided. I can’t. I’d feel better either way.”

“Once,” I said.

“Once. He made no sound at all. I have heard a hive go quiet when somebody sets down a hat too close, and it was very like.”

“You hung it back.”

“My hand did. It hadn’t held that hammer in thirty years and it went to the left-hand nail like a swallow to the same beam. Face out. Ned’s way.” Her mouth moved. “Caught by a nail, after all that.”

“Then I put out the lamp. One does. I stood in the dark with Aubrey at my feet, and heard a step in the lane. You walk like somebody counting stairs, Dot; I’d know it in my sleep. You were humming, flat, the one from the music round that your team got wrong. You came up past the window, and I held my breath, and I thought: if she looks in, I shall tell her everything, and be glad. And you went by. You didn’t look.”

“No,” I said.

It came out quite steady. I had carried that dark window for nine days, and I had expected the saying of it to weigh more.

“I was angry with you for about a minute, which wasn’t reasonable. Then I put the strip on, because I wanted to see what I was doing, and I waited for it, flicker and stammer and light, and that’s the headache. It’s quite true. I only put it at Easter because it seemed the safer end of the year. I do try to tell the truth about small things. It saves effort.”

“The stove,” I said.

“I lit it with your own kindling and burned what he’d written. Mrs P. in the mor. He had put that down for you, so as not to forget. I couldn’t burn the book. It’s the one thing I’m not able to do. I took his key off the bench, your green wool, and locked up behind me.”

“And the cupboard.”

“Ned lent me that key for the Saturdays, in 1955. I expect he wrote fetch back. He never did fetch it back, and I never offered. I took it to my wedding in my coat pocket. In thirty-four years I never turned it once, until the Saturday you said to Kit, with the door wide open, that Ned had kept a notebook. You’ve never learned to lower your voice, Dot. You tell the whole lane everything in a whisper.”

“Where is it?”

“In the honey-house, in the biscuit tin with the Christmas paper. I held it over the stove and I couldn’t. I couldn’t burn his hand either. You may have it back when they’ve done with it.” She looked at me sideways. “It isn’t a bad hand, you know. You only think it is.”

“And Quire.”

“Three months, in eighty-six. Sardines, because a sardine tin wants only a key, and the cat wasn’t hard to please. On the back step at six, before you were up. You’d forgotten to feed anything, my dear, yourself included, and I thought, I can’t mend that, but I can see to the cat. I’m sorry about the cupboard. I couldn’t leave her loose with the window open and the harbour at the bottom of the lane. The milk was only manners.”

“You might have said. In eighty-six.”

“You’d have had to thank me.”

The foot had stopped swinging. She looked down at the water.

“I loved him, Dot. It was no news to Ned. He was kind about it, which is worse than the other. He gave me the frame for a wedding present, like handing a woman a hat when she’s asked for the sea. And you had him, and you didn’t need him. The week he died you forgot to feed a cat, and by the Wednesday you had the shop open. I sat in the honey-house three days with the bees and a pot of tea going cold, and I couldn’t open anything.”

“I was not good at it,” I said. “I was only upright.”

“It looks very much the same from the pews.”

I had no answer, and said so by saying nothing, which is not my habit.

“He told me about the dot, you know.”

“The Pellow dot,” I said.

“In my first week. A pin-prick at the foot of the last gathering of everything he finished, with the point of the awl. So they know somebody was here. He’d not have told you; it was a pupil’s thing. When I had the last gathering of the Carne open on the frame in March, there it was. I could have cut that gathering out and sewn in a leaf of the day-book. I sat with my thumb on it for the best part of an afternoon.” She looked at her thumb. “I left it. I thought somebody who knew would find it. I think I wanted somebody to.”

“I had to sit down,” I said.

“Yes. I thought you would.”

“And Pieter,” I said.

“He put a note in my handbag at the Lantern while the lemonades were being fetched. The quay, five to eleven; he should like to speak of the paper. The Tarts went home at a quarter to, and I went round by Net Loft Row. He had a leaf with him still, in his paperback, too beautiful to sell. He had worked out the lion paper and the honey, and he would write to the police from Rotterdam, as a courtesy, so that I might speak to them first. Another courteous man. I seem to have spent this summer among them.”

“He was standing at the edge with the leaf in his hand, looking at the water. Low water twenty-five past nine, I thought, so a young flood over mud, and nobody about. A foreign gentleman, a drop of drink, a dark quay.” The foot swung once. “I pushed him. I did not wait to see.”

“He might have drowned.”

“That was the idea, my dear.”

She said it in the level voice, the voice of someone reading out her own minutes, and it was the level that I could not bear. I would have borne a shout. I found I had stood up and was shaking all down my front, and I sat down again on the mooring post, for the look of the thing.

“He’s awake,” I said. “He has been since yesterday, and this morning he spoke.”

“I thought so. You told me he was asleep with your whole face. You go pink to the ears, Dot, you always have.” Her shoulders came down about an inch, and I saw it. “I’m glad. I should like that written down somewhere, that I’m glad. It’s the one thing in all this I would have back.”

The weed at the edge of the Slip stood up straight in the water and leaned neither way.

“I’ve always liked the top of the tide,” she said. “Well. That’s the minutes.” She slid down from the rail, small and round, with her sash straight and the Book in the crook of her left arm. “There’s one more item.”

“Morwenna.”

“Ned would be so cross with me. Good calf.”

She threw it left-handed, underarm, the way one tosses a posy at a wedding, out over the rail and high, and the Regatta Book turned once in the low sun with its red label flashing and came down in the green water a yard off the gig’s bow.

It floated. A big book will, for a moment, on the air in its spine. Then the sea began to find the way in, and Jago Rowe came down the length of the Provident in three strides and said, “No. Not that, Morwenna,” in his voice like a slow tide. He leaned out on his enormous arm, the one with the anchor gone to a blur, and took the Regatta Book out of the sea by its spine as a man takes a loaf from a hot oven, and set it streaming on the Slip at my feet.

“Oh, Jago,” said Morwenna, quite gently, as one speaks to a dog that has brought back a stick one had not meant to throw.

There was a noise from the head of the Slip: a constable covering a hundred feet of wet concrete in boots. Garrow had come to the top behind her, with half an egg sandwich still in his hand. He looked at the sandwich, and at the woman by the rail, and said, in a voice I had not heard from him before, “Constable Kitto. If you would.”

Demelza stopped in front of Morwenna with her plait come out from under her helmet, breathing hard. “Morwenna Hext,” she said, “I am arresting you on suspicion of the murder of Aubrey Trevithick, and of the attempted murder of Pieter de Vries. You do not have to say anything unless you wish to do so, but what you say may be given in evidence.”

“Yes, my handsome,” said Morwenna. “I rather thought you might.” She took the cake tin out of her bag and pressed it into my hands. Her fingers were warm and dry and perfectly steady. “Eat, Dot. You’ll want it before the day’s out. It’s a day old, but it’s a day old in the right way.”

Demelza took her elbow, as one steers a person off a kerb, and they went up the Slip together, the small round figure in the sash and the short square one in the helmet, past Garrow, who stood aside and for once in his life said nothing at all.

I knelt on the concrete by the Book. For the first time since the tent nobody was looking at me, and I discovered that I did not mind. The sea had done what a week of suspicion had not: it had got into the glue. Wheat paste will hold for ten years if you keep it dry, but it has never learned to refuse water. That is why we use it. It lets go, for those who know how to ask.

I slid the bone folder from my bag into the seam of the back board, where the water had gone in ahead of me, and eased. The board opened like the lid of a pie. Between the two skins of millboard, flat and brown and cold, lay the leaves.

I lifted them out one at a time on the flat of my left thumb and laid them in a row on the warm concrete, where the sun had come round the lifeboat house and found them. The ink had not run. It does not, on old rag, if you are quick: the iron has had three hundred and fifty years to make up its mind. A pilot’s careful brown hand, a mile at a time, telling a stranger which rocks to keep well open. Twenty of them lay along the Slip in the sun, spread like a hand of cards put down by a player with nothing left to hide, and the tide stood at the top and did not move, in no hurry whatever.

chapters.title: A Second Dot
chapters.html:
It rained the whole of the last Sunday in July, the steady, well-meaning rain that Trevenna keeps for days when it would like to be left alone, and by ten o’clock the Bindery smelled of clove from the shop door to the yard.

I had been up since five with the paste. The seals had come off on the Monday, peeled away with a razor blade by DC Pascoe, who apologised to the door and then to me. Inspector Garrow had telephoned on the Tuesday and called me Mrs Pellow, without the dear, and I had not known where to put the receiver. Morwenna had made a statement of eleven pages, signing every one, and Garrow said it was the first he had ever read that did not want its commas moved. She was to be tried at Truro in the autumn. Kit had come home on the Saturday night in the back of the same white Ford, with his bootlaces in a paper bag, and slept fourteen hours on my settle with Quire sitting on his chest and hissing at him, which is how you know she is fond.

Imogen had buried her father on the Monday, with Mr Nance giving the hymn and half the Lantern in the churchyard wet to the knee, and at the lychgate I put the swan ring into her hand. She tried it on her thumb, where it turned, and said “Accurate,” and nearly smiled. Mr Nance had since had a letter of three lines from her, selling him back the Psalter for the nine hundred pounds Aubrey paid, to be settled when the roof was mended; he showed it to me in the street and apologised for weeping. The Institute met on the Wednesday and voted, with Doris Rosevear abstaining and Gwen Trewhella shouting that she had been in favour for the last ten minutes, to keep Ronald Hext at Gwithian House out of the bunting fund until Christmas. So it turned out that the position could be reversed after all, though it took seven women and an urn.

And I was seen. I do not know how else to put it. A woman I had not spoken to since 1974 crossed the Hard to tell me she had always thought it was Morwenna. People held doors.
